title: `dialect_impala()` quotes identifiers with double quotes, which Impala rejects
description:
On dbplyr 2.6.0, queries against an Impala ODBC connection (Cloudera driver) fail because identifiers are double-quoted. Impala parses double-quoted text as a string literal. This worked on 2.5.2. The proposed fix is in #1871. I'm filing this to document the failure on a live connection, which goes beyond the `tbl()` field-discovery failure #1871 describes.

## The driver and dbplyr disagree on the same connection

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), driver = "Cloudera ODBC Driver for Impala", ...)

DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, "x")
#> <SQL> `x`
dbplyr::escape(dbplyr::ident("x"), con = con)
#> <SQL> "x"
```

## Failure on a real query

```r
tbl(con, in_schema("<schema>", "<table>")) %>%
  slice_max(batch_detail_id, by = load_dt)
#> Error in `collect()`:
#> ! Failed to collect lazy table.
#> Caused by error in `<fn>`:
#> ! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [Cloudera][ImpalaODBC][HY000].
#> ✖  (110) Error while executing a query in Impala: : ParseException: Syntax error in line 198:
#> • FROM "<schema>_...
#> • ^
#> • Encountered: STRING LITERAL
#> • Expected: DEFAULT, UNNEST, IDENTIFIER
```

## Reprex without a database

```r
library(dbplyr)
con <- simulate_impala()
sql_query_fields(con, ident("my_table"))
#> <SQL> SELECT *
#> FROM "my_table" AS "q01"
#> WHERE (0 = 1)
```

## Workaround confirmed on a live connection

Applying backtick quoting (the change in #1871) resolves both the `tbl()` and the `slice_max()` failures:

```r
dialect_impala_bt <- function() {
  new_sql_dialect(
    "impala",
    quote_identifier = function(x) dbplyr:::sql_quote(x, "`"),
    has_window_clause = TRUE
  )
}
con2 <- with_dialect(con, dialect_impala_bt())

escape(ident("x"), con = con2)
#> <SQL> `x`

tbl(con2, in_schema("<schema>", "<table>")) %>%
  slice_max(batch_detail_id, by = load_dt)
#> # Database: Impala 4.0.0.7.3.1.400-100
#> (runs successfully)
```

## Environment

- dbplyr 2.6.0 (fails); 2.5.2 (works)
- odbc 1.7.2
- Cloudera ODBC Driver for Impala 2.6.17.1026
- Impala 4.0.0.7.3.1.400-100

title: `n_distinct` with two arguments produces unexpected results
description:
When using `n_distinct` with two unnamed arguments, `dbplyr` treats the second as `na.rm =` and ignores it, silently producing surprising results (especially if the na.rm warning has already been displayed in the last 8 hours). The issue can be reproduced simply with:
```r
translate_sql(n_distinct(x, y), con = simulate_snowflake())
# <SQL> COUNT(DISTINCT "x") OVER ()
```

A more complete reprex comparing to behaviour on a local dataframe:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
})

df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2), y = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2), z = 1:6)
df_db <- copy_to(memdb(), df)

# A random operation that displays the na.rm warning
sum_x <- df_db |> summarise(sum(x)) |> pull()
#> Warning: Missing values are always removed in SQL aggregation functions.
#> Use `na.rm = TRUE` to silence this warning
#> This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.

# For a local dataframe, these produce different results
df |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, y)) |>
  pull()
#> [1] 4
df |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, na.rm = y)) |>
  pull()
#> [1] 2

# For a database table, they produce the same result
df_db |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, y)) |>
  pull()
#> [1] 2
df_db |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, na.rm = y)) |>
  pull()
#> [1] 2

# Behaviour in other scenarios
df_db |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull()
#> Error in `n_distinct()`:
#> ! unused argument (y)

df_db |> 
  summarise(n_distinct(x, y, z)) |>
  pull()
#> Error in `n_distinct()`:
#> ! unused argument (z)
```

<sup>Created on 2026-10-20 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I suggest that `n_distinct(x, y)`, `n_distinct(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)`, and , `n_distinct(x, y, z)` should all produce an error like "Error in `n_distinct()`: `dbplyr` does not yet support `n_distinct` on multiple columns`.

title: `copy_to.Spark SQL` doesn't properly account for mixed finite/infinite
description:
`copy_to()` signals an error when trying to create a temporary view with mixed finite and infinite types.

Below are some tests with finites, infinites, and NA

``` r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- dbConnect(databricks(), httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_HTTPPATH"))
df <- data.frame(x = c(1:2, NA, Inf, -Inf))
copy_to(con, df[1:3, , drop = FALSE], overwrite = TRUE)
copy_to(con, df[3:5, , drop = FALSE], overwrite = TRUE)
try(copy_to(con, df, overwrite = TRUE))
#> Error in try(copy_to(con, df, overwrite = TRUE)) : 
#>   ! ODBC failed with error 00000 from
#>   [Simba][Hardy][INVALID_INLINE_TABLE.INCOMPATIBLE_TYPES_IN_INLINE_TABLE][INVALID_INLINE_TABLE.INCOMPATIBLE_TYPES_IN_INLINE_TABLE].
#> ✖  (80) Syntax or semantic analysis error thrown in server while executing
#>   query. Error message from server:
#>   org.apache.hive.service.cli.HiveSQLException: Error running query:
#>   org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: Invalid inline table. Found inco
#> • <SQL> 'CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW `df` AS
#> •  SELECT CAST(`x` AS DOUBLE) AS `x`
#> •  FROM (
#> •  SELECT NULL AS `x`
#> •  WHERE (0 = 1)
#> • 
#> •  UNION ALL
#> • 
#> •  VALUES (1.0), (2.0), (NULL), ('Infinity'), ('-Infinity')
#> •  ) AS `values_table`'
#> ℹ From 'nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1805'.
try(copy_to(con, df[-3, , drop = FALSE], overwrite = TRUE))
#> Error in try(copy_to(con, df[-3, , drop = FALSE], overwrite = TRUE)) : 
#>   ! ODBC failed with error 00000 from
#>   [Simba][Hardy][INVALID_INLINE_TABLE.INCOMPATIBLE_TYPES_IN_INLINE_TABLE][INVALID_INLINE_TABLE.INCOMPATIBLE_TYPES_IN_INLINE_TABLE].
#> ✖  (80) Syntax or semantic analysis error thrown in server while executing
#>   query. Error message from server:
#>   org.apache.hive.service.cli.HiveSQLException: Error running query:
#>   org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: Invalid inline table. Found inco
#> • <SQL> 'CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW `df[-3, , drop = FALSE]` AS
#> •  SELECT CAST(`x` AS DOUBLE) AS `x`
#> •  FROM (
#> •  SELECT NULL AS `x`
#> •  WHERE (0 = 1)
#> • 
#> •  UNION ALL
#> • 
#> •  VALUES (1.0), (2.0), ('Infinity'), ('-Infinity')
#> •  ) AS `values_table`'
#> ℹ From 'nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1805'.
```

<sup>Created on 2026-10-20 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I believe the issue comes from trying to properly fit `Infinite`.  Using `(double('Infinity'))` instead of `('Infinity')` seems to work:

``` sql
SELECT CAST(`x` AS DOUBLE) AS `x`
  FROM (
    SELECT NULL AS `x`
    WHERE (0 = 1)

    UNION ALL

    VALUES (1.0), (2.0), (NULL), (double('Infinity')), (double('-Infinity'))
)
```

|x|
|---|
|1|
|2|
|null|
|Infinity|
|-Infinity|

title: Error "In dbplyr you cannot use a variable created in the same `summarise()`"
description:
This error is new in version 2.6.0. This would work fine before:

```r
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)

# For this test, create a SQLite database with the 'cars' table:
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(conn = con, name = "cars", value = cars, overwrite = TRUE)

# Test: use sum() twice in the same `summarize()`:
carsTable <- tbl(con, "cars")
carsTable |>
  summarize(sum = sum(speed),
            sumSqr = sum(speed * speed))
# Error in `summarize()`:
#   ℹ In argument: `sumSqr = sum(speed * speed)`
# Caused by error:
#   ! In dbplyr you cannot use a variable created in the same `summarise()`.
# ✖ `sum` was created earlier in this `summarise()`.
# ℹ You need an extra `mutate()` step to use it.
```

It can of course be trivially fixed by renaming the `sum` variable, or using `base::sum()`, but just to raise awareness of this unexpected side-effect.

title: Make sql_cast generic to allow other translations
description:
PostgreSQL supports `EXPR::TYPE` as an alternative to `CAST(EXPR AS TYPE)`.

If users prefer that translation, it's currently unavailable. Could we make `sql_cast()` a generic to support dispatch on the SQL flavor so that downstreams could get this custom translation if preferred?

Of course `CAST(EXPR AS TYPE)` should always be supported, so this is just a matter of preference in the exact SQL text that gets generated. And operator precedence needs to be considered, e.g. `CAST(1000 * x AS INT64)` needs to be `(1000 * x)::INT64`, so we'd probably wind up translating `(EXPR)::TYPE` for safety, not quite as "nice".

Related to #177.

title: Redshift translations for interval functions fail
description:
## Description

In #1740, interval translations were improved for Postgres by taking advantage of the `MAKE_INTERVAL()` function.

Unfortunately, `MAKE_INTERVAL()` isn't available in Redshift; the unit is mistaken for a column identifier, and an opaque error message is produced.


## Example

```r
# Suppose a table called `lookups.calendar` exists, containing a date-type column called `date`
q <- dplyr::tbl(redshift$connect(), I("lookups.calendar")) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    date = date + lubridate::days(1),
    .keep = "none"
  )


# Redshift inherits the translation from backend-postgres...
dplyr::show_query(q)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "date" + MAKE_INTERVAL(days => 1) AS "date"
#> FROM lookups.calendar


# ... but because MAKE_INTERVAL() doesn't exist, when we try to execute the query, the
# unit is interpreted as an identifier & we get an opaque error
dplyr::collect(q)
#> Error:
#> ! Failed to collect lazy table.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Failed to prepare query : ERROR:  column "days" does not exist in calendar
```

title: SAP HANA backend canot create temporary tables
description:
I am trying to use `copy_to` to copy a table to a SAP HANA instance so that I can join against it. Presumably this should use a local temporary table. I can create a non-temporary table, but attempting to create a temporary table throws an error. The [SAP HANA docs](https://help.sap.com/docs/hana-cloud-data-lake/performance-and-tuning-for-data-lake-relational-engine-basics/temporary-tables) on temporary tables are kind of unclear, but I think the correct query syntax should be something like `DECLARE LOCAL TEMPORARY TABLE`, whereas dbplyr tries to just use `CREATE TABLE` (based on the error message). I'm guessing this mismatch in syntax is the reason for the error, but I'm not certain.

title: BigQuery: single backslash in string literals since dbplyr 2.6.0 (Illegal escape sequence), regression vs 2.5.1
description:
## Brief description of the problem

With the BigQuery backend (via `bigrquery`), a regex string literal containing `\` is emitted with a single backslash in dbplyr 2.6.0, but with a doubled backslash in 2.5.1. BigQuery treats `\` as an escape character in string literals, so the 2.6.0 output is rejected with:

```
Syntax error: Illegal escape sequence: \. [invalidQuery]
```

Expected: the backslash is doubled so the generated SQL is valid (as in 2.5.1).

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(bigrquery)

# Dummy connection
con <- DBI::dbConnect(bigrquery::bigquery(), project = "reprex")

packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '2.6.0'

translate_sql(str_detect(x, "^a\\.b$"), con = con)
#> dbplyr 2.6.0: <SQL> REGEXP_CONTAINS(`x`, '^a\.b$')    # single backslash -> invalid on BigQuery
#> dbplyr 2.5.1: <SQL> REGEXP_CONTAINS(`x`, '^a\\.b$')   # doubled backslash -> valid

lazy_frame(x = "a", con = con) |>
  filter(str_detect(x, "^a\\.b$")) |>
  show_query()
#> 2.6.0:
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (REGEXP_CONTAINS(`x`, '^a\.b$'))
#>
#> 2.5.1:
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df`.*
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (REGEXP_CONTAINS(`x`, '^a\\.b$'))

# Collecting the 2.6.0 query against a real table raises:
#> ! ... Syntax error: Illegal escape sequence: \. [invalidQuery]
```

title: dplyr::filter_out implementation is broken with Teradata (an maybe others ?)
description:
Hello,

Summary : This issues describes a problem with filter_out and Teradata, and also offers a solution : a PR is ready to be submitted anytime you like :) 

- Fork branch : https://github.com/rplsmn/dbplyr/tree/fix/filter_out_teradata
- Contributors : @vincentbiot and @rplsmn

## Description

The `filter_out` translation doesn't work in Teradata, here's a minimal reprex, output, and suggested change: 

## The bug

###  Code

```r
con <- dbConnect(teradata())
tbl(con, I("my_schema.my_table")) |>
    dplyr::filter_out(my_var == "foo")
```

The error 

```
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error in `<fn>`:
! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [RStudio][ODBC Teradata Driver][Teradata
  Database].
✖ (-3707)Syntax error, expected something like ')' between ')' and '='.
• <SQL> 'SELECT TOP 21 "my_table".*
• FROM my_schema.my_table
• WHERE (CASE WHEN (("my_var" = 'foo') = (TRUE)) OR (("my_var" = 'foo') IS NULL AND (TRUE) IS
  NULL) THEN 0 ELSE 1 END = 1)'
ℹ From nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1620.
```

## Inspect the SQL

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

con <- dbplyr::simulate_teradata()

lf <- dbplyr::lazy_frame(a = c(1:3), b = c("a", "b", "c"), c = c("x1", "x2", "x3"))
lf |> 
  dplyr::filter_out(
    b == "a"
  )
```

Result : 

```
<SQL>
SELECT *
FROM "df"
WHERE (CASE WHEN (("b" = 'a') = (TRUE)) OR (("b" = 'a') IS NULL AND (TRUE) IS NULL) THEN 0 ELSE 1 END = 1)
```

In Teradata, booleans as a type don't exist. 
Here, `(("b" = 'a') = (TRUE))` or `AND (TRUE) IS NULL` cannot work. 
So, when one wants to build boolean chains, it often needs to be quite verbose by building chains of `CASE WHEN X THEN 1 ELSE 0 = 1 END`

Suggested change to (similar to other backend-specific changes like sqlite) `is_distinct_from`

```r
sql_translation.sql_dialect_teradata <- function(con) {
  sql_variant(
    sql_translator(
      .parent = base_odbc_scalar,
      is_distinct_from = \(x, y)
        sql_glue(
            "CASE WHEN(
                CASE WHEN ({x}) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END = 1
                OR CASE WHEN ({x}) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END IS NULL
                )
            THEN 0 ELSE 1 END = 1"
        ),
        (...)
    )
)
```

The unit tests for filter_out don't test for some of the backends covered by `{dbplyr}`, including Teradata which explains why this fell through the gaps !
I've added a unit test (expect_translation) for the backend-aware `is_distinct_from` for Teradata, and another one for verb-filter `filter_out`.

Please note that all this was tested in an environnement with access to Teradata, but unable to perform all the tests of this package.

Thank you for your time, ha ve a great day.
Cheers
Raphael

title: Inconsistent translation of filter conditions to SQL in SQL Server/ODBC
description:
I have noticed that dbplyr inconsistently translates filter conditions to sql.

In particular, it does translate `filter(condition)` to `WHERE (cast("condition" AS "BIT") = 1)` if it is a stand-alone query or the LHS of a join, but not if it is the RHS of a join.

I can confirm that this problem does not occur with SQLite. 

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(DBI)

con <- odbc::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(), 
  Driver = "ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server",
#... (server, user, pwd)
  encoding = "UTF-8"
  )

boolean_test <- tibble(a = 1:3, b1 = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE), b2 = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))

DBI::dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "#boolean_test",
  value = boolean_test,
  temporary = TRUE
)

q1 <- tbl(con, sql("select * from #boolean_test")) %>% filter(b1)
show_query(q1)

q2 <- tbl(con, sql("select * from #boolean_test")) %>% filter(b2)
show_query(q2)

j1 <- left_join(q1, q2)
show_query(j1)
```
result:
```
> show_query(j1)
<SQL>
SELECT "LHS".*
FROM (
  SELECT "q01".*
  FROM (select * from #boolean_test) "q01"
  WHERE (cast("b1" AS "BIT") = 1)
) "LHS"
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT "q01".*
  FROM (select * from #boolean_test) "q01"
  WHERE ("b2")
) "RHS"
  ON (
    "LHS"."a" = "RHS"."a" AND
    "LHS"."b1" = "RHS"."b1" AND
    "LHS"."b2" = "RHS"."b2"
  )
```
with the correct translation for b1, and the incorrect translation for b2.

This causes an error if the data is actually queried:

```
> left_join(q1, q2)
Joining with `by = join_by(a, b1, b2)`
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error in `<fn>`:
! ODBC failed with error 42000 from [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server][SQL Server].
✖ An expression of non-boolean type specified in a context where a condition is expected, near ')'.
• Statement(s) could not be prepared.
• <SQL> 'SELECT TOP 21 "q01".*
• FROM (
•  SELECT "LHS".*
•  FROM (
•  SELECT "q01".*
•  FROM (select * from #boolean_test) "q01"
•  WHERE (cast("b1" AS "BIT") = 1)
•  ) "LHS"
•  LEFT JOIN (
•  SELECT "q01".*
•  FROM (select * from #boolean_test) "q01"
•  WHERE ("b2")
•  ) "RHS"
•  ON (
•  "LHS"."a" = "RHS"."a" AND
•  "LHS"."b1" = "RHS"."b1" AND
•  "LHS"."b2" = "RHS"."b2"
•  )
• ) "q01"'
ℹ From nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1787.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

title: `dialect_spark_sql()` quotes identifiers with `"`, but Databricks/Spark SQL expects backticks
description:
Thanks for implementing ADBC support here! I've been testing it with Databricks, and I think `dialect_spark_sql()` is currently using the wrong identifier quoting. `dialect_spark_sql()` is documented as the Databricks Spark SQL backend, but it currently quotes identifiers with double quotes. Databricks/Spark SQL uses backticks for delimited identifiers by default.

Minimal reprex:

```r
library(dbplyr)

packageVersion("dbplyr") # Current git version
#> [1] '2.5.2.9000'

translate_sql(x + 1, con = dialect_spark_sql())
#> <SQL> "x" + 1.0

sql_query_fields(
  dialect_spark_sql(),
  sql("catalog.schema.table")
)
#> <SQL> SELECT *
#> FROM (catalog.schema.table) AS "q01"
#> WHERE (0 = 1)
```

I would expect backticks here:

```sql
`x` + 1.0

SELECT *
FROM (catalog.schema.table) AS `q01`
WHERE (0 = 1)
```

This matters for working with Databricks because dbplyr uses `sql_query_fields()` during `tbl()` column discovery. With an ADBC Databricks connection, this fails before the table can be created:

```r
library(DBI)
library(adbi)
library(adbcdrivermanager)
library(dbplyr)

# Using the latest build from https://github.com/adbc-drivers/databricks
# To build the `.so`, I did:
# cd rust
# cargo build --features ffi

databricks_driver <- adbc_driver(
  "./rust/target/debug/libdatabricks_adbc.so",
  entrypoint = "AdbcDriverInit"
)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  adbi::adbi(databricks_driver),
  uri = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_HOST"),
  "databricks.http_path" = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_SQL_PATH"),
  "databricks.auth.type" = "access_token",
  "databricks.access_token" = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_TOKEN")
)

tbl(con, I("catalog.schema.table"))
#> Error in `dbplyr_query_fields()`:
#> ! Can't query fields.
#> i Using SQL: SELECT * FROM catalog.schema.table AS "q02" WHERE (0 = 1)
#> Caused by error:
#> ! [PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR] Syntax error at or near '"q02"'
```

A workaround I have is:

```r
dialect_databricks <- function() {
  new_sql_dialect(
    "spark_sql",
    quote_identifier = function(x) sql_quote(x, "`"),
    has_window_clause = TRUE
  )
}

con <- with_dialect(con, dialect_databricks())
```

That makes the field-discovery query use backticks and works for me.

---

Docs:
- Databricks identifiers: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-identifiers
- Spark identifiers: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-identifier.html
- Databricks KB for the exact double-quote alias failure: https://kb.databricks.com/using-double-quotes-in-a-query-causes-a-syntax-error

title: `months()` / `days()` generate `MAKE_INTERVAL(months => 1.0)` on PostgreSQL, breaking queries in dev version (pre-2.60)
description:
Hi folks! The new PostgreSQL translation for lubridate interval functions (`months()`, `days()`, etc.) introduced in the development version switches from `CAST('1.0 months' AS INTERVAL)` to `MAKE_INTERVAL(months => 1.0)`. The old approach worked because PostgreSQL's interval string parser accepts '1.0 months' as a valid literal (the float was harmless inside the string). `MAKE_INTERVAL`, however, has strictly typed `int` parameters, so passing 1.0 (R's default double representation of 1) produces invalid SQL and causes an error. See reprex below:

```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)

packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] ‘2.5.2.9000’

con <- simulate_postgres()
tbl <- lazy_frame(x = "2020-01", con = con)

# months(1) — idiomatic R, 1 is a double by default
tbl |> mutate(y = months(1)) |> sql_render()
#> <SQL> SELECT *, MAKE_INTERVAL(months => 1.0) AS "y"
#>       FROM "df"
```

Running this against a real PostgreSQL connection fails:
~~~
Error in `dplyr::collect()`: Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error:
! Failed to prepare query: ERROR: function make_interval(months => numeric) does not exist
HINT: No function matches the given name and argument types.
      You might need to add explicit type casts.
~~~

The previous translation (`dbplyr@2.5.2`) used `CAST('1.0 months' AS INTERVAL)`, which worked because PostgreSQL's interval string parser accepts '1.0 months' as a valid interval string just fine:
~~~
tbl |> mutate(y = months(1)) |> sql_render()
#> <SQL> SELECT `df`.*, CAST('1.0 months' AS INTERVAL) AS `y`
#>       FROM `df`
~~~

**Expected behaviour**
months(1) and days(1) (and others) should produce `MAKE_INTERVAL(months => 1)`, the argument should be coerced to an integer literal when rendering to `MAKE_INTERVAL`, since that is the only valid type for its named parameters. `months(1)` is common practice in R, and the translation layer should not require callers to know about PostgreSQL's `MAKE_INTERVAL` type constraints.

title: `as_ident_or_sql()` rejects glue strings and produces a cryptic internal error due to `call = call` in dev version (pre-2.6.0)
description:
Hi folks! `as_ident_or_sql()` (a [new function](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/main/R/ident.R#L48) in the current dev version added as part of a [refactor](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/commit/c57cb1c6030f452cb4e0df996ee9f3be0a092aba#diff-edc7374cc979134cfa56c21f1e37d6048944b8ee7a90b9090daee4f64d48ad35L49) to `in_catalog()` and `in_schema()`) introduced two unintended behaviors that combined produce a cryptic internal `rlang` error when calling those functions:

(1) it uses `rlang::is_bare_character()` to validate inputs, which rejects character subclasses like `glue` strings even though they are functionally identical to plain strings (may be overly strict? given that `is.character(glue::glue("x"))` is `TRUE`);

(2) it passes `call = call` to `cli::cli_abort()`, but `call` is not defined in scope, so R silently resolves it to the primitive `base::call`, which `rlang` rejects, masking (1) entirely. A fix for this could be to add `call` as a function parameter, with for example `as_ident_or_sql(x, call = rlang::caller_call())`.

See reprex for the error:
```r
# pak::pak("tidyverse/dbplyr") # to install dev version
library(dbplyr)
library(glue)

packageVersion("dbplyr")
# [1] ‘2.5.2.9000’

# glue strings are character subclasses (functionally identical to plain strings),
# but `is_bare_character()` rejects them, hitting the broken error branch
in_catalog(
  catalog = "MY_DB",
  schema = "MY_SCHEMA",
  table = glue("my_table")
)

in_schema(schema = "MY_SCHEMA", table = glue("my_table"))
```
**Error**
~~~
Error in `rlang::abort()`:
! `call` must be a call or environment, not a primitive function.
---
Backtrace:
    ▆
 1. └─dbplyr::in_catalog(catalog = "MY_DB", schema = "MY_SCHEMA", table = glue("my_table"))
 2.   ├─base::structure(...)
 3.   └─dbplyr:::as_ident_or_sql(table)
 4.     └─cli::cli_abort(...)
 5.       └─rlang::abort(call = call)
 6.         └─rlang:::validate_signal_args(...)
 7.           └─rlang::stop_input_type(...)
 8.             └─rlang::abort(message, ..., call = call, arg = arg)
 ~~~

title: Snowflake dialect broken by named `WINDOW` clause syntax in dev version (pre-2.6.0)
description:
Hi folks, we saw the upcoming `dbplyr@2.6.0` release issue (#1833) and wanted to test the dev version against our internal packages before the release, since they don't live on CRAN and wouldn't surface in standard pre-release testing.

We found that the dev version generates SQL using a named `WINDOW` clause (e.g. `OVER "win1" ... WINDOW "win1" AS (...)`) for window functions in grouped `mutate()` calls. **Snowflake does not support named window clause syntax and rejects this SQL with a compilation error**. The reprex below demonstrates the SQL translation  change:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
# pak::pak("tidyverse/dbplyr") # to test with dev version
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)

con <- simulate_snowflake()
df <- tbl_lazy(
  data.frame(group_id = 1L, category = "a", event_date = Sys.Date(), ref_date = Sys.Date()),
  con = con
)

df |>
  group_by(group_id, category) |>
  mutate(
    result = case_when(
      any(event_date > ref_date)  ~ "after",
      any(event_date <= ref_date) ~ "before"
    )
  ) |>
  show_query()
```
dev version output (fails in Snowflake):
~~~
SELECT
  *,
  CASE
WHEN (BOOLOR_AGG("event_date" > "ref_date") OVER "win1") THEN 'after'
WHEN (BOOLOR_AGG("event_date" <= "ref_date") OVER "win1") THEN 'before'
END AS "result"
FROM "df"
WINDOW "win1" AS (PARTITION BY "group_id", "category")
~~~
`dbplyr@2.5.2` output (works in Snowflake):
~~~
SELECT
  `df`.*,
  CASE
WHEN (BOOLOR_AGG(`event_date` > `ref_date`) OVER (PARTITION BY `group_id`, `category`)) THEN 'after'
WHEN (BOOLOR_AGG(`event_date` <= `ref_date`) OVER (PARTITION BY `group_id`, `category`)) THEN 'before'
END AS `result`
FROM `df`
~~~

Running the first SQL against a live Snowflake connection produces the following error:
~~~
! ODBC failed with error 00000 from .
✖ SQL compilation error:
• syntax error line 7 at position 48 unexpected '"win1"'.
• syntax error line 8 at position 49 unexpected '"win1"'.
• syntax error line 719 at position 2 unexpected 'WINDOW'.
• syntax error line 719 at position 59 unexpected ')'.
~~~

The inline `OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` form generated by `dbplyr@2.5.2` works correctly. The named clause form appears to be a side effect of the dialect/window clause refactor in the dev version (may be the `supports_window_clause()` removal [noted in NEWS.md](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/main/NEWS.md#extensions)).

title: `filter_out()` support
description:
`filter_out()` may be kind of tricky for dbplyr to support since SQL itself doesn't have support for something like this, so it would have to be translated into a `WHERE` somehow.

This is tricky due to 3 value logic with `NULL`, meaning you can't just translate `filter_out(df, ...)` into `WHERE NOT (...)`

Inspired by https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27503379/use-a-calculated-column-in-a-where-clause, I wonder if you can use a derived table that computes the expressions "as is" and then have an outer `WHERE` that keeps `FALSE` and `NULL`.

i.e., I think:

```r
df <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, NA), y = c(1, NA, 3))

filter_out(df, x == 1, y == 3)
```

translates to

```sql
SELECT derived.x, derived.y
FROM (
  SELECT df.x, df.y, (df.x = 1) & (df.y = 3) AS dbplyr_filter_out_condition 
  FROM df
) AS derived
WHERE derived.dbplyr_filter_out_condition = FALSE OR derived.dbplyr_filter_out_condition IS NULL;
```

I think it would be infinitely harder to try and rewrite the `...` of the `filter_out()` as equivalent `filter()` conditions, i.e. `filter(df, x != 1 | is.na(x), y != 3 | is.na(y))`. I think that requires a lot of case by case context on exactly how to flip the condition.

Another option without the derived table is

```sql
SELECT *
FROM df
WHERE ((x = 1) & (y = 3)) = FALSE OR ((x = 1) & (y = 3)) IS NULL;
```

which seems simpler on the surface, but I worry about the fact that the condition is duplicated, especially if it is non-deterministic for some reason.

title: Implement an ADBC backend
description:
There are two ways of installing adbc drivers:

* Wrapped in R packages, e.g. `pak::pak("adbcsqlite")`
* Using `dbc`, e.g. `dbc install sqlite`

Then you can generate an DBI compatible connection with adbi:

```R
con1 <- DBI::dbConnect(adbi::adbi("adbcsqlite"), uri = ":memory:")
con2 <- DBI::dbConnect(adbi::adbi(adbcdrivermanager::adbc_driver("sqlite")), uri = ":memory:")
```

It'll be easiest to test with `adbcsqlite` since that keeps everything in R package space, even though we probably expect most people will use dbc in practice.

@ianmcook supplied this translation of driver names to SQL dialects that would be a good place:

```
bigquery: bigquery
duckdb: duckdb
dremio: flightsql
gizmosql: flightsql
starrocks: flightsql
mssql: mssql
mariadb: mysql
mysql: mysql
tidb: mysql
vitess: mysql
cedardb: postgresql
citus: postgresql
cockroachdb: postgresql
cratedb: postgresql
neon: postgresql
paradedb: postgresql
postgresql: postgresql
timescaledb: postgresql
yellowbrick: postgresql
yugabytedb: postgresql
redshift: redshift
snowflake: snowflake
sqlite: sqlite
trino: trino
```

We're currently missing some way to reliably extract the driver name from the connection. @eitsupi suggested `con@database$driver$name`, but that [doesn't work for me](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1581#issuecomment-3778201396).

title: Interesting behavior with list lookup with `$` following a `rename()`
description:
In the first example, the lookup seems to access `Quux` instead of `quux` . Why?

I tend to use and also recommend `!!` to be explicit about which values are "pasted" into the expression "at call time" (via `enquo()`) . I have heard different opinions about this, interested in the current recommendations.

Originally filed as https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-r/issues/1730.

``` r
options(conflicts.policy = list(warn.conflicts = FALSE))
library(dplyr)

tbl <- tibble::tibble(Quux = LETTERS[1:3])
duck_tbl <-
  dbplyr::copy_inline(DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite()), tbl) |>
  compute()
duck_tbl
#> # Source:   table<`dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`> [?? x 1]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.51.2 []
#>   Quux 
#>   <chr>
#> 1 A    
#> 2 B    
#> 3 C

ltr <- list(quux = "A", Quux = "B")

# Unexpected:
duck_tbl |>
  rename(quux = Quux) |>
  filter(quux == ltr$quux) |>
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `Quux` AS `quux`
#> FROM `dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`
#> WHERE (`Quux` = 'B')

# Workaround:
duck_tbl |>
  filter(Quux == !!ltr$quux) |>
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`.*
#> FROM `dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`
#> WHERE (`Quux` = 'A')

# Correct:
duck_tbl |>
  filter(Quux == ltr$quux) |>
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`.*
#> FROM `dbplyr_96gH0U8VF5`
#> WHERE (`Quux` = 'A')
```

title: Implement `%notin%`
pivot_wider doesn't accept "native" lambdas like values_fun = \(x) max(x, na.rm=TRUE)
description:
It looks like we're required, if supplying a lambda, to use {purrr} style, but I don't see that documented:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/d5184b3e2d5b9fb82f3e509b5996cbd5f58b5562/R/verb-pivot-wider.R#L496-L510

As {tidyr} local backends don't have a problem with the native lambda, I think this is a bug, but maybe there's a reason why this should just be documented as WAI instead.

----

Reprex:

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tidyr)
library(dbplyr)

# Create a small in-memory SQLite table with duplicate keys
# so that pivot_wider requires a values_fn to aggregate
df <- memdb_frame(
  id = c(1, 1, 2),
  name = c("a", "a", "b"),
  value = c(10, 20, 30)
)
df |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = name, 
    values_from = value, 
    values_fn = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# Error in `pivot_wider()`:
# ! Can't pivot column value:
# Caused by error:
# ! Can't convert `values_fn$value`, `<fn>`, to a function.
# Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.

# no problem for local equivalent
df |> 
  collect() |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = name, 
    values_from = value, 
    values_fn = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#      id     a     b
#   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
# 1     1    20    NA
# 2     2    NA    30
```

title: Feature request: first-class `guard` argument to `tbl()` that propagates through verbs and joins
description:
Written by Claude, reviewed and tweaked by hand.

Follow-up to tidyverse/duckplyr#919.

### Problem

Packages that wrap `dplyr::tbl()` sometimes need to attach an object whose lifetime must extend at least as long as any tbl derived from the original. In duckplyr's case, `as_tbl()` registers a temporary DuckDB view and attaches a finalizer ("scope guard") that drops the view once no derivative tbl references it anymore — so the view sticks around through arbitrarily long verb chains and disappears promptly after the last `collect()`. Other use cases are conceivable.

There's currently no supported way to do this. Two approaches have been tried, both fragile:

1. **Attach to the tbl itself** — `attr(out, "duckplyr_scope_guard") <- guard`. Works for verbs that mutate in place (attributes survive by R copy semantics), but silently breaks in joins (the RHS tbl is consumed and its attributes dropped) and anywhere a verb rebuilds via `dplyr::make_tbl()`. This is what caused the osdc revdep failure in the dbplyr 2.6.0 cycle.

2. **Attach to `out$lazy_query`** — the fix shipped in tidyverse/duckplyr#919. The lazy_query tree is the durable spine of a dbplyr tbl (every verb wraps the prior query as `$x`, joins keep both sides as `x_lq` / `y_lq`), so a root-node attribute stays GC-reachable across all derivative tbls including joins. Empirically robust against current dbplyr `main`, but it reaches into dbplyr internals and could break the next time the lazy_query layout changes.

### Proposed API

A first-class, optional `guard` argument to `dplyr::tbl()` (or a dbplyr-specific entry point) that dbplyr propagates as an internal contract:

```r
out <- dplyr::tbl(con, name, guard = scope_guard)
```

Propagation semantics:

- Single-input verbs (`mutate`, `filter`, `select`, `arrange`, `summarise`, `head`, `group_by`, …) carry the guard forward unchanged.
- Joins and other multi-input verbs union the guards from both sides, e.g. `joined$guard <- c(lhs$guard, rhs$guard)`. A list/vector of guards is fine; what matters is that every guard from any input tbl remains reachable from the result.
- `collect()` / `compute()` / `copy_to()` need not do anything special — they just need to keep the guard reachable until the result is materialised, which falls out naturally if it's stored on the tbl/lazy_query.
- Guards should be opaque to dbplyr — any R object, used only for its GC-reachability. dbplyr shouldn't call or inspect them.

### Why this belongs in dbplyr

The propagation rules (especially the join case) are dbplyr-internal: external packages can't implement them without depending on lazy_query internals, which is what we're trying to avoid. A documented `guard` slot on the tbl, with a guarantee that dbplyr preserves reachability across its verbs, is the smallest contract that lets downstream packages (duckplyr today, plausibly others) tie resource lifetimes to dbplyr objects safely.

### Users other than duckplyr

**Other temp-object backends.** Same shape as duckplyr, different engine:
- `arrow::to_duckdb()` and `duckdb::duckdb_register()` register an Arrow/data.frame as a DuckDB view; the view needs unregistering when the tbl is gone.
- Snowflake/BigQuery/Athena/Databricks backends that create a session-scoped resource per tbl — temporary stage, result-cache handle, session-scoped UDF, named query result.
- Spark's `createOrReplaceTempView()` (sparklyr) — currently cleaned up only on session end.

**dbplyr's own `copy_to(temporary = TRUE)` and `compute()`.** Today cleanup is implicit (dies with the connection). A guard slot would let these drop the temp object the moment no tbl references it — meaningful in Shiny / Plumber / long-running R sessions where temp objects pile up.

**File-backed sources owned by the package.** A wrapper that downloads/decompresses/materializes a remote file into a local Parquet/CSV/DuckDB file and points a tbl at it. The file should be deleted when the last derivative tbl is collected. Applies to arrow `open_dataset()` against a temp directory, duckdb `read_parquet()` against a downloaded file, etc.

**Snapshot / transaction pinning.** Iceberg / Delta / database MVCC: pin a snapshot ID or hold a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction open so a multi-step pipeline sees a consistent view. Release the pin when all derivative tbls go away. Same shape — opaque handle whose lifetime tracks the tbl.

**Federated queries.** (An extension of the `copy_to()` case?) A wrapper that joins two backends by materializing one side as a temp object in the other engine ends up with *two* guards (one per materialization) — exactly the join case the proposal already handles via `c(lhs$guard, rhs$guard)`.

title: `dbplyr::pull()` behavior with quosures
description:
In [a recent `srvyr` issue](https://github.com/gergness/srvyr/issues/204), I'm having trouble with some code that uses `pull()` with quosures. I think the underlying problem is this difference in behavior when a dataset is local vs a `dbplyr` one:

``` r
library(RSQLite)

local_df <- data.frame(x = 1:4)

xquo <- rlang::quo(x)

local_df |> pull(!!xquo, !!nmquo)
```

title: [Feature] Add an optional argument to unlock GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (ROLLUP/CUBE)
description:
Greetings, 

When working with Teradata or DuckDB, a commonly used feature by data scientists here is to use `GROUP BY ROLLUP` (or `CUBE`) to get sets of grouped results for an aggregate.

Adding this option to dbplyr would unlock a cool feature, without necessarily changing `dplyr` (here's a 2014 issue with @hadley opposing the implementation in 2017 : https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/236) 

For the actual implementation, this is not a standard sql_translation job, but rather a change to [group_by.tbl_lazy](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/d5184b3e2d5b9fb82f3e509b5996cbd5f58b5562/R/verb-group_by.R#L26) and to [sql_clause_group_by](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/d5184b3e2d5b9fb82f3e509b5996cbd5f58b5562/R/sql-clause.R#L63)

We'd need to simply paste "ROLLUP" or "CUBE" in front of the "GROUP BY" in the later one, depending on an arg.
For example, it could be a  `.sets` argument accepting `c(NULL, 'rollup', 'cube')` to `group_by.tbl_lazy` ?

I am willing to work on a PR to demo an implementation :-) 

NB : I also found it in the following dbplyr-covered backends, but I do not use them : SAP HANA, Apache Hive, MySQL (ROLLUP only), PostgresSQL, Snowflake, Spark

## References

- Teradata : https://docs.teradata.com/r/Enterprise_IntelliFlex_VMware/SQL-Data-Manipulation-Language/SELECT-Statements/GROUP-BY-Clause/GROUPING-SETS-Option
- DuckDB : https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/query_syntax/grouping_sets

- Hive : https://hive.apache.org/docs/latest/language/enhanced-aggregation-cube-grouping-and-rollup/#cubes-and-rollups
- MySQL : https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.7/en/group-by-modifiers.html

Thank you for your time.
Cheers
Raphael

title: Support Azure Synapse SQL
description:
Synapse (Azure Synapse Analytics) is a SQL dialect very similar to SQL Server and in many environments uses the same driver. Most translations in backend-mssql.R work for both, but Synapse does not support DATEDIFF_BIG. The current mssql backend emits DATEDIFF_BIG here:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/ce9c71188cb9b5d676bc7c99f83f001edef9221e/R/backend-mssql.R#L498C17-L498C29

**Problem**
- SQL Server has DATEDIFF_BIG and DATEDIFF. DATEDIFF_BIG is safer for very large differences (returns bigint), while DATEDIFF returns int.
- Synapse does not provide DATEDIFF_BIG (only DATEDIFF), so generated SQL containing DATEDIFF_BIG fails on Synapse.

**Desired behavior**
-Keep DATEDIFF_BIG for SQL Server where it is supported.
-Translate to DATEDIFF when the target is Synapse.

@hadley what approach do you think it would work best? Should a new backend be defined for synapse or we can apply some logic to the already existing Sql Server one? 95% of the SQL will be the same so I don't know how useful will be to create a whole new backend file.

Happy to try to open a PR if you point me to the appropiate approach.

For reference, a previous PR changed IFF to CASE to support both SQL Server and Synapse: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/1773

FYI @edward-burn

title: Support slice_head() and slice_tail() on database backends
description:
# Issue Draft: Support `slice_head()` and `slice_tail()` on database backends

## Problem

`slice_head()` and `slice_tail()` throw errors on database backends, even though `head()` works fine using `LIMIT`. This creates an inconsistent user experience.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(con, mtcars)

# This works
tbl(con, "mtcars") %>%
  head(5) %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars`
#> LIMIT 5

# But this throws an error
tbl(con, "mtcars") %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)
#> Error in `slice_head()`:
#> ! `slice_head()` is not supported on database backends.
#> ℹ Please use `slice_min()` instead.
```

## Why this is inconsistent

Both `head()` and `slice_head()` face the same "undefined row order" issue that the documentation warns about:

> "databases don't really have a sense of row order, so what 'first' means is subject to interpretation"
> — `verb-head.R`, lines 9-10

Yet `head()` is supported while `slice_head()` is not. Users who have already called `arrange()` would reasonably expect `slice_head()` to work.

## Proposed solution

### Case 1: Without `by` parameter

Simply delegate to `head()`:

```r
slice_head.tbl_lazy <- function(.data, ..., n, prop, by = NULL) {

  if (!missing(prop)) {
    cli_abort("{.arg prop} is not supported on database backends")
  }

  by_quo <- enquo(by)
  if (quo_is_null(by_quo)) {
    # No grouping: delegate to head()
    return(head(.data, n = n %||% 1L))
  }

 # With `by`: use slice_by() - see Case 2
  # ...
}
```

### Case 2: With `by` parameter

Use the existing `slice_by()` infrastructure (which already powers `slice_min()`, `slice_max()`, `slice_sample()`):

```r
# With `by`: use row_number() window function
size <- list(type = "n", n = n %||% 1L)
slice_by(.data, order_by = list(), size, {{ by }}, with_ties = FALSE)
```

This would translate to:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col) AS q01
  FROM table
)
WHERE q01 <= 5
```

### For `slice_tail()`

Similar approach, but with descending order or using a subquery pattern.

## Related

- Issue #394 listed `slice_head()` and `slice_tail()` as targets but only `slice_min()`, `slice_max()`, and `slice_sample()` were implemented.
- The `slice_by()` helper function already exists and handles the `by` parameter logic.

## Questions for maintainers

1. Is there a technical reason why `slice_head()`/`slice_tail()` were left unimplemented in #394?
2. Would a PR implementing this approach be welcome?
3. For `slice_tail()`, is there a preferred SQL pattern? (e.g., reverse order + LIMIT, or window function with DESC)

title: expand() using LEFT JOIN without 'ON' is not allowed in GoogleSQL
description:
This is #836 redux, I think.

GoogleSQL requires an `ON` clause, so the current translation of `expand()` doesn't work. Here's the BigQuery definition:

https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#join_conditions

> You must use a join condition when you perform a conditional join operation.

(my understanding is "conditional join" includes `LEFT JOIN`)

Thus this translation fails:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/d5184b3e2d5b9fb82f3e509b5996cbd5f58b5562/R/verb-expand.R#L69-L73

This _could_ be a problem for the downstream to update their `expand()` S3 method, though currently it's a bit awkward since we'd probably want to first copy-paste the other part of the implementation:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/d5184b3e2d5b9fb82f3e509b5996cbd5f58b5562/R/verb-expand.R#L29-L64

So I think the way forward is to either:

 1. Use a new generic specifically for that end part of the `expand()` implemenation to allow downstream to define a narrower generic
 2. Use `ON 1=1` to satisfy the `ON` requirement (I checked this does WAI)

NB: I see the comment there about SQLite, but I'll also note that simply replacing `LEFT JOIN` with `CROSS JOIN` _does_ work for GoogleSQL.

I can't come up with a  verified {bigrquery} reprex since I don't have a project to run against, but something like this should do it:

```r
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(bigrquery::bigquery(), ...)

conn %>%
  tbl(sql("
  SELECT 1 AS a, 'a' AS b
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 2 AS a, 'b' AS b
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1 AS a, 'b' AS b
  ")) %>%
  tidyr::expand(a, b)
```

title: Adding filter creates a qualified select * which causes error
description:
We use a DB2 flavored SQL database. Ever since {dbplyr} was updated past version 2.3.4, an error occurs in certain combinations of commands.

It appears this is due to a `SELECT` statement having a qualified name combined with `*`. This appears to occur under certain circumstances, such as when `filter()` is used. If the quotes are removed or the entire qualifier with up to the catalog is provided, it works. However, I do not know how this can be enforced. Specifying specific columns also works as `*` is no longer used. 

I believe this is related in some capacity to this prior issue: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1480 

Perhaps there is a simple solution Ive missed to adjust quoting in column selection with `*`?

## Example 

Due to the nature of the system being DB2, it is hard to create a reprex. However, I have provided some pseudocode and example outputs to help elucidate the issue.

Setup Connection 
```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
               "DB2", # DSN for our DB2
                uid = Sys.getenv("myuid"),     
                pwd = Sys.getenv("mypwd"), timeout = 10)
```

**Works** - the select * does not have a quoted qualifier
```r

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT MYCATALOG.MYSCHEMA.MYTABLE.*
FROM MYCATALOG.MYSCHEMA.MYTABLE.
WHERE MYCOLUMN != 'SOMEVALUE'"

```

**Fails** - due to a qualified select *
```r
mytbl <-tbl(con, in_catalog(sql("MYCATALOG"), sql("MYSCHEMA"), sql("MYTABLE")))
 mytb  %>%
  filter(MYCOLUMN != "SOMEVALUE") %>%
  show_query() # collect()
```

```
! ODBC failed with error 00000 from [IBM][CLI Driver][DB2/AIX64].
✖  SQL0204N "MYTABLE" is an undefined name.  SQLSTATE=42704

<SQL> 'SELECT "MYTABLE".*
FROM MYCATALOG.MYSCHEMA.MYTABLE
WHERE ("MYCOLUMN " != 'SOMEVALUE')'
```

description:
When running `coalsc` on a database table, spurious quotation marks are added to the output and collected results. They are not actually "there" in the database. 

``` r
library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag

library(dbplyr)
#>

#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql

# Repro uses an in-memory DuckDB database
con <- dbConnect(duckdb(), dbdir = ":memory:")  # in-memory DB [1](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/list)

df1 <- tibble::tibble(
  A = c("c","a"),
  B = c("c","a"),
  C = c("c", NA_character_)
)

dbWriteTable(con, "tbl1", df1, overwrite = TRUE)

tb1 <- tbl(con, "tbl1")
x <- c("A", "B", "C")

# Baseline: remote print of original table (no quotes)
tb1
#> # Source:   table<tbl1> [?? x 3]
#> # Database: DuckDB v1.3.0 [unknown@Linux 5.10.247-246.989.amzn2.x86_64:R 4.4.1/:memory:]
#>   A     B     C    
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1 c     c     c    
#> 2 a     a     <NA>

#> # Source:   SQL [?? x 3]

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
```

title: duckdb: as.double / as.numeric treated as "AS NUMERIC"
description:
~~``as.integer()``~~ ``as.numeric()`` is converted to ``AS NUMERIC``. In duckdb, this is an [alias to DECIMAL(18, 3)](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/data_types/overview#general-purpose-data-types).

Similar to other databases (https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/379, https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/408), ``AS DOUBLE`` is what we need.

```r

> packageVersion("duckdb")
[1] ‘1.4.0’
> packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] ‘1.1.4’
> packageVersion("dbplyr")
[1] ‘2.5.1’
>
> con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), ":memory:")
>
> # Write a double to a table first
> DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "table", data.frame(a = c(0.0091792656587473)))
>
> # Casting the value gives surprising results
> dplyr::tbl(con, "table") |> dplyr::mutate(b = a * 1e6, c = as.double(a) * 1e6)
# Source:   SQL [?? x 3]
# Database: DuckDB 1.4.0 [lentinj@Linux 6.17.13+deb14-amd64:R 4.5.2/:memory:]
        a     b     c
    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 0.00918 9179.  9000
> dplyr::tbl(con, "table") |> dplyr::mutate(b = a * 1e6, c = as.double(a) * 1e6) |> dplyr::show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT "table".*, a * 1000000.0 AS b, CAST(a AS NUMERIC) * 1000000.0 AS c
FROM "table"
```

``copy_inline()`` implicitly casts to numeric, so the end result is particularly surprising there, but basically the same bug:

```r
> dbplyr::copy_inline(con, data.frame(a = c(0.0091792656587473))) |> dplyr::show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT CAST(a AS NUMERIC) AS a
FROM (
  SELECT NULL AS a
  WHERE (0 = 1)

  UNION ALL

  VALUES (0.0091792656587473)
) values_table
> dbplyr::copy_inline(con, data.frame(a = c(0.0091792656587473))) |> dplyr::mutate(b = a * 1e6)
# Source:   SQL [?? x 2]
# Database: DuckDB 1.4.0 [lentinj@Linux 6.17.13+deb14-amd64:R 4.5.2/:memory:]
      a     b
  <dbl> <dbl>
1 0.009  9000
```

title: `sql` in `in_catalog` breaks with `filter`
description:
I am having trouble generating reproducible example because I don't know how to mock catalogs and table valued functions but effectively issue is:

```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)

tbl(con, in_catalog("Datawarehouse", "DBO", sql("MyTableValuedFunction(Param1, Param2)"))) %>%
  show_query
```

title: Support for union() --> UNION DISTINCT
description:
BigQuery doesn't support unqualified `UNION` clauses:

https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#union

Everything must be `UNION ALL` or `UNION DISTINCT` (the latter being what's usually intended by `UNION` without `ALL`, but clearer to the reader).

Currently, it's not easy to make this tweak in a flavor:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/572693098d0098018b6bb2d1e88b650d2e1e1580/R/db-sql.R#L671-L684

I could write my own `sql_query_union()` method, but that would require copy-pasting most of the logic in the default DBIConnection method.

Is the right approach to expose another method, akin to `sql_join_suffix()`, that returns the valid `UNION` operators?

```r
sql_union_operators.DBIConnection <- function(con) c("UNION", "UNION ALL")

sql_union_operators.BigQueryConnection <- function(con) c("UNION DISTINCT", "UNION ALL")
```

title: allow users to set `copy_to(in_transaction = FALSE, ...)` so that `rows_*()` methods can be used with begin/commit/rollback SQL transactions
description:
SQL transactions is a power feature in ensuring that your database works as intented. Since the `DBI` package doesn't support nested transactions and there has been no active discussion on this topic on the package forums, `dbplyr` should allow users to opt out of using transactions with `db_copy_to()` and `copy_to()` methods. This way users could write their own logic around insert/updating/deleting data via the very handy `rows_*()` methods.

The work required for this feature is minimal, since `copy_to()` and `db_copy_to()` already have this argument. The problem is that there is no way to set this argument when using `rows_*()` methods. Too possible approaches come to mind.

1. Create a new dbplyr option: `dbplyr_in_transaction` which defaults to `TRUE` and use this as the default argument in `db_copy_to()` and `copy_to()` methods (tested this approached in my fork `samssann/dbplyr@f-in-transaction-option`)
2. Add `in_transaction` argument to `rows_*()` methods and let it pass through to the copy methods

An example using option 1

``` r
# pak::pkg_install("samssann/dbplyr@f-in-transaction-option")
# pak::pkg_install("RSQLite")

library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tibble)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE Ponies1 (
   id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
   name TEXT,
   cutie_mark TEXT
)")
#> [1] 0
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE Ponies2 (
   id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
   name TEXT,
   cutie_mark TEXT
)")
#> [1] 0

ponies1 <- tbl(con, "Ponies1")
ponies2 <- tbl(con, "Ponies2")

# does not work since dbplyr_in_transaction = TRUE
rlang::with_options(
  dbplyr_in_transaction = TRUE,
  dbplyr:::with_transaction(
    con = con,
    in_transaction = TRUE,
    code = {
      rows_append(ponies1, tibble(name = "a1", cutie_mark = "b1"), in_place = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
      rows_append(ponies2, tibble(name = "a2", cutie_mark = "b1"), in_place = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
    }
  )
)
#> Error: cannot start a transaction within a transaction
ponies1
#> # Source:   table<Ponies1> [0 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#> # ℹ 3 variables: id <int>, name <chr>, cutie_mark <chr>
ponies2
#> # Source:   table<Ponies2> [0 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#> # ℹ 3 variables: id <int>, name <chr>, cutie_mark <chr>

# works since dbplyr_in_transaction = FALSE
rlang::with_options(
  dbplyr_in_transaction = FALSE,
  .expr = dbplyr:::with_transaction(
    con = con,
    in_transaction = TRUE,
    code = {
      rows_append(ponies1, tibble(name = "a1", cutie_mark = "b1"), in_place = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
      rows_append(ponies2, tibble(name = "a2", cutie_mark = "b1"), in_place = TRUE, copy = TRUE)
    }
  )
)
ponies1
#> # Source:   table<Ponies1> [1 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#>      id name  cutie_mark
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>     
#> 1     1 a1    b1
```

title: Translate 'as(x, "TYPE")' --> 'CAST(x AS TYPE)'?
description:
We generally support specific vector casts like `as.character()`:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/e6e5dc6ecd03124e2771bd22d56bd1fa5b519dd9/R/backend-mysql.R#L88-L92

This is most natural for R vector types; allowing generic `as(x, "TYPE")` to drop directly into a `CAST()` call would naturally extend to _all_ object types that a given SQL flavor supports, _especially_ if it's something backend-specific that might look unnatural as an `as.*` R call.

title: Inline `*_join()` + `mutate()`, `filter()` and `distinct()`
description:
`*_join()` always produces a subquery if followed by other verbs:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2)
lf3 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, c = 3)

lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, z = 3)
left_join(lf, lf2, by = "x") %>% 
  mutate(y = y + 1, z = z + 1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`, `z` + 1.0 AS `z`
#> FROM (SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `z`
#> FROM `df` AS `LHS`
#> LEFT JOIN `df` AS `RHS`
#> ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
#> ) `q01`

# could be
# SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`, `z` + 1.0 AS `z`
# FROM `df` AS `LHS`
# LEFT JOIN `df` AS `RHS`
# ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

Depending on the verb this should be quite easy or not. E.g. in `sql_build()` we have to translate the symbol `x` to ``LHS`.`x`` and this has to be done everywhere. For example in `sql_build.op_filter()` we need to pass this alias to `translate_sql_()`

```r
where_sql <- translate_sql_(op$dots, con, context = list(clause = "WHERE"))
```

title: Summarise query generation
description: i.e. how does `filter()` eventually flow through to the corresponding query generation.

title: Inline filter after a join
description:
This:

```R
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, z = 3)
lf |> filter(x == 1) |> left_join(lf2, by = "x")
```

currently generates

```sql
SELECT "LHS".*, "z"
FROM (
  SELECT "df".*
  FROM "df"
  WHERE ("x" = 1.0)
) AS "LHS"
LEFT JOIN "df2"
  ON ("LHS"."x" = "df2"."x")
```

but since `WHERE` is computed after the join, and we know how to rename the symbols, it could be:

```sql
SELECT "df".*, "z"
FROM "df"
LEFT JOIN "df2"
  ON ("df"."x" = "df2"."x")
WHERE ("df"."x" = 1.0)
```

title: Feature request: implement `bind_rows()`
description:
`bind_rows()` in dplyr allows efficiently combining a list of data frames into a single data frame by wrapping `vec_rbind`. This does not work for dbplyr `tbl` objects.

This is a common pattern so it would be good to implement it without needing to collect the data locally. The SQL equivalent is `UNION`, so a way to implement it would be to reduce the list using the existing `union` or `union_all` (I think dbplyr's implementation would match union_all) translation, e.g.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.2.3
library(purrr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

# Create random slices of mtcars
tables <-
  1:5 |>
  map(function(n) {
    tbl_name <- paste0("mtcars_", n)
    copy_to(con, slice_sample(mtcars, n = 3), tbl_name)

    tbl(con, tbl_name)
  })

reduce(tables, union) |>
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars_1`
#> UNION
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars_2`
#> UNION
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars_3`
#> UNION
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars_4`
#> UNION
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `mtcars_5`
```

<sup>Created on 2023-08-02 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


This would be a straightforward way to implement it, and it produces a good translation that is similar to what someone would manually write. I think some checks would need to be done when using `select *` to ensure that column order matches, as some SQL engines check only that column types align, not column names.

It would be good also to support the `.id` argument to append a column with the list name for each item. This could be achieved by running `mutate` on each item prior to the reduce operation.

title: slice_min() differs from dplyr behavior in the presence of NULLs

title: Options to control how table names are qualified in SELECT clause
description:
I am in the early stages of experimenting with dbplyr as a front end to an Apache DataFusion backend (with some adbi/adbc serving as the driver). Early appearances are that when querying from a table in a non-public schema `dbplyr` generates SQL like

```{sql}
SELECT my_table.* FROM my_schema.my_table ...
```

The generated table/schema are actually quoted, but that doesn't make a difference to the backend one way or the other. What does matter is that the table name resolution rules fail for this backend in this case; both `SELECT *` and `SELECT my_schema.my_table.*` would work, as would versions with quotes.

I found a few superficially similar, but narrower in scope, issues, several of which were all marked as resolved by #1656; the most similar is probably #1577 but unlike in that case the quotes seem to be irrelevant. And indeed, I have installed this branch and it resolves some straightforward cases for me (though requiring a patch to `adbi` that specifies using dbplyr's 2nd edition interface). From the PR title and description, I'm hopeful this could fully solve the issue (single-table queries no longer using qualifiers at all and multi-table ones using aliases anyways).

There is a mention in the PR that

> ... I'll make it optional and only enable for Oracle and teradata.

When there is a design for this, will that option be publicly accessible (e.g. through a `sql_options` argument, or a generic that the DBI connection can set)?

title: dplyr grouped distinct does not split-apply-combine calculations, but dbplyr does
description:
Hello--it appears that dplyr's grouped distinct applies calculations to the whole frame, while dbplyr uses a partition to apply calculations within groups.

reprex using dplyr v1.0.10:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(g = c("a", "a", "b"), x = c(1, 2, 3))
df %>% group_by(g) %>% distinct(avg = mean(x))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Groups:   g [2]
#>   g       avg
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 a         2
#> 2 b         2

memdb_frame(df) %>% group_by(g) %>% distinct(avg = mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)) %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `g`, AVG(`x`) OVER (PARTITION BY `g`) AS `avg`
#> FROM `dbplyr_001`
```

title: Inline `*_join()` + `distinct()`
description:
```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1, .name = "lf2")

left_join(
  lf,
  lf2,
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  distinct(y.x) %>% 
  show_query(cte = TRUE)
```

produces

```sql
WITH `q01` AS (
  SELECT `df`.`x` AS `x`, `df`.`y` AS `y.x`, `lf2`.`y` AS `y.y`
  FROM `df`
  LEFT JOIN `lf2`
    ON (`df`.`x` = `lf2`.`x`)
)
SELECT DISTINCT `y.x`
FROM `q01`
```

Instead it could be

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT `df`.`y` AS `y.x`
FROM `df`
LEFT JOIN `lf2`
  ON (`df`.`x` = `lf2`.`x`)
```

title: Add `.order` and `.frame` arguments to `mutate()`.
description:
Back in 2017, @Hadley suggested "there are two possible APIs" for implementing what became `window_frame()` and `window_order()` (see tidyverse/dplyr#2874; @edgararuiz-zz).

At the time, I believe there was no `.by` argument to `mutate()`, so the `window_frame()`/`window_order()` approach seemed to make most sense. At that time one choice was: 

```r
df %>%
  group_by(gvkey) %>%
  window(
    .order = vars(datadate),
    .frame = (-3, 0),
    
    sale_ttm = sum(sale),
    cogs_ttm = sum(cogs),
    sga_ttm = sum(sga)
  )
  ```

But now this could be something like:

```r
df |>
  mutate(
    sale_ttm = sum(sale),
    cogs_ttm = sum(cogs),
    sga_ttm = sum(sga),
    .by = gvkey,
    .order = vars(datadate),
    .frame = (-3, 0)
  )
```

This would seem to have the merit of making it easier for `dbplyr` to infer that a window function was being sought (currently there are cases where `dbplyr` does not get the hint).

I am surprised that I have only one instance of `window_frame()` in my [book](https://iangow.github.io/far_book/ffjr.html#replication-of-ffjr). It seems like a very handy pattern (e.g., moving averages, windowed regressions).

I had a comical exchange with ChatGPT about this this afternoon (Australia time) (see [here](https://chatgpt.com/share/66ed3e66-2cb0-800b-9dfe-e3e0e0a27d97)).

``` r
memdb_frame(x = 1:2, y = 1:2) %>%
```

```r
mf1 <- memdb_frame(x = 1:2, y = 1:2)
```

title: Produce shorter SQL for multiple mutates
description:
The generated SQL is way more nested than it would have to be. It would be great if we could shorten the queries 

## Nested Mutates
This is probably not very common but maybe there is an easy fix.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2)
lf %>% 
  mutate(
    x = x + 1,
    x = x + 1,
    y = y + 1,
    y = y + 1
  )
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
#> FROM (SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
#> FROM (SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y`
#> FROM `df`) `q01`) `q02`

# could be
# SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
# FROM (SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
# FROM `df`) `q01`
```

## Group Followed by Multiple Mutates

```r
lf %>% 
  group_by(x) %>% 
  mutate(x = x + 1) %>% 
  mutate(y = y + 1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
#> FROM (SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y`
#> FROM `df`) `q01`

# could be
# SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y` + 1.0 AS `y`
# FROM `df`
```

<details>

## Mutate Followed by Filter

Fixed by #792

```r
lf %>% 
  mutate(x = x + 1) %>% 
  filter(y == 1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM (SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y`
#> FROM `df`) `q01`
#> WHERE (`y` = 1.0)

# could be
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x` + 1.0 AS `x`, `y`
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (`y` = 1.0)
```

## Joins
Moved to its own issue #722
This feels pretty common to me

</details>

``` r
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1)
```

title: Issues with quoted identifiers and CTEs
description:
After completing #1558, I discovered there were some other issues with CTEs, namely, dbplyr quoted tables names inconsistently and incorrectly.

I created this test case to generate the two different issues I encountered.

```r
test_that("CTE quoting works right", {
  lf1 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2, .name = "lf1")
  lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, z = 2, .name = "lf2")

  # The query is nonsensical, because I took a failing query from the wild and
  # whiddled it down to the minimum amount of code required to reveal two
  # separate quoting issues when using CTEs

  double_it <- function(.data, column_name) {
    .data %>%
      mutate(
        "{ column_name }" := .data[[column_name]] * 2
      )
  }

  skinny <- function(column_name) {
    lf1 %>%
      double_it(column_name) %>%
      mutate(
        column_name = column_name,
        .keep = "none"
      )
  }

  tall_tbl <- purrr::map(c("x", "y"), skinny) %>%
    purrr::reduce(dplyr::union_all)

  query <- tall_tbl %>%
    left_join(tall_tbl, by = join_by(column_name)) %>%
    left_join(tall_tbl, by = join_by(column_name)) %>%
    sql_render(sql_options = sql_options(cte = TRUE)) %>%
    expect_snapshot()
})
```

The output produced for this snapshot is the following:

```sql
WITH `q01` AS (
    SELECT `x` * 2.0 AS `x`, `y`
    FROM `lf1`
  ),
  `q02` AS (
    SELECT 'x' AS `column_name`
    FROM `q01`
  ),
  `q03` AS (
    SELECT `x`, `y` * 2.0 AS `y`
    FROM `lf1`
  ),
  `q04` AS (
    SELECT 'y' AS `column_name`
    FROM `q03` AS `q01`
  ),
  `q05` AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM `q02`
  
    UNION ALL
  
    SELECT *
    FROM `q04`
  ),
  `q06` AS (
    SELECT 'x' AS `column_name`
    FROM ```q01``` AS `q01`
  ),
  `q07` AS (
    SELECT 'y' AS `column_name`
    FROM ```q03``` AS `q01`
  ),
  `q08` AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM `q06`
  
    UNION ALL
  
    SELECT *
    FROM `q07`
  ),
  `q09` AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM '`q06`'
  
    UNION ALL
  
    SELECT *
    FROM '`q07`'
  )
  SELECT `...1`.`column_name` AS `column_name`
  FROM `q05` AS `...1`
  LEFT JOIN `q08` AS `...2`
    ON (`...1`.`column_name` = `...2`.`column_name`)
  LEFT JOIN `q09` AS `...3`
    ON (`...1`.`column_name` = `...3`.`column_name`)
```

Here are the two issues I noticed:

- If you look at the definition for CTE `q06`, you'll see the FROM clause has incorrectly triple-quoted the `q03` identifier
- If you look at the definition for CTE `q09`, you'll see the FROM clause has incorrectly applied single quotes around the `q06` identifier

Either of these issues render the SQL statement invalid and unable to run on a database.

title: BUG - muliple joins fail in MS Access - expecting additional parenthesis ?
description:
Hello,

I noticed multiple successive joins fail in MS Access.
For example, using the industrial emission DB available at https://sdi.eea.europa.eu/data/ff47e25d-5d4c-491d-b9ce-de17ca61fe6d

```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

odbcListDataSources()
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), 
                 DSN="EPRTR")

sites <- tbl(con, "1_ProductionSite") %>% 
  select(Site_INSPIRE_ID) 
  

facilities <- tbl(con, "2_ProductionFacility") %>% 
  select(Parent_Site_INSPIRE_ID, Facility_INSPIRE_ID )

installations <- tbl(con, "3_ProductionInstallation") %>%
  select(Parent_Facility_INSPIRE_ID, Installation_INSPIRE_ID) 

join <- facilities %>%
  left_join(y= installations, by=c("Facility_INSPIRE_ID"="Parent_Facility_INSPIRE_ID") )%>% 
  left_join(y=sites, by=c("Parent_Site_INSPIRE_ID"="Site_INSPIRE_ID") )

 join %>% show_query()

```

We get the query

```SQL
SELECT
  `Parent_Site_INSPIRE_ID`,
  `Facility_INSPIRE_ID`,
  `Installation_INSPIRE_ID`
FROM `2_ProductionFacility`
LEFT JOIN `3_ProductionInstallation`
  ON (`2_ProductionFacility`.`Facility_INSPIRE_ID` = `3_ProductionInstallation`.`Parent_Facility_INSPIRE_ID`)
LEFT JOIN `1_ProductionSite`
  ON (`2_ProductionFacility`.`Parent_Site_INSPIRE_ID` = `1_ProductionSite`.`Site_INSPIRE_ID`)
```

This query fails in Access with the message:

```
Syntax error (missing operator) in query expression '(`2_ProductionFacility`.`Facility_INSPIRE_ID` =
  `3_ProductionInstallation`.`Parent_Facility_INSPIRE_ID`)
```

However, similar queries generated by Access have parenthesis around the first join. Adding parenthesis to the query generated by dplyr and copy/paste to Access allows the query to run successfully.

```SQL
SELECT
  `Parent_Site_INSPIRE_ID`,
  `Facility_INSPIRE_ID`,
  `Installation_INSPIRE_ID`
FROM (
`2_ProductionFacility`
LEFT JOIN `3_ProductionInstallation`
  ON (`2_ProductionFacility`.`Facility_INSPIRE_ID` = `3_ProductionInstallation`.`Parent_Facility_INSPIRE_ID`)
)
LEFT JOIN `1_ProductionSite`
```

title: Export a mask akin to rlang::.data for custom SQL functions
description:
A useful feature of dbplyr is automatically passing through unknown calls straight into SQL, e.g. some flavors support `ANY_VALUE()` to take a value from a column arbitrarily during aggregation:

```r
conn |>
  tbl("my_schema.table") |>
  group_by(grp) |>
  summarize(some_x = ANY_VALUE(x)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  show_query()
```

Will give something like

```sql
SELECT grp, ANY_VALUE(x) AS some_x
FROM my_schema.tbl
GROUP BY grp
```

However, within packages, this presents the classic issue with `R CMD check` notes that `ANY_VALUE()` is an undefined function, from the static R checker's point of view.

rlang offers `.data` and `.env` masks for this purpose:

https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/dot-data.html

Could dbplyr offer something similar, e.g. an `.sql` mask we could use as:

```r
conn |>
  tbl("my_schema.table") |>
  group_by(grp) |>
  summarize(some_x = .sql$ANY_VALUE(x)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  show_query()
```

title: sql escape for 'non-translated' function in window context
description:
In the context of the following issue: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1527

Something like this does not work at the moment (generated sql does ignores window options) for spark sql backend:
```r
dbplyr::lazy_frame(rep_df) |> 
  group_by(user_id) %>%
  dbplyr::window_order(dates) %>%
  dbplyr::window_frame(-Inf, -1) %>%
  mutate(list_amount = sql("collect_list(amount)")) %>% 
  dbplyr::sql_render()
```

In general, would it be better to generate the sql one would expect by replacing whatever that it there in the sql call. 

In this case, it is:

```sql
SELECT
`df`.*,
collect_list(`amount`) OVER (PARTITION BY `user_id` ORDER BY `dates` ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS `list_amount`
FROM `df`
```

<ins>Why is this required</ins>: There is no way to generate this sql chunk via `dbplyr` and thereby breaks one's workflow. Its practically impossible to cover all "translations" that some backend offers. Would it make sense to create a meaningful "escape hatch"? 

<ins>Personally</ins>, for a serious dbplyr user like me, I will be forced to switch to some other tool say pyspark (which I do not want to) for day-to-day work or do some monkey patching with `sdf_sql` with handwritten sql (I choose dbplyr for convenience and elegance).

title: Multiple left joins fails in MS Access
description:
dbplyr 2.4.0.9000  Microsoft Access 2019, 64 bit
(Edited 1.12.2023 to make case clearer)

I have seen #1130, but I am using the github version of tidyverse

```
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
a <- lazy_frame(patient = "a", adate = "11.01.2020", con = simulate_access())
b <- lazy_frame(patient = "a", bdate = "12.01.2020", con = simulate_access())
c <- lazy_frame(patient = "a", cdate = "13.01.2020", con = simulate_access())

a  |> left_join(b) |>
  select(patient, adate, bdate )
``` 

Works after replacing "FROM df" by FROM 'a' etc.

```
SELECT `df_LHS`.*, `bdate`
FROM `a` AS `df_LHS`
LEFT JOIN `b` AS `df_RHS`
ON (`df_LHS`.`patient` = `df_RHS`.`patient`)
```

One more join

```
a  |> left_join(b) |> left_join(c) |>
  select(patient, adate, bdate, cdate )
```
Fails after replacing "FROM df"

```
SELECT `df...1`.*, `bdate`, `cdate`
FROM `a` AS `df...1`
LEFT JOIN `b` AS `df...2`
ON (`df...1`.`patient` = `df...2`.`patient`)
LEFT JOIN `c` AS `df...3`
ON (`df...1`.`patient` = `df...3`.`patient`)
```

which looks reasonable . Run it or paste it directly into an Access Query, it errors

```
Syntax error (missing operator) in Query
(`df...1`.`patient` = `df...2`.`patient`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...3`
  ON (`df...1`.`patient` = `df...3`.`patient`)
```

The problem is in the periods. This is ok:
```
SELECT `df1`.* FROM `a` AS `df1`
```

This fails

```
SELECT `df.1`.* FROM `a` AS `df.1`
```


**Workaround**: Use a collect() between the joins. Ok for smaller data sets.

**Cross-test**: a manually created join is fine:

```
SELECT a.patient, a.adate, b.bdate, c.cdate
FROM (a LEFT JOIN b ON a.patient = b.patient) LEFT JOIN c ON b.patient = c.patient;
```

Sample test database attached

[testdb.zip](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/files/13510712/testdb.zip)

--- Another cross-test ---

With sqlite, the following works fine

```
SELECT `a...1`.*, `bdate`, `cdate`
FROM `a` AS `a...1`
LEFT JOIN `b` AS `b...2`
  ON (`a...1`.`patient` = `b...2`.`patient`)
LEFT JOIN `c` AS `c...3`
  ON (`a...1`.`patient` = `c...3`.`patient`)

```

title: `copy_to` creates tables with invalid column names
description:
I use dbplyr with a database where some column names are invalid.
If a table with invalid column name is copied to the data base, invalid
names are changed to valid ones. Thus when using `copy_to`, the table in the
database might have column names than are different from the original data frame.

This was no problem in dbplyr 2.1.1, but in dbplyr 2.2.1 the returned tbl object
contains the old (invalid) column names instead of the new correct ones. This leads
to bugs when working with the table.

A closer look into the code showed that the following line led to the problem:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blame/main/R/verb-copy-to.R#L86

Before the line was changes, the column names were read from the table. Now it is
assumed that they are the same as the ones in the data frame. This assumption isn't
true in my case and I think that there are also other data bases where this isn't
necessarily true (random example: https://www.techtalkcorner.com/parquet-files-column-names-with-spaces/).

Can we either
- get back to the old behaviour in `copy_to` to read the column names from the table or
- add a parameter to switch the behavior (use column names from data frame or read them from table)?

title: dblyr::rows_upsert  and rows_update with ROracle connection (OraConnection) fail
description:
dplyr::rows_upsert (in_place=TRUE) with ROracle connection  fails because dbplyr::sql_query_upsert.OraConnnection puts a semicolon at the end of the query. Without that semicolon the query works just as expected.

dplyr::rows_update with OraConnection produces "update from " query that is not supported by Oracle. 
This is most likely due to fact that there is no sql_query_update.OraConnection method in dbplyr.

Update can be done in Oracle by merge without the insert part.
