title: filter generates buggy SQL when comparing with list element
description:
When using tbl via dbplyr, filter generates correct SQL when comparing a column with an R scalar variable, but when using $ syntax to access value in a list, buggy sql is generated. The reprex below produces errors both with Postgres and SQLite connections, though more of the generated SQL is visible with Postgres

```r
library(DBI)
library(dbplyr)

init_table <- function(con) {
  # dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE a")
  dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE a (a_id INTEGER, a_value VARCHAR)")
  dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO a (a_id, a_value) VALUES (1, 'value 1')")
}

test_filter <- function(con) {
  tbl_a <- tbl(con, "a")
  # This works fine
  id <- 1
  tbl_a %>% filter(a_id == id)
  # This blows up
  l <- list(id = 1)
  tbl_a %>% filter(a_id == l$id)
}

slCon <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())
init_table(slCon)
test_filter(slCon)
# SQLite: Error in `collect()`:
# ! Failed to collect lazy table.
# Caused by error:
# ! near "AS": syntax error

# pgCon=dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), host = "...", user = "...")
# init_table(pgCon)
# test_filter(pgCon)
# Error in `collect()`:
# ! Failed to collect lazy table.
# Failed to prepare query: ERROR:  syntax error at or near "AS"
# LINE 3: WHERE ("a_id" = (1.0 AS "id").1.0)
```
Something is wrong with the SQL quoting in this case.

title: ODBC complex query fails to collect() while it did in an earlier version
description:
In our app, we generate some complex queries via metaprogramming. When using a JDBC connection, the query works no problem. However, with the same app in Docker containers we have to use an ODBC connection instead. The connection itself works, we pull some data from the database. When it comes to the complex query, we get a non-informative error message:  
" Warning: Error in collect: Failed to collect lazy table.
 Caused by error:
 ! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1526: 00000: [Informix][Informix ODBC Driver]General error.
   1: shiny::runApp"

I'll provide an example of the query below with fake names. Sorry for it being hard to comprehend (its difficult for us too :))
```r
inner_join(
  inner_join(
    tbl(my_odbc_connection, 'table1'),
    tbl(my_odbc_connection, 'table2')  %>%
      rename_with( ~ paste0(.,'_t2')) , 
    by = c('key1' = 'key_t2'),
    suffix = c('_left_table2', '_right_table2')
    ),
  tbl(my_odbc_connection, 'table3') %>% 
    rename_with( ~ paste0(.,'_t3')) ,
  by = c('key3' = 'key_t3'),
  suffix = c('_left_table3', '_right_table3')
  )  %>% 
collect()
```

After lots of trial and error, here's what made even this work as intended: **using dbplyr 2.1.1**.
I've heard there's been some issues with 2.4.0, but we also used 2.3.4 and 2.3.3, with the same error.
So, it seems we found our fix, hopefully this could point to specific parts that cause this issue elsewhere :)

title: Use of `as.Date()` in `filter()` returns an error in dbplyr 2.4.0 for Oracle databases
description:
We work with a lot of Oracle databases and have experienced some queries that breaks when updating to dbplyr 2.4.0. When using `as.Date()` in a `filter()` it doesn't translate to the right sql-statement. I have tried with a reprex below.

For dbplyr 2.3.4:
``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
  
lazy_frame(DATE_VAR = as.Date("2021-12-31"), con = simulate_oracle()) %>% 
  filter(DATE_VAR == as.Date("2021-12-31")) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM (`df`) 
#> WHERE (`DATE_VAR` = DATE '2021-12-31')

utils::packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '2.3.4'
```
<sup>Created on 2024-01-16 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

For dbplyr 2.4.0:
``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
  
lazy_frame(DATE_VAR = as.Date("2021-12-31"), con = simulate_oracle()) %>% 
  filter(DATE_VAR == as.Date("2021-12-31")) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df`.*
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (`DATE_VAR` = DATE 2021-12-31)

utils::packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '2.4.0'
```
<sup>Created on 2024-01-16 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

We get the following error when running with our database:
```r
Error in `collect()`:
  ! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error in `.oci.SendQuery()`:
  ! ORA-00936: missing expression
```

In dbplyr 2.4.0 the sql-statement's where-clause has `DATE 2021-12-31` and dbplyr 2.3.4 has `DATE '2021-12-31'`. So the apostrophes around the date are missing in dbplyr 2.4.0. Is this the expected behaviour?

Thanks for the great work on the package.

title: Performance and usability of joins with `copy = TRUE` to Snowflake
description:
**Performance**
When using `copy = TRUE` to create a temporary table with data from my local environment, I consistently see execution times over ten minutes, even for very small datasets.  I believe this is because `db_write_table()` is called using a `name` argument that does not specify a catalog or schema, leading to an expensive call to `dbExistsTable()`.  This belief is reinforced by much better performance (< 5s) after hacking explicit schema and warehouse names into `db_copy_to()`:
```
# db-io.R, top of `db_copy_to()`
table <- as_table_ident(table)
vctrs::field(table, 'catalog') <- 'MY_FAVORITE_LITERAL_CATALOG'
vctrs::field(table, 'schema') <- 'AND_SCHEMA'
```

**Usability**
A related, arguably separate, issue is the need to set a current working catalog and schema on a connection (using `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`) prior to any use of `copy = TRUE`, if no default exists.  While these "current" values enable table creation and write operations via the query interface (`CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT INTO`), `dbExistsTable()` wraps a direct library call to `SQLTables()` and does not interact with them.  This was declared "not worth the effort" in #1099, and I respect that may remain the judgement, though the state of both table naming and data warehouse relevance have evolved since then.

**Opportunity**
Let this be a feature request to call `db_write_table()` / `dbWriteTable()` using a fully qualified name, in order to avoid asking the driver to list all catalogs and schemas, and eliminate the need to set a current schema and catalog.

Of course, this raises a design question: _sure, but what catalog and schema do we use?_  Where to put temporary tables for a generic data warehouse backend is not obvious to me.  To kick off brainstorming, choices might include:
* Extract catalog and schema from an existing table (hard, per previous discussion, and lacks flexibility -- users may wish to specify a location with no or few tables for better performance)
* User-specified schema and warehouse via options or environment variables (my favorite idea so far)
* Require "current" schema and warehouse in query interface (contrary to above request), and collect via `CURRENT_WAREHOUSE()` and `CURRENT_SCHEMA()` (I don't like this idea but do think it could work)

Thanks again to @hadley and @detule for the [recent collaboration on name-escaping in `odbc`](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/pull/618).  As promised, this issue aims at solving `copy = TRUE` further up the stack, building from that earlier foundational work.  cc @fh-mthomson.  Happy seasonal holidays to all `dbplyr` friends.

title: `db_sql_render()` doesn't pass three dots
description:
I have a package `RPresto` that extends the `db_sql_render()` generic for Presto connections ([code link](https://github.com/prestodb/RPresto/blob/master/R/dbplyr-db.R#L180)). The extended `db_sql_render()` function has an added argument, `use_presto_cte`. The call stack goes from `dbplyr::db_sql_render()` to `RPresto::db_sql_render.PrestoConnection()`, so the passing of the `use_presto_cte` arg relies on the three dot ellipsis in `dbplyr::db_sql_render()`. However, in dbplyr 2.4.0, `db_sql_render()` doesn't pass on the ellipsis (see [code link](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/main/R/db.R#L76)).

Happy to provide a quick PR to add the ellipsis passing to the function.

title: Dates in MS SQL aren't escaped properly
description:
```r
library(dbplyr)
escape(as.POSIXlt("2022-12-31 12:59:15"), con = simulate_mssql())
## <SQL> '2022-12-31T12:59:15Z'
## should be: 
## <SQL> '2022-12-31T12:59:15'
```

`T-SQL` does not allow for the time zone letter to be added to the literal (cf. [the specifications for time literals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/datetime-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver16#supported-string-literal-formats-for-datetime)).

Thus, we would need to specify an own `sql_escape_datetime` routine for `Microsoft SQl Server` where we remove the (forced) conversion to `UTC`:

```r
`sql_escape_datetime.Microsoft SQL Server` <- function (con, x)  {
    x <- strftime(x, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
    sql_escape_string(con, x)
}
```

title: Smart handling of rowwise vs. vectorized operations.
description:
In the following reprex I show a very simple SQL query that I can't figure out how to replicate using `dbplyr` translation.

The operation is to calculate a random number based on the value in an existing column. Because there is no vectorized function for this in R, using `dplyr` I need to either call `map` or use `rowwise`.  However, neither of these translates properly to SQL.

This is a general issue in that SQL is naturally rowwise, while R tries to be vectorized as much as possible for efficiency.

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(tidyverse)

### Create in-memory DB
con = dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), location=":memory:")
#> Error in dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), location = ":memory:"): could not find function "dbConnect"

### Create local table
df = tibble(A = 1:10)

### Write table to database
dbWriteTable(con, "tmp", df, overwrite=T)
#> Error in dbWriteTable(con, "tmp", df, overwrite = T): could not find function "dbWriteTable"

### Read lazy table from DB
dbf = tbl(con, "tmp")
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'con' not found


### Perform operation in the database:
### Create random integer based on value in column A
dbGetQuery(con, "select A, abs(random() % A) as B from tmp")
#> Error in dbGetQuery(con, "select A, abs(random() % A) as B from tmp"): could not find function "dbGetQuery"

### Try doing the same with local table
df %>% mutate(B = sample(1:A, 1))
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `B = sample(1:A, 1)`.
#> Caused by warning in `1:A`:
#> ! numerical expression has 10 elements: only the first used
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>        A     B
#>    <int> <int>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     2     1
#>  3     3     1
#>  4     4     1
#>  5     5     1
#>  6     6     1
#>  7     7     1
#>  8     8     1
#>  9     9     1
#> 10    10     1
df %>% mutate(across(A, ~sample(1:.x, 1), .names="B"))
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `across(A, ~sample(1:.x, 1), .names = "B")`.
#> Caused by warning in `1:A`:
#> ! numerical expression has 10 elements: only the first used
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>        A     B
#>    <int> <int>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     2     1
#>  3     3     1
#>  4     4     1
#>  5     5     1
#>  6     6     1
#>  7     7     1
#>  8     8     1
#>  9     9     1
#> 10    10     1
df %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(B = sample(1:A, 1))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>        A     B
#>    <int> <int>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     2     1
#>  3     3     3
#>  4     4     4
#>  5     5     5
#>  6     6     1
#>  7     7     4
#>  8     8     6
#>  9     9     2
#> 10    10     5
df %>% mutate(B = map_dbl(A, ~sample(1:.x, 1)))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>        A     B
#>    <int> <dbl>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     2     2
#>  3     3     1
#>  4     4     4
#>  5     5     2
#>  6     6     1
#>  7     7     1
#>  8     8     5
#>  9     9     3
#> 10    10     4

### Try doing the same with lazy table
dbf %>% mutate(B = sample(1:A, 1)) %>% show_query()
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'dbf' not found
dbf %>% mutate(across(A, ~sample(1:.x, 1), .names="B")) %>% show_query()
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'dbf' not found
dbf %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(B = sample(1:A, 1)) %>% show_query()
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'dbf' not found
dbf %>% mutate(B = map_dbl(A, ~sample(1:., 1))) %>% show_query()
#> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos): object 'dbf' not found
```

<sup>Created on 2023-10-25 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Quite honestly, my preference would be for dplyr to, by default, `map` non-vectorized operations. I'm having trouble thinking of a situation where the meaning isn't implicitly clear. That doesn't mean there aren't.

Alternatively, find a way to deal with the situation where `rowwise` is used so that code can be used for both local and lazy tables.

Or maybe in `dplyr` have a way to explicitly specify whether a given operation is to be done row-wise or column-wise. Consider this:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
tb = tibble(A = list(c(1,2), c(3,4)))
tb %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(B = sum(A))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   A             B
#>   <list>    <dbl>
#> 1 <dbl [2]>     3
#> 2 <dbl [2]>     7
tb %>% mutate(B = map_int(A, ~sum(.)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   A             B
#>   <list>    <int>
#> 1 <dbl [2]>     3
#> 2 <dbl [2]>     7
```

<sup>Created on 2023-10-25 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I think the following should produce the outputs shown:

``` r
tb %>% mutate(B = rowwise(sum(A)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   A             B
#>   <list>    <dbl>
#> 1 <dbl [2]>     3
#> 2 <dbl [2]>     7
tb %>% summarize(s = colwise(sum(A)))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   s        
 #>  <list>   
#> 1 <dbl [2]>
tb %>% summarize(s = colwise(sum(A))) %>% pull(s)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 4 6
```

There would be no question how those are to be evaluated or translated to SQL

title: Translate `str_starts()` to `REGEXP_INSTR` instead of `INSTR` for Snowflake
description:
Snowflake doesn't have a `INSTR` function. As such, I think the following `stringr` functions are affected:

- str_detect() when `fixed()` is used
- str_ends()
- str_starts()

```r
x <- c("XXX", "XXY", "YXXX")

#####
# str_detect()
#####
lazy_frame(TOKEN=x,con = simulate_snowflake()) %>%
  filter(
    stringr::str_detect(TOKEN, fixed("XXX"))
  )
<SQL>
SELECT `df`.*
FROM `df`
WHERE (INSTR(`TOKEN`, 'XXX') > 0)

#####
# str_starts()
#####
lazy_frame(TOKEN=x,con = simulate_snowflake()) %>%
  filter(
    stringr::str_starts(TOKEN, fixed("XXX"))
  )
<SQL>
SELECT `df`.*
FROM `df`
WHERE (INSTR(`TOKEN`, 'XXX') = 1)

#####
# str_ends()
#####
lazy_frame(TOKEN=x,con = simulate_snowflake()) %>%
  filter(
    stringr::str_ends(TOKEN, fixed("XXX"))
  )
<SQL>
SELECT `df`.*
FROM `df`
WHERE (INSTR(`TOKEN`, 'XXX') = ((LENGTH(`TOKEN`) - LENGTH('XXX')) + 1))
```

title: Include generated SQL in error messages
Can we add custom translations ?
description:
In `sql_substr()` we have an example showing us how to add a new variant.

I think I understand the general mechanism, `sql_variant()` receives  "translators" which are environments containing functions creating strings of class "sql". I see also that `sql_translator()` has a `.parent` arg so we can inherit from a higher level translator.

But I don't quite understand how to idiomatically add a new translation to an existing variant. 

A hack that I think will work OK for my project is to edit the `base_odbc_scalar`, `base_odbc_agg`, and `base_odbc_win` environments directly since they're exported and not locked, another would be to overwrite `dbplyr:::sql_translation.Oracle` (Since that's Oracle in my case) but seems a bit clunky as well.

I thought about using a super class of my "Oracle" too but it seems I'd have to set new methods for at least `tbl()` and probably more, that seems like a rabbit hole.

My use case FWIW is to add a series of functions such as `count_if()`, which don't exist in neither R or Oracle, I'd like also to implement some translations from str_replace to REGEXP_EXTRACT, the general idea is that I'd like this code to work the same before or after collecting.

Can you recommend a way to go at this ?

title: resolve R CHECK warning on use of TO_DATE in Oracle
description:
I have a package which connects to Oracle via dbplyr.
In some of the package functions I use `TO_DATE` to filter values by date, like in the following example:

```R
flight_list <- function(con = NULL, wef, til) {
  wef <- lubridate::as_datetime(wef, tz = "UTC") |> format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
  til <- lubridate::as_datetime(til, tz = "UTC") |> format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

  # get a connection eventually
  if (is.null(con)) {
    con <- db_connection(schema = "XYYZ")
  }
  # bind to the flights table
  flt <- dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::in_schema("MMM", "FLIGHT")))
  flt |>
    dplyr::filter(
      TO_DATE(wef, "yyyy-mm-dd hh24:mi:ss") <= .data$LOBT,
      .data$LOBT < TO_DATE(til, "yyyy-mm-dd hh24:mi:ss")
}
```

This functionally works but upon checking the package (R CHECK) I get the following:

```
  flight_list: no visible global function definition for 'TO_DATE'
``` 

Is there a way to avoid/silence these warnings?

title: `slice_sample()` does not interact correctly with `set.seed()` when working with an SQLite database.
description:
I'm not too sure if this issue sits within `dbplyr` or `RSQLite`, but the `slice_sample()` function does not appear to be taking account of a seed set via `set.seed()` when using an SQLite database.

If I set a seed, then run `slice_sample()`, then later set the same seed, and run `slice_sample()` again, the sampled table is different.

For comparison, when undertaking these sample operations using a Microsoft SQL Server database, the expected behaviour is observed (i.e., the two sampled tables are identical).

```r
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)


tbl <- tibble(n = 1:30)
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_table", tbl)

set.seed(100)
sample1 <- slice_sample(tbl(conn, "test_table"), n = 3)

set.seed(100)
sample2 <- slice_sample(tbl(conn, "test_table"), n = 3)

identical(sample1, sample2)
```

title: Add a function to check if `schema` exists in a database
description:
It would be nice to have a function checking if the `schema` exists in a database. It would be a good feature to work on schedule with databases and caching results (e.g. pulling tables if a given `schema` exists).

For the time-being I don't see any other way to check it with classic error handling which is a bit cumbersome:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

tmp <- tempfile()
DBI::dbExecute(con, paste0("ATTACH '", tmp, "' AS aux"))

dplyr::copy_to(con, mtcars, dbplyr::in_schema("aux", "df"), temporary = FALSE)

# this one exists
dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::in_schema("aux", "df"))

# this does not
tryCatch({
  dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::in_schema("aux2", "df"))
},
error = function(e) {
  print("no schema")
})
```

title: Add support for Databricks backend
description:
Thanks to the default "DBI" translation, most of the `dplyr`/`dbplyr` operations work. There are Databricks specific operations, for example `var()`,  currently marked as not-supported by `dbplyr`, due to the fact that `var()` is not in the default translation. Databricks uses "Spark SQL", which is underpinned by the Hive SQL syntax. My suggestion would be to use the same SQL variance  currently in use for the Hive backend support. 

The second issue uncovered, is that `copy_to()` does not work. The Databricks back-end does not support transactions. So I think a custom `db_copy_to()` function will be needed here.

The following `reprex` contains the specific code that can be used to connect to Databricks using a PAT. It also contains confirmation that `var()` is supported in Databricks. The confirmation is in calling SQL directly via `DBI`, and then attempting

title: Only select required columns
description:
```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 2, b = 3)

left_join(
  lf,
  lf2 %>% 
    group_by(x) %>% 
    summarise(
      a = sum(a, na.rm = TRUE),
      b = sum(b, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  select(x, y, a)
```

With the PRs for inlining `select()` before and after a `*_join()` merged this gives

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `a`
FROM `df` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT `x`, SUM(`a`) AS `a`, SUM(`b`) AS `b`
  FROM `df`
  GROUP BY `x`
) `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

The part `` SUM(`b`) AS `b` `` is not necessary and could be left out automatically.

title: Approximate number of rows ?
description:
Counting rows can be slow on databases, but this information is often stored (though not necessarily up to date) in meta tables. Could we have a way to fetch it through dbplyr ?

Displaying it in the header when printing would seem like a net win at least ? And there could be a new verb `db_approx_count()` mentioned in `?count`.

chatgpt got me this as a start: 

1. MySQL:
   In MySQL, you can use the `SHOW TABLE STATUS` command to get information about a table, including the number of rows. The query would look like this:

   ```sql
   SHOW TABLE STATUS LIKE 'your_table_name';
   ```

   In the result set, you can find the row count under the column `Rows`.

2. PostgreSQL:
   In PostgreSQL, you can use the `pg_stat_all_tables` system view to get statistics about all tables in the database. The query would look like this:

   ```sql
   SELECT schemaname, tablename, n_live_tup AS row_count
   FROM pg_stat_all_tables
   WHERE schemaname = 'your_schema_name' AND tablename = 'your_table_name';
   ```

   The `n_live_tup` column represents the number of live (non-deleted) rows in the table.

3. SQL Server:
   In SQL Server, you can use the `sys.dm_db_partition_stats` dynamic management view to get row count information. The query would look like this:

   ```sql
   SELECT OBJECT_NAME(object_id) AS table_name, row_count
   FROM sys.dm_db_partition_stats
   WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('your_schema_name.your_table_name') AND index_id IN (0, 1);
   ```

   The `row_count` column provides the number of rows in the specified table.

4. Oracle:
   In Oracle, you can use the `ALL_TABLES` or `USER_TABLES` data dictionary views to get information about tables, including the number of rows. The query would look like this:

   ```sql
   SELECT table_name, num_rows
   FROM all_tables
   WHERE owner = 'YOUR_SCHEMA_NAME' AND table_name = 'YOUR_TABLE_NAME';
   ```

   The `num_rows` column contains the number of rows in the specified table.

title: Efficiency of `anti_join()` implementation in SQLite
description:
The SQL translation of `anti_join` is very inefficient when working with large SQLite tables. I believe this isn't technically a `dbplyr` issue, but since faster anti joins are possible with different SQL syntax I am posting this here. I'm not super experienced with SQL, so I might be missing something important about the generalizability of the `dbplyr` generated SQL code, but the performance difference is noteworthy.

Background:
I'm using `dbplyr`  to work with a moderately large dataset A (c. 4 million rows) that has an alphanumeric record identifier. About 5% of these identifiers are not represented in a related table B and when trying to identify missing records using an anti join noticed that `dbplyr::anti_join(A, B)` operations on this table do not complete in reasonable time, eventhough other operations such as `left_join(A, B)` are fast.

Looking into this further I realised that `dbplyr::anti_join` is translated to 
```sql
SELECT * FROM `A` WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM `A`
  WHERE (`A`.`id` = `B`.`id`)
)
```

Whereas doing the anti join using an SQL left join is much faster 
```sql
SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id WHERE B.id IS NULL
```
Even at much smaller table sizes (1e4 rows) the performance difference is substantial (2 orders of magnitude on my machine)

reprex:
```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)

# Create db with dplyr ----------------------------------------------------
con_dplyr <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), path = ":dbname:")

#make large df

# Add table to database
tbl_size = 1e4
A <- tibble(value = rnorm(tbl_size)) %>% tibble::rownames_to_column( var = 'id')
B <- tibble(id = sample(A$id, size = .95*tbl_size)) %>% mutate(nchar = nchar(id))
dplyr::copy_to(con_dplyr, A, "A", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)
dplyr::copy_to(con_dplyr, B, "B", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)

rm_A = tbl(con_dplyr, 'A')
rm_B = tbl(con_dplyr, 'B')

#this is a fast left join
left_join(rm_A,rm_B) %>% collect()

#this is a slow anti join
anti_join(rm_A,rm_B) %>% collect()

#this is a fast anti join
DBI::dbGetQuery(con_dplyr, 'SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id WHERE B.id IS NULL')

#comparing the different SQL statements via DBI::dbGetQuery
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
left_join_is_null = DBI::dbGetQuery(con_dplyr, 'SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id WHERE B.id IS NULL'),
where_not_exists = DBI::dbGetQuery(con_dplyr, 'SELECT *
FROM A
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM B
  WHERE (A.id = B.id)
)'),
times = 5)

DBI::dbDisconnect(con_dplyr)
```

title: dbplyr 2.4.0 breaks duckdb's ability to treat files as tables
description:
DuckDB can execute `SELECT` statements directly on files (CSV, Parquet etc) without needing to use a function. In this case, the file name is treated as the table name. This is explained in the docs: https://duckdb.org/docs/archive/0.9.1/data/parquet/overview.

Previously this functionality worked fine with `dbplyr`, up until 2.3.4. However with the upgrade to 2.4.0, it fails. With the below example I'm querying a specific file called `metadata.0.2.3.parquet`, but you can replace it with any parquet file and the same issue will occur:
```r
duckdb::duckdb() |>
    DBI::dbConnect(drv = _, read_only = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::tbl("metadata.0.2.3.parquet")
```
```
It looks like you tried to incorrectly use a table in a schema as source.
ℹ If you want to specify a schema use `in_schema()` or `in_catalog()`.
ℹ If your table actually contains "." in the name use `check_from = FALSE` to silence this message.
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error:
! rapi_prepare: Failed to prepare query SELECT "metadata.0.2.3.parquet".*
FROM "metadata.0.2.3.parquet"
LIMIT 11
Error: Binder Error: Referenced table "metadata.0.2.3.parquet" not found!
Candidate tables: "metadata"
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

This may be related to #1388, but the error messages are somewhat different.

title: Support Firebird-Backends in tbl()?
description:
Hi all,

I'm not 100% sure if my issue should be addressed here or over at [r-dbi](https://github.com/r-dbi/DBI). 

It would be nice to support Firebird-Databases when using the function `tbl()`.

By default this function generates a SQL-Statement of a given query  with a `LIMIT 11` clause to reduce the printed output in the console. However, this is not valid Firebird-SQL syntax and must be handled via [SELECT] `FIRST 11` [*].

Is there any chance to include this some time?

Kind regards,
Philipp

Error for a given query is below

```
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dbplyr)

con_dbi <- dbConnect(odbc(), "our_database")

MY_TABLE<- tbl(con_dbi, "MY_TABLE")

print(MY_TABLE)

dbDisconnect(con_dbi)

Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error:
11 en unknown - line 3, column 70: [Devart][ODBC][Firebird]Dynamic SQL Error
<SQL> 'SELECT *
FROM "MY_TABLE"
LIMIT 11'
```

title: ODBC with Databricks - Temp Tables vs Views

Hey there,

One of the [primary recommendations](https://docs.databricks.com/en/sparkr/rstudio.html#connect-using-rstudio-desktop) for interfacing with Databricks is via dbplyr translation to Spark SQL through the Databricks ODBC driver (using it in a similar way to any other backend). However, Spark SQL apparently doesn't support temporary tables, only temporary views, which is a major breaking change to all `compute()` calls within my code (and possibly some joins and other things I've not yet run into as well).

No great way to make this a reprex, but wanted to understand any workarounds that may exist and/or request an argument or package-level option to switch between temporary `views` and `tables` interchangeably to avoid issues with `compute()`. The naive workaround at the moment is to just override `dbplyr::compute()` in my code with a user-defined function that takes and returns the generated SQL query, thus allowing the `compute()` calls to remain and not actually compute anything.

The other way of connecting to Databricks remotely, via Sparklyr and Databricks-Connect, is also having its own fair share of issues at the moment, otherwise that would be the workaround I'd adopt.

title: Translation of as.Date in Oracle is not correct in version 2.4
description:
Hello,

In version 2.4 the translation of as.Date is not correct, I think the error is generated by the migration to `glue_sql2` https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/83045c593a69c0d981bad0051cf63be24e923c49/R/backend-oracle.R#L118

In the previous version the conversion of as.Date() was `DATE '2023-01-01'` and now it is `DATE 2023-01-01`, so the problem is that the quotes are missing from the value of the date. I think it would be fixed by adding the .val in the following way: `glue_sql2(sql_current_con(), "DATE {.val x}")`

Regards,

title: incorrect SQL generated when summarize called with no arguments in multi-step analytical pipe chain
description:
# Problem

Calling `summarize()` with no arguments breaks in the context of a multi-step chain requiring window functions.

# Reprexes

## Query Results

- *Expected behavior:* the results generated by the two grouped filter pipe chains should have the same rows, except that the first one will have the `n` column and the second one won't. 
- *Actual behavior:* the one that assigns `n` in `summarize` returns 7 rows and the one that doesn't returns 6.

```r
library(RSQLite)
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql

mtcars_db <- tbl_memdb(mtcars)

# start with this grouped summary
mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = 'drop')
#> # Source:   SQL [7 x 4]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#>     cyl    vs    am    n
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     4     0     1     1
#> 2     4     1     0     3
#> 3     4     1     1     7
#> 4     6     0     1     3
#> 5     6     1     0     4
#> 6     8     0     0    12
#> 7     8     0     1     2

# tack on a cyl grouped filter to the above - it does nothing, as expected
mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  filter(n() > 1)
#> # Source:   SQL [7 x 4]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#> # Groups:   cyl
#>     cyl    vs    am     n
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     4     0     1     1
#> 2     4     1     0     3
#> 3     4     1     1     7
#> 4     6     0     1     3
#> 5     6     1     0     4
#> 6     8     0     0    12
#> 7     8     0     1     2

# the last column `n` is irrelevant, so if we drop it we should still get the same 7 rows
# but we actually get 6
mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(.groups = 'drop') %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  filter(n() > 1)
#> # Source:   SQL [6 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 [:memory:]
#> # Groups:   cyl
#>     cyl    vs    am
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     4     1     0
#> 2     4     1     1
#> 3     6     0     1
#> 4     6     1     0
#> 5     8     0     0
#> 6     8     0     1
```

## show_query diagnostic

- In the first version of the grouped filter, `filter(n() > 1)` triggers the generation of ```COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY `cyl`)```, which is needed to do the grouped filter by `cyl`. 
- In the second version, the query generator doesn't realize it needs to do this. Instead it generates a `COUNT(*)` for the # of rows associated with each (cyl, vs, am) group, which we didn't ask for, and the WHERE clause uses that column.

```r
library(RSQLite)
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql

mtcars_db <- tbl_memdb(mtcars)

mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`, `n`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY `cyl`) AS `q01`
#>   FROM (
#>     SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`, COUNT(*) AS `n`
#>     FROM `mtcars`
#>     GROUP BY `cyl`, `vs`, `am`
#>   )
#> )
#> WHERE (`q01` > 1.0)

mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(.groups = 'drop') %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`, COUNT(*) AS `q01`
#>   FROM `mtcars`
#>   GROUP BY `cyl`, `vs`, `am`
#> )
#> WHERE (`q01` > 1.0)
```

## variant with n1 instead of n

Just in case it's helpful - the working code also works if we do `n1 = n()` instead of `n = n()` in the first summarize, which distinguishes it more clearly from the `n()` in the filter:

```r
library(RSQLite)
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql

mtcars_db <- tbl_memdb(mtcars)

mtcars_db %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs, am) %>%
  summarize(n1 = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`, `n1`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY `cyl`) AS `q01`
#>   FROM (
#>     SELECT `cyl`, `vs`, `am`, COUNT(*) AS `n1`
```

title: Use purrr::map function for bulk-saving data frames to database
description:
I have many data frames which I want to save into database. It works fine in manual way:

``` r
mydf <- tribble(
    ~col1, ~col2, ~col3,
    50, 500, 5000,
    1000, 2000, 3000
  )
  
  mydf2 <- tribble(
    ~col1, ~col2, ~col3,
    0, 1, 2,
    666, 777, 888
  ) 
  
  
  schema <- "test_schema"
  
  db_name <- dbplyr::in_schema(schema, "mydf")
  
  dplyr::copy_to(
    con,
    mydf,
    name = db_name,
    overwrite = T,
    temporary = F
  )


db_name <- dbplyr::in_schema(schema, "mydf2")
  
  dplyr::copy_to(
    con,
    mydf2,
    name = db_name,
    overwrite = T,
    temporary = F
  )
```

I created this function utilizing purrr::map() to automate the process:

``` r
myschema <- "test_schema"
  
df_list <- c("mydf", "mydf2")

  
  save_to_db <- function(df_to_save) {
    
    df_to_save <- get(df_to_save)

    db_name <- dbplyr::in_schema(myschema, deparse(substitute(df_to_save)))
    

    dplyr::copy_to(
      con,
      df_to_save,
```

title: compute fails with JDBC connections because it calls dbSendQuery instead of dbSendUpdate
description:
The [compute](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/collapse.tbl_sql.html) function throws an error when used with JDBC database connections. This happens because it uses `dbSendQuery` instead of `dbSendUpdate`, the appropriate method for data manipulation type SQL statements that don't return anything.

The commands below should provide everything you need to convince yourself of this. It's almost completely reproducible except you have to set up your own database and RJDBC connection. [This issue](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1359) has a method for doing that using docker.


```
# [not shown - set up your own RJDBC connection object]

library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

# test compute() ---------------------------------------------------------

tbl(con, sql('select 1'))  %>% compute()

Error in `dplyr::db_save_query()`:
! Can't save query to "dbplyr_001".
Caused by error in `dbSendQuery()`:
! Unable to retrieve JDBC result set
  JDBC ERROR: [Vertica][JDBC](11300) A ResultSet was expected but not generated from query "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE 
"dbplyr_001" AS
SELECT *
FROM (select 1) "q01"
". Query not executed. 
  Statement: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE 
"dbplyr_001" AS
SELECT *
FROM (select 1) "q01"
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

# test dbSendQuery() ---------------------------------------------------------
 
RJDBC::dbSendQuery(con, "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mytest as select 1")

Error in RJDBC::dbSendQuery(con, "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mytest as select 1") : 
  Unable to retrieve JDBC result set
  JDBC ERROR: [Vertica][JDBC](11300) A ResultSet was expected but not generated from query "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mytest as select 1". Query not executed. 
  Statement: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mytest as select 1

# test dbSendUpdate() - no error ---------------------------------------------------------

RJDBC::dbSendUpdate(con, "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mytest as select 1")

```


# Root Cause Analysis

I'm having some difficulty understanding what package(s) are responsible for the wrong method ultimately getting called. I think this is the key: we have this call chain

DBI::dbExecute -> DBI::dbSendStatement -> RJDBC::dbSendQuery

Which should instead be

DBI::dbExecute -> DBI::dbSendStatement -> RJDBC::dbSendUpdate

The [DBI documentation](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/dbsendstatement) says 

> dbSendStatement() comes with a default implementation that simply forwards to [dbSendQuery()](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/dbsendquery), to support backends that only implement the latter.

... and RJDBC does not implement `dbSendStatement`.

title: Generating temporary column (using window function) for filtering causes error in dbplyr 2.3.1
description:
Generating temporary column (using window function) for filtering causes error in dbplyr version 2.3.1.
Dbplyr version 2.3.0 does not have this issue.
Dbplyr version 2.3.1 changelog mentions a **breaking change** which does not seem applicable to this, given its description, but this could be a side-effect of fix for issue #1103.

Below reprex uses dbplyr version 2.3.0 where query is constructed without issues.

``` r
library(dplyr)
```

Below reprex also consists of an example with successful query construction which does not use the temporary column in it. For this case, the table alias and column alias are both `q01`. Wouldn't it interfere with understandability for someone reading the generated SQL? dbplyr version 2.3.0 uses `q01` to denote table alias and `q02` to denote column alias for the same example.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
```

title: MSSQL Incorrect Translation of Boolean and row_number while Filtering Zero Rows
description:
I'm trying to filter all rows from a table to handle certain edge cases where I want to pass a table forward for use in joins but just have it be empty if necessary. Typically, a `filter(FALSE)` is all that I need to do, but when connected to an MS SQL Server via `odbc` and the `freetds` driver, there's some translation hiccups that prevent the two most common patterns for this from happening. 

My guess is that, `TRUE` and `FALSE` are being incorrectly translated to numerics instead of booleans? And the `row_number()` translation could probably rely on some sort of sensible default windowing scheme

Reprex:
``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dbplyr))

df <- tibble(a = 1:10) 

db_rs <- tbl_lazy(df = df, con = simulate_redshift())
db_sq <- tbl_lazy(df = df, con = simulate_sqlite())
db_ms <- tbl_lazy(df = df, con = simulate_mssql())

# Successful in their respective DBs
db_rs %>% filter(FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (FALSE)
db_sq %>% filter(FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (0)

# Fails in Microsft SQL Server 
db_ms %>% filter(FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (0)
db_ms %>% filter(row_number() == -1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `a`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS `q01`
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
#> WHERE (`q01` = -1.0)

# Workarounds
db_ms %>% filter(row_number(a) == -1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `a`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT
#>     *,
#>     CASE
#> WHEN (NOT((`a` IS NULL))) THEN ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((`a` IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `a`)
#> END AS `q02`
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
#> WHERE (`q02` = -1.0)
db_ms %>% filter(1 != 1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (1.0 != 1.0)
```

title: Regression: migrating from build_sql() to glue_sql2() lost escaping
description:
# Problem summary
In https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/1228, most references to `build_sql()` where replaced with `glue_sql2()`.

This subtly broke some fundamental SQL translations, since `escape()` methods were no longer being applied.

# Reprex (using Snowflake as my motivating example)

## Previously:
```r
local_con(dbplyr::simulate_snowflake())
months = function(x) {
  build_sql("INTERVAL '", x, " month'")
}
months(1)
  <SQL> INTERVAL '1.0 month'
```

## current translation, which fails:
```r
months = function(x) {
  glue_sql2(sql_current_con(), "INTERVAL '{x} month'")
}
months(1)

Error in `.transformer()`:
! `value` must be a string or scalar SQL, not the number 1.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

# Solutions considered
1. [hacky] Manually add `escape(x)`  in applicable calls to `glue_sql2()` (e.g., #1350 to mitigate breaking Snowflake translations)
2. [robust] Migrate relevant `escape()` functionality from `build_sql()` to `gluesql2()` (https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/main/R/build-sql.R#L32-L44)

title: Feature Request: Some mechanism for partially evaluating functions
description:
A major feature of `dbplyr` is the ability to reuse code whether it is held in memory in R or remotely in SQL, so for example the `case_when` function can be used interchangeably:

```{r}
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "mtcars", mtcars)

mtcars_remote <- tbl(con, "mtcars")

mtcars %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = case_when(
      mpg <= 15 ~ "Bad",
      mpg >= 25 ~ "Good",
      .default = "Fine"
    )
  )
# same results
mtcars_remote %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = case_when(
      mpg <= 15 ~ "Bad",
      mpg >= 25 ~ "Good",
      .default = "Fine"
    )
  )
```
But if I want to encapsulate my own `case_when` statement into a function I lose interoperability

```{r}
my_case_when <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    x <= 15 ~ "Bad",
    x >= 25 ~ "Good",
    .default = "Fine"
  )
}
# still works
mtcars %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = my_case_when(mpg)
  )

# doesn't work because it tries to evaluate my function in SQL
mtcars_remote %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = my_case_when(mpg)
  )

# bang bang makes it evaluate in R, but now it's too eager because it wants to evaluate mpg in R too
mtcars_remote %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = !!my_case_when(mpg)
  )
```
Proposal: some sort of `sql_var` function that indicates to the bang bang to evaluate up to the point where the variable wrapped in `sql_var` needs to be evaluated and then pass evaluation onto SQL. 

```{r}
# hopefully an interface like this could work
mtcars_remote %>%
  mutate(
    mpg_bucket = !!my_case_when(sql_var(mpg))
  )
```

Maybe there's already a way to do this with `rlang` that I'm not aware of. In my work, we maintain a collection of complex `case_when` wrappers for translating ICD10 codes into different disease classifications, and being able to reuse that code with `dbplyr` would be really great.

title: na.rm = TRUE not respected in pmin/pmax for Snowflake
description:
As discussed in https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/118, the default translations for `pmin()` and `pmax()` are `LEAST` and `GREATEST`, respectively.

However, for Snowflake (akin to Oracle), [LEAST](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/least) and [GREATEST](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/greatest) do the following (in contrast to many other backends, discussed with Snowflake [here](https://community.snowflake.com/s/question/0D50Z00009LHFw1SAH/greatest-and-null-values) and a community-identified workaround [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74527418/how-to-use-greatest-in-snowflake-with-null-values)):
> If any of the argument values is NULL, the result is NULL.

Accordingly:
* when providing `na.rm = TRUE` to `pmin()` and `pmax()`, it's silently ignored currently (related to  https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/479)
* The [default, periodic messaging for na.rm = FALSE in check_na_rm()](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/5bae6a8acc8d79f338bbf73396a8002ad19b984e/R/translate-sql-helpers.R#L241-L254)) is not accurate.

I'd expect either:
1. [preferred] `na.rm = TRUE` is supported OR
1. [interim] `na.rm = TRUE` errors when called on Snowflake (and does not warn when `na.rm = FALSE`)

Illustrative Code (masking company Snowflake instance):
```r
conn_snowflake <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string = "<company>")
id_temp <- DBI::Id(schema = "TEST", table = "TEST")

test_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  a = c(1, NA, 3),
  b = c(NA, 2, 4)
)

dbplyr::copy_to(
  conn_snowflake,
  test_tbl,
  name = id_temp,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

tbl_sf <- conn_snowflake %>%
  tbl(id_temp)

# expected behavior: correctly ignores NA for `min()` / `max()`
tbl_sf %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    min_a = min(a, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_b = min(b, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_a = max(a, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_b = max(b, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Source:   SQL [1 x 2]
# Database: Snowflake 7.22.1[michael.thomson@Snowflake/TEST]
  min_a min_b max_a max_b
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     2     3     4

na_rm <- TRUE # toggle TRUE or FALSE

# unexpected behavior: both return NA for each na.rm = TRUE and FALSE
tbl_sf %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    pmin_a_b = pmin(a, b, na.rm = na_rm),
    pmax_a_b = pmax(a, b, na.rm = na_rm)
  )

# Source:   SQL [3 x 4]
# Database: Snowflake 7.22.1[michael.thomson@Snowflake/TEST]
      a     b pmin_a_b pmax_a_b
  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1     1    NA       NA       NA
2     3     4        3        4
3    NA     2       NA       NA
```

title: rows_update truncates very long text (json) upon insertion
description:
I am working with a remote MySQL database trough dplyr / dbplyr. I stumbled upon a strange behaviour today that puzzles me.

I am inserting a very long text (JSON) into a column with Type LONGTEXT (which has enough space to store the string in the db)

I experienced truncation of the string to maximum 65535 characters (byte limit for e.g. TEXT columns) when using `dplyr::rows_update` . When using an alternative approach using DBI directly this truncation does not occur. 

My current naive thinking goes into the direction of the 'copy_to()' mechanisms. I saw in the source of `dbplyr` that the method `dbplyr::detect_col_types()` for class `DBIConnection` returns NULL. So if the new df is created in the remote DB with default col Types (e.g. TEXT vs LONGTEXT) this would explain this behaviour. https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/09cb67969634f25574d78fb45b20aa28de01a4c0/R/rows.R#L775

Am I trying to use dbplyr outside of its intended usage? If yes believe this should at least be documented / warned. 

This is the code i execute:
```
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)

# Establish the database connection
con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), Driver = "MySQL ODBC 8.0 ANSI Driver",
                 Server = "your_server", Database = "your_database",
                 User = "your_username", Password = "your_password",
                 timeout = 10)

# Create a sample data frame with long JSON data
json_data <- paste(rep('{"key":"', 100000), "a", rep('"}', 100000), collapse = "")
json_data <- paste0('{"data": "', json_data, '"}')

df <- data.frame(id = 1:3, json = rep(json_data, 3))

print(nchar(json_data))

# Create Table in remote database with name `temp_table` with a column `json` set to LONGTEXT
query <- "
  CREATE TABLE temp_table (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    json LONGTEXT
  )
"
dbExecute(con, query)

# Use dplyr to update the remote database table

tbl(con, "temp_table") %>%
  rows_update(df,by = c("id"), copy=TRUE, in_place = TRUE, unmatched='ignore')

resDplyr <- tbl(con,"temp_table") %>%
  dplyr::collect()

nchar(resDplyr$json[1])


# DBI method -----------------------------------------------------------------
update_statement <- "UPDATE temp_table SET json = ? WHERE id = ? "


# Iterate over the rows in the data frame and update the database
for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
  # Get the values for the current row
  json_data <- df$json[i]
  id <- df$id[i]
  
  # Execute the update statement with the current row values
  dbExecute(con, update_statement, list(json_data, id))
}

resDBI <- tbl(con,"temp_table") %>%
  dplyr::collect()

nchar(resDBI$json[1])

# Close the database connection
dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: Support `str_detect(strings, fixed(pattern))` for all DB backends
description:
`dbplyr` tries to create a subset of the tidyverse that will work on both database backends, and in-memory tibble backends. Unfortunately there are currently *no* string-matching functions in that subset, because certain backends (e.g. SQLite) don't support regex by default.

My proposal is therefore to support the "fixed strings" versions of common string matching functions, because (to my knowledge), all SQL backends support the `LIKE` operation.

The way I would envisage this working is:

```r
DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:") |>
    dplyr::tbl("table_name") |>
    dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(some_column, fixed("foo")))
```

This would translate to something like `SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE some_column LIKE %foo%`.

However, this would fail, because it requires full regex support:
```r
DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:") |>
    dplyr::tbl("table_name") |>
    dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(some_column, "foo"))
```

I imagine this could be implemented using an `sql_translator` input that provides an `str_detect` implementation that fails when the input pattern is anything other than `fixed`. In theory this could be extended to support `base::grep(fixed=TRUE)` and other similar functions.

title: FR: Nudge users via thin wrapper methods for tbl_lazy methods of names(), $
description:
Successor to #997, #1010.

That issue/PR was about defining a `names.tbl_lazy()` method that behaves more like what new users might expect out of running `names()` on a lazy table, namely that it returns the column names.

But as discussed (https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/1010#issuecomment-1322274125), this is a bit fraught because other basic R functions like `str()` induce some implicit requirements on consistency among `names()` and related operators like `$`, `[`, and `[[`, so we decided against creating such a method and instead forcing users to call `colnames()`.

Nevertheless, I think it's still helpful to nudge users in the right direction if they're using `names()` on a `tbl_lazy` object, since the value will be confusing and very few users will actually want the results.

The same can be said for `$` -- even if it doesn't return a column, I would guess that's what the vast majority of people who wind up using `$` on a `tbl_lazy` object will have intended.

We can improve the UX here by turning these methods into simple wrappers that nudge the user the first time they use `names()`, but then fall silent to get out of their hair, e.g. (rough sketch)

```r
names.tbl_lazy = function(x) {
  if (!cache$warned) { cache$warned <- TRUE; message("Did you mean colnames()?") }
  NextMethod("names")
}
```

title: Misinterpreted na.rm = TRUE argument when translated into SQL conditional function, if()
description:
Below is an example which demonstrates the use of na.rm = TRUE argument for pmin() function.
The arguments are translated incorrectly into SQL and the condition appear as "arg1 <= arg2 and ... and **argN-1 <= TRUE**".
Similar is the case with pmax() function.
The obvious workaround at this point is to substitute NA as something to get these functions work.

``` r

#> 
#> Attaching package: 'sparklyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter
library(dbplyr)

#> [1] 0

mpgs <- mpg %>% copy_to(sc, ., "mpg", ovewrite = TRUE)

mpgs_r <- mpgs %>% 
  mutate(
    myvar = pmin(
      case_when(cty > hwy ~ hwy, TRUE ~ as.integer(NA)),
```

title: Incorrect SQL translation for paste0 on bigquery
description:
paste0 translates to concat_ws on bigquery when it should translate to concat as far as I can tell. Here is my reprex.


``` r
library(bigrquery)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
bq_auth(path = Sys.getenv("BIGQUERY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON_PATH"))

cdm_schema <- Sys.getenv("BIGQUERY_CDM_SCHEMA")
schema <- Sys.getenv("BIGQUERY_SCRATCH_SCHEMA")

con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  bigrquery::bigquery(),
  project = Sys.getenv("BIGQUERY_PROJECT_ID"),
  dataset = schema
)

DBI::dbWriteTable(con, paste0(schema,".temp_table"), data.frame(a = "a", b = "b"), overwrite = TRUE)

dplyr::tbl(con, paste0(schema,".temp_table"))
#> Warning: <BigQueryConnection> uses an old dbplyr interface
#> ℹ Please install a newer version of the package or contact the maintainer
#> This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
#> # Source:   table<synpuf_110k_results.temp_table> [1 x 2]
#> # Database: BigQueryConnection
#>   b     a    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 b     a

dplyr::tbl(con, paste0(schema,".temp_table")) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(ab = paste0(a, b))
#> # Source:   SQL [1 x 3]
#> # Database: BigQueryConnection
#>   b     a     ab   
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1 b     a     ab

dplyr::tbl(con, paste0(schema,".temp_table")) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(ab = paste0(a, b)) %>%  dplyr::show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, CONCAT(`a`, `b`) AS `ab`
#> FROM `synpuf_110k_results.temp_table`

dplyr::tbl(con, paste0(schema,".temp_table")) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(ab = CONCAT(a, b))
#> # Source:   SQL [1 x 3]
#> # Database: BigQueryConnection
#>   b     a     ab   
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1 b     a     ab

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: `as.Date()` now throws an error (version 2.3.2) when querying a Teradata server.
description:
I had a previously running code to query a Teradata server that is no longer running after updating (dbplyr, R, and odbc).
The issue seems to be related to how `as.Date()` is being translated into SQL. Using `show_query()`, in the prior versions it came as CAST("X" AS DATE), now SELECT DATE "X" which throws an error when trying to pull the data.

I know it is related to the update because the code still runs on a VM running older versions and querying the same server.
The updates are: R 4.2 to 4.3, dplyr 1.0.10 to 1.1.2, dbplyr 2.2.1 to 2.3.2, odbc 1.3.3 to 1.3.4, and DBI is the same 1.1.3.

Below are comparison of the two queries.

```r
   library (dplyr)
   library (DBI)
   library (odbc)
   connection <- dbConnect(odbc(), "Teradata")

   tbl(connection, "Teradata_table") %>% 
   head() %>% 
   select(POSIXct_POSIXt_var) %>% 
   mutate(date_var= as.Date(POSIXct_POSIXt_var)) %>% 
   show_query()
```
The old version brings 
```
<SQL>
   SELECT "POSIXct_POSIXt_var", CAST("POSIXct_POSIXt_var" AS DATE) AS "date_var"
   FROM (
     SELECT TOP 6 *
     FROM "Teradata_table"
   ) "q01"
```
Now results in: 

```
 <SQL>
   SELECT TOP 6 "POSIXct_POSIXt_var", DATE "POSIXct_POSIXt_var" AS "date_var"
   FROM "Teradata_table"

```

The latter throws an error when trying to pull the data as such: 

```r
   tbl(connection, "Teradata_table") %>% 
   head() %>% 
   select(POSIXct_POSIXt_var) %>% 
   mutate(date_var = as.Date(POSIXct_POSIXt_var)) %>% 
   as_tibble()
```
Results in: 

> (-3706)Syntax error: expected something between the word 'POSIXct_POSIXt_var' and the 'AS' keyword.

While I had a good suggestion for a walk around on my [SO post](https://stackoverflow.com/q/76282760/13695652) by using `sql('CAST ("var" AS DATE)')` to replace `as.Date()`,  I feel this might need to be addressed here to retain `as.Date()` functionality for Teradata use. A more experience [user](https://stackoverflow.com/users/1082435/wibeasley) on SO suggested that the issue might be related to [this commit](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/commit/83045c593a69c0d981bad0051cf63be24e923c49#diff-c4f086980e5692d16e3337acd7bfefe3a9315135688133ee4f24ea2944ccba3bL113). I hope this helps.

title: joins fail on Oracle because of multiple quoting
description:
This is similar to #1091 
Although a fix was merged there, I still see the issue with current   dbplyr 2.3.1 using an Oracle backend with pool.

This describes the problem, but is not a strictly reprocible example (I don't know how to mock a oracle database).

```r
r$> con
<Pool> of OraConnection objects
  Objects checked out: 0
  Available in pool: 1
  Max size: Inf
  Valid: TRUE
```


```r
 tbl(con, dbplyr::in_schema("s", "df1")) %>%
        dplyr::inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("s", "df2")) ,
                          by = "x") %>% 
      dplyr::show_query()
```

Gives

```r
SELECT
  """s"".""df1"""."x" AS "x",
  "col2"
FROM ("s"."df1") """s"".""df1"""
INNER JOIN ("s"."df2") """s".""df2"""
  ON ("""s"".""df1"""."x" = """s"".""df2"""."x")
```

and fails with 

```
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error in `.oci.SendQuery()`:
! ORA-01741: illegal zero-length identifier
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

likekly because of the **multiple quotes** inserted. I don't know why or where they come from.


The proposed fix in #1091 using `x_as` and `y_as` works, but is ugly (in fact on `x_as` is needed):

```r
 tbl(con, dbplyr::in_schema("s", "df1")) %>%
        dplyr::inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("s", "df2")) ,
                          by = "x", x_as = "x", y_as = "y") %>% 
      dplyr::show_query()
```

```r
SELECT
  "x"."x" AS "x",
FROM ("s"."df1") "x"
INNER JOIN ("s"."df2") "y"
  ON ("x"."x" = "y"."x")
```

Downgrading `dbplyr` to `2.2.1` also fixes the issue (uses `LHS` and `RHS` as names), but is also ugly to fix versions.

```r
SELECT
  "x"."x" AS "x",
FROM ("s"."df1") "LHS"
INNER JOIN ("s"."df2") "RHS"
  ON ("LHS"."x" = "RHS"."x")
```

The [tests](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/1095/files#diff-e17acee6ea41d52e9c4f034ff34330261bbb194c818b6f3c60b3afd00b1b9c0c) are using SQLite, and work. So I assume it's a Oracle specific problem?

Any ideas what's going on or where / how to fix this?
I am not too deep in the dbplyr code-basis, I ssupect it's in the name creation....

title: Inline `filter()` in `semi/anti_join()`
description:
```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 2, b = 3)

semi_join(
  lf,
  lf2 %>% 
    filter(a == 1),
  by = "x"
)
```

Currently produces

```sql
SELECT *
FROM `df` AS `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM (
    SELECT *
    FROM `df`
    WHERE (`a` = 1.0)
  ) `RHS`
  WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
)
```

But could be

```sql
SELECT *
FROM `df` AS `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM
  FROM `df` AS `RHS`
  WHERE (`RHS`.`a` = 1.0) AND (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
)
```

title: Support `relationship` parameter in join verbs
description:
dplyr added a `relationship` parameter to join verbs in v1.1.1, which throws an error if provided to dbplyr.

The issue I am experiencing is for some unit tests that run across both local and lazy tables. dplyr throws a warning if there is a many-to-many relationship, which can be silenced by providing the `relationship` parameter, but this then causes the lazy table tests to fail.

I don't think dbplyr necessarily needs to support the check (would probably have to be an extra query to check if it is violated), but it would be good if it would accept the parameter.


title: query optimisation - distinct + count
description:
Hello, thanks for the package

these two queries produce the same result, however one takes 100x the other on Postres, MySQL and sqlite. Any chance the first slow query could be converted in the backend to the second?

## slow 688 seconds on postgres

```r
pg_tbl |>  
distinct(tissue, file_id) |>
 count(tissue) |> 
print() |> 
system.time()


   user  system elapsed 
  ..   ..   688.908 

```

explain

```r
<SQL>
SELECT `tissue`, COUNT(*) AS `n`
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT `tissue`, `file_id`
  FROM `metadata`
)
GROUP BY `tissue`

<PLAN>
  id parent notused                               detail
1  2      0       0              CO-ROUTINE (subquery-1)
2  6      2       0 SCAN metadata USING INDEX idx_tissue
3 16      2       0         USE TEMP B-TREE FOR DISTINCT
4 22      0       0                    SCAN (subquery-1)
5 25      0       0         USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY
```

## fast 3 seconds on postgres
```r
> pg_tbl |> 
group_by(tissue) |> 
summarise(unique_files = file_id |> distinct() |> count()) |> 
print() |>
 system.time()


   user  system elapsed 
  0.123   0.007   3.018
```
explain

```r
<SQL>
SELECT `tissue`, count(distinct(`file_id`)) AS `unique_files`
FROM `metadata`
GROUP BY `tissue`

<PLAN>
  id parent notused                               detail
1  7      0       0 SCAN metadata USING INDEX idx_tissue
2 38      0       0  USE TEMP B-TREE FOR count(DISTINCT)
```

title: slice_* function issue with data masking
description:
There is an issue when `slice_*` calls are translated to SQL when the `order_by` parameter uses `.data$` notation rather than a bare symbol name. The generated SQL erroneously prefixes .data to the order by clause, which causes the query to fail.

```r
# Expected behaviour (using local df)
mtcars %>%
  group_by(.data$cyl) %>%
  slice_max(.data$mpg)

# Returns 1 row per group, ordered by MPG

# Observed behaviour (fails)
rem_mtcars <- copy_to(connection, mtcars)
rem_mtcars %>%
  group_by(.data$cyl) %>%
  slice_max(.data$mpg)

# This works
rem_mtcars %>%
  group_by(.data$cyl) %>%
  slice_max(mpg)
```

An example of the generated SQL is

`
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY "cyl" ORDER BY ".data"."mpg" DESC)
`

The translation works fine when using `arrange`, it is only for the window functions I have observed the issue.

I've tested this with Redshift and SQLite with the same output.

title: Pass `DBI::Id()` to `DBI::dbWriteTable()`
description:
Extracted from #1099.

For odbc connections, dbplyr currently calls `dplyr::db_write_table` (effectively `DBI::dbWriteTable` / `odbc:::odbc_write_table`) with a plain string as the `name` argument (`dbplyr_003`, etc).  On backends with many schemas and tables, this leads to very bad performance (~15 minutes of hang for me), as iteration over all schemas and tables is needed to find a match (via `odbcConnectionColumns`).

When an `Id` is supplied as the `name` argument to `odbc::odbc_write_table` instead, its catalog, schema, and table names are [passed to `odbc::odbcConnectionColumns`, and ultimately `SQLColumns` on the driver](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/111cedfe2aacb1ca4f87016814fb7d295f7dfb3f/R/Connection.R#L145), enabling much faster execution.

I think it's important, then, that an `Id` encapsulating the schema and table names is passed to `db_write_table` in `db_copy_to.DBIConnection`.

title: Improve on how to create table identifiers
description:
Overall, they severely lack vector properties

* the class is lost when subsetting

``` r
ident("a", "b")[1]
#> [1] "a"
```

* combining changes the class to sql and quotes with backticks

``` r
c(ident("a"), ident_q("b"))
#> <SQL> `a`
#> <SQL> b
```

* `in_schema()` and `in_catalog()` can be coerced to a length 2 resp. 3 character which already caused a couple of issues

``` r
paste0("Can't write to table: ", in_schema("schema", "table"))
#> [1] "Can't write to table: schema" "Can't write to table: table"
paste0("Can't write to table: ", in_catalog("catalog", "schema", "table"))
#> [1] "Can't write to table: schema"  "Can't write to table: table"  
#> [3] "Can't write to table: catalog"
```

* wrapping doesn't work nicely. It simply quotes (and always uses backticks as quotes) and it isn't idempotent e.g. 

``` r
ident(ident(ident("a")))
#> <IDENT> ```a```
```


Then there is `as.sql()` which is used to:

* escape a table name, e.g. `as.sql(table, con = con)` (this is the most common use)
* in `in_schema()` and `in_catalog()`
* in `win_over()` to prepare `partition` and `order`. This doesn't even feel like the right use.

Overall, the handling of table identifiers is too fiddly and difficult to get right which caused a couple of issues like repeated quoting or issues with incorrect handling of `in_schema()` or `in_catalog()`.
The table identifiers should be build upon vctrs and the issues above be fixed this way.

Open questions:

* Is it necessary to accept arbitrary SQL?
* Is support for quoted identifiers needed? And how exactly? Can e.g. the schema be quoted and the table not? Or should it be possible to pass in a fully qualified name `schema.table`?


Challenges:

* Combining e.g. `in_schema()` and `ident()` doesn't make much sense with the current class system. It would make more sense to have a single class for table identifiers instead. This would obviously be a big breaking change.
* A common class should be build upon record objects. Unfortunately, they don't support names so a workaround is needed.

title: Query text not deterministic
description:
Hi,

this is similar to issue #336.
In my case the column naming seems to be non-deterministic. When issuing `show_query()` for the first time after loading the dbplyr package the result is different than all the followup usages of `show_query()`. All the subsequent uses will result in the same query text though.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

table <- tbl_lazy(tibble(col1 = c(1,2), col2 = c(1,2)), dbplyr::simulate_hana())

# q1
table %>%
  select(col1) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = col2, by = col1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `col1`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT `col1`, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY `col1` ORDER BY `col2` DESC) AS `q01`
#>                                                                             ^^^
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
#> WHERE (`q01` <= 1)

# q2
table %>%
  select(col1) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = col2, by = col1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `col1`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT `col1`, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY `col1` ORDER BY `col2` DESC) AS `q02`
#>                                                                             ^^^
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
#> WHERE (`q02` <= 1)

# q2 - result stabilizes
table %>%
  select(col1) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = col2, by = col1)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `col1`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT `col1`, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY `col1` ORDER BY `col2` DESC) AS `q02`
#>                                                                             ^^^
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
#> WHERE (`q02` <= 1)
```

title: rows_insert requires that for each row, the value in each column must be different from everything else in that column
description:
Either I'm misunderstanding the documentation or there's a bug in ```rows_insert()```. If the former (much more likely), I'm happy to try to patch the documentation.

The [docs for rows_insert()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/rows.html) say (from dplyr), "```rows_insert()``` adds new rows (like ```INSERT```). By default, key values in ```y``` must not exist in ```x```." Does this mean that in any table, for each row, the value in each column must be different from everything else in that column? Surely that isn't right, yet it seems to be the case:

```r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
  library(DBI)
})

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())

# Create database with one table and three columns: id, fruit, colour
create_db <- "CREATE TABLE fruits(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, fruit TEXT, colour TEXT)" |> as.sql(con)
DBI::dbExecute(con, create_db)
#> [1] 0

fruits <- tbl(con, "fruits")

# Apples can be red
red_apple <- tibble(fruit = "apple", colour = "red")

# Insert into the database; primary key autoincrements and id will be assigned
rows_insert(fruits, red_apple, copy = TRUE, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
#> Matching, by = "fruit"

fruits
#> # Source:   table<fruits> [1 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 []
#>      id fruit colour
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 apple red

# Apples can also be green
green_apple <- tibble(fruit = "apple", colour = "green")

# This new row should be added to the database
rows_insert(fruits, green_apple, copy = TRUE, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
#> Matching, by = "fruit"

# But it isn't!
fruits
#> # Source:   table<fruits> [1 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 []
#>      id fruit colour
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 apple red

# To be added both values must be different from anything in the table
lemon <- tibble(fruit = "lemon", colour = "yellow")
rows_insert(fruits, lemon, copy = TRUE, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
fruits
#> # Source:   table<fruits> [2 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.41.2 []
#>      id fruit colour
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 apple red
#> 2     2 lemon yellow

```

title: MSSQL Incorrect Translation of between() when not used in filter context
description:
Hey there, stumbling into some more issues related to SQL translations w/ booleans in MSSQL. In this case, the translation for `dplyr::between()` is the same in both a `mutate`/`summarize` context (which doesn't work) and in a `filter` context (which does). 

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dbplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(lubridate))

lf <-
    lazy_frame(tibble(
        a = 1:10,
        b = 2
    ),
    con = simulate_mssql())

# Succeeds (stock translation)
lf %>% filter(between(x = a, left = b, right = 5))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (`a` BETWEEN `b` AND 5.0)

# Fails (stock translation)
lf %>% mutate(c = between(x = a, left = b, right = 5))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, `a` BETWEEN `b` AND 5.0 AS `c`
#> FROM `df`

# Succeeds (possible new translation)
lf %>% mutate(c = case_when(between(
    x = a, left = b, right = 3
) ~ TRUE, .default = FALSE))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, CASE WHEN (`a` BETWEEN `b` AND 3.0) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS `c`
#> FROM `df`

# Succeeds (possible new translation)
lf %>% mutate(c = if_else(condition = between(
    x = a, left = b, right = 3
), true = TRUE, false = FALSE))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, IIF(`a` BETWEEN `b` AND 3.0, 1, 0) AS `c`
#> FROM `df`
```

title: MariaDB doesn't support `RETURNING` in update queries
description:

As per the MariaDB documentation, "RETURNING" can only be used in INSERT, REPLACE and DELETE queries.

title: Bug in sql_query_upsert for oracle backend
description:
I'm not sure if i'm just oblivious to something here but the SQL generated by sql_query_upsert for an Oracle connection seems to have a bug in it. It's referencing a table called 'excluded' which doesn't seem to be invloved in anything. It also failed to wrap the ON clause in parenthesis which I think is required by oracle.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql

dbplyr::sql_query_upsert( con = simulate_oracle(),
                          table = ident("t1"),
                          from = ident("t2"),
                          by = c("a"),
                          update_cols = c("b")
)
#> <SQL> MERGE INTO `t1`
#> USING `t2` AS `...y`
#>   ON `...y`.`a` = `t1`.`a`
#> WHEN MATCHED THEN
#>   UPDATE SET `b` = `excluded`.`b`
#> WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN hi tim
#>   INSERT (`a`, `b`)
#>   VALUES (`...y`.`a`, `...y`.`b`)
#> ;
```

<sup>Created on 2023-05-22 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I've found that the following changes to the sql_query_upsert.Oracle function in  backend-oracle.R resolve the issue:

```  # https://oracle-base.com/articles/9i/merge-statement
  parts <- rows_prep(con, table, from, by, lvl = 0)
  update_cols_esc <- sql(sql_escape_ident(con, update_cols))
  #update_values <- sql_table_prefix(con, update_cols, ident("excluded"))
  update_values <- sql_table_prefix(con, update_cols, from)
  update_clause <- sql(paste0(update_cols_esc, " = ", update_values))

  insert_cols <- c(by, update_cols)
  insert_cols_esc <- escape(ident(insert_cols), parens = FALSE, con = con)
  insert_values <- sql_table_prefix(con, insert_cols, ident("...y"))

  clauses <- list(
    sql_clause("MERGE INTO", table),
    sql_clause("USING", parts$from),
    #sql_clause_on(parts$where, lvl = 1),
    sql_clause("ON", parts$where, sep = " AND", lvl = 1, parens = TRUE),
    sql("WHEN MATCHED THEN"),
    sql_clause("UPDATE SET", update_clause, lvl = 1),
    sql("WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN"),
    sql_clause_insert(con, insert_cols_esc, lvl = 1),
    sql_clause("VALUES", insert_values, parens = TRUE, lvl = 1),
    sql_returning_cols(con, returning_cols, table),
    sql(";")
  )
```

title: `remote_name()` for `in_schema()` etc
description:
The documentation says

> `remote_name()` gives the name remote table, or `NULL` if it's a query

But what exactly is meant by "name" when a table is specified via `in_schema()`, `in_catalog()` or `DBI::Id()`?

At the moment `remote_name()` returns these objects as they are. But from the name I'd rather expect to get a string.

I think:

* `remote_name()` should simply return the name of a table, e.g. for `in_schema("my schema", "my table")` it should return `"my table"`. If the table was created via `ident_q()` or `sql()` it returns `NULL`
* we add another function `remote_table()` that returns a table identifier e.g. for `in_schema("my schema", "my table")` it should return `in_schema("my schema", "my table")`. If the table was created via `ident_q()` or `sql()` it should return them as they are.

title: MSSQL Incorrect Translation for !is.na()
description:
When using `!is.na()` in any context while submitting queries to my MSSQL Server, my ODBC driver isn't happy about a syntax error. It appears using the `~` in the query creates an issue, where the most appropriate translation for `!is.na(x)` should probably be `x IS NOT NULL`. 

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dbplyr))

lf <- lazy_frame(tibble(a = 1:10, b = 2), con = simulate_mssql())

# Fails
lf %>% mutate(c = !is.na(a))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, CAST(IIF(~(`a` IS NULL), 1, 0) AS BIT) AS `c`
#> FROM `df`

# Succeeds
lf %>% mutate(c = is.na(a))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, CAST(IIF((`a` IS NULL), 1, 0) AS BIT) AS `c`
#> FROM `df`

# Succeeds
lf %>% mutate(c = sql('CAST(IIF((`a` IS NOT NULL), 1, 0) AS BIT)'))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, CAST(IIF((`a` IS NOT NULL), 1, 0) AS BIT) AS `c`
#> FROM `df`
```

<sup>Created on 2023-04-07 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Specifically, the error is:
```
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error:
! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1752: 00000: [FreeTDS][SQL Server]Statement(s) could not be prepared.  [FreeTDS][SQL Server]Incorrect syntax near 'q01'.  [FreeTDS][SQL Server]Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'IS'. 
<SQL> 'SELECT TOP 11 *, CAST(IIF(~("a" IS NULL), 1, 0) AS BIT) AS "c"
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM "#dbplyr_005"
) "q01"'
```

but when substituting with raw SQL like above, things work as expected.

I'm not sure if this is an indicator of a broader issue with how the MSSQL implementation expects to apply the "not operator" to non-existent boolean types using "bits" (MSSQL Server doesn't support booleans, which is a facepalm), but I was definitely having issues trying to invert a `TRUE` or `1` value in any way using `!` via dbplyr.

title: Prefix `*` with table alias
description:
As described in https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/908 for Oracle and https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/966 for Teradata, specifying new columns after SELECT * is not possible with [Exasol-Database](https://github.com/exasol) neither. Most likely there are other RDBMS that do not support this.

I like the use of star instead of repeating every columnname, it's very convenient and makes it easier to inspect the generated SQL-query.  IMHO adding the alias as a prefix to the star would be a more generic solution to these problems:

Following dplyr-pipe
```
tbl(db, "my_table") %>%
  mutate(
    new_col = "any_value"
  ) %>% show_query()

```
sould translate to:
```
<SQL>
SELECT "t1".*, 'any_value' AS new_col
FROM "my_table" as "t1"
```
Of course, every derived table e.g.  `select "sub1".* from (select * from "my_table") "sub1"` has to be declared with an alias too.
Would it be possible to prefix every star with an table alias?

Thanks!

title: Is there a way to render_sql with schema
description:
I'm using Sybase, which I know there isn't a back end for.  I've gotten pretty far just connecting with JDBC.  But one of the issues I'm working through right now is that Sybase really seems to want you to call tables including the schema name.  `dbplyr::render_sql` strips those out, even if the original object I started with was created using the `dbplyr::in_schema` method.

Is there an option that can be specified somewhere to force `dbplyr` to hang onto the schema I specified at the beginning?  Or if that isn't possible, just to force it to render with a default schema I specify?
