title: Name collision in `compute(temporary = FALSE)`
description:
By default, calling `compute` creates a table with name "dbplyr_n". Although temporary tables are isolated between sessions, if a user calls temporary = FALSE without explicitly setting a name, then the table is persisted using the dbplyr_ name. Other users using dbplyr on the same database can then experience collisions when calling `compute` as the generated table name already exists. Best practice would be to avoid persisting these temp tables without specifying a name, but it can happen.

Possible solutions:
1. Allow user to set an option to replace the default "dbplyr_" prefix with something unique to them
2. Don't allow user to set temporary = FALSE without specifying a table name
3. Check if generated table name exists before trying to create it, and create another one if not
4. Use a suffix of random letters instead of sequential numbers

Option 1 relies on the user to set the option, and they could still potentially collide with their own tables.
Option 2 should stop the problem at the root, but would be a breaking change.
Option 3 is undesirable IMO due to extra call to DB, and theoretically could result in many calls if all generated names were taken.
Option 4 would be a reasonable solution and miniscule probability of collisions

title: Translate nzchar()
description:
I think `nzchar()` has an ANSI representation as `x <> ""`.

We could also be more precise and take `keepNA` into account:

 - `nzchar(x, keepNA = TRUE)` ➡️  `x <> ""`
 - `nzchar(x, keepNA = FALSE)` ➡️  `(x IS NULL OR x <> "")`

```
! Can't copy to table "dbplyr_003"
Caused by error in `dplyr::db_write_table()` at dbplyr/R/db-io.R:56:8:
! Can't write table "dbplyr_003".
Caused by error in `new_result()`:
! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1594: 00000: Cannot perform CREATE TEMPTABLE. This session does not have a current schema. Call 'USE SCHEMA', or use a qualified name.
```

**Thoughts**
The call to `copy_to` enabling `copy = TRUE` passes a `unique_table_name` and the connection object:
```
# verb-copy-to.R:94
auto_copy.tbl_sql <- function(x, y, copy = FALSE, ...) {
  copy_to(x$src, as.data.frame(y), unique_table_name(), ...)
}
```
I imagine it would be safe to use the same schema where `x` is stored as the destination for `y`.  Could we extract the schema name from `y` here and update the third argument as `in_schema(schema_name, unique_table_name())`?  This raises a related question about the best way to extract a schema name from a lazy tbl; I've been taking an inelegant approach by inspecting `some_tbl$[ops | lazy_query]$x[$x[$x ...]]]` but there's likely something I'm missing.

**Further**
For odbc connections, dbplyr currently calls `dplyr::db_write_table` (effectively `DBI::dbWriteTable` / `odbc:::odbc_write_table`) with a plain string as the `name` argument (`dbplyr_003`, etc).  On backends with many schemas and tables, this leads to very bad performance (~15 minutes of hang for me), as iteration over all schemas and tables is needed to find a match (via `odbcConnectionColumns`).

When an `Id` is supplied as the `name` argument to `odbc::odbc_write_table` instead, its catalog, schema, and table names are [passed to `odbc::odbcConnectionColumns`, and ultimately `SQLColumns` on the driver](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/111cedfe2aacb1ca4f87016814fb7d295f7dfb3f/R/Connection.R#L145), enabling much faster execution.

I think it's important, then, that an `Id` encapsulating the schema and table names is passed to `db_write_table` in `db_copy_to.DBIConnection`.

---
dbplyr version: current `main` (`861b08fc4b538822299fb8cb414a98a6b066ad0d`)
R version: 4.2.2

title: "ambiguous column name" SQL translation error in development version
description:
With the development version of `dbplyr`, I'm getting an "ambiguous column name" error with `full_join` (but not `left_join`) when the two tables have at least one column name in common that contains at least one capital letter and is not a `join_by` column. This error does not occur with the current CRAN version (dbplyr 2.3.2). A full reproducible example is below, but first, here are the SQL translations with the development version and the current CRAN version, so you can see how they differ.

#### SQL translation with development version (dbplyr@505ca70):
```sql
SELECT
  COALESCE(`d1`.`KEY1`, `d2`.`KEY1`) AS `KEY1`,
  COALESCE(`d1`.`KEY2`, `d2`.`KEY2`) AS `KEY2`,
  `VAR` AS `VAR.x`,
  `vAr0` AS `vAr0.x`,
  `d1`.`var1` AS `var1.x`,
  `var2`,
  `VAR` AS `VAR.y`,
  `vAr0` AS `vAr0.y`,
  `d2`.`var1` AS `var1.y`,
  `var3`
FROM `d1`
FULL JOIN `d2`
  ON (`d1`.`KEY1` = `d2`.`KEY1` AND `d1`.`KEY2` = `d2`.`KEY2`)
```

#### SQL translation with version 2.3.2:
```sql
SELECT
  COALESCE(`d1`.`KEY1`, `d2`.`KEY1`) AS `KEY1`,
  COALESCE(`d1`.`KEY2`, `d2`.`KEY2`) AS `KEY2`,
  `d1`.`VAR` AS `VAR.x`,
  `d1`.`vAr0` AS `vAr0.x`,
  `d1`.`var1` AS `var1.x`,
  `var2`,
  `d2`.`VAR` AS `VAR.y`,
  `d2`.`vAr0` AS `vAr0.y`,
  `d2`.`var1` AS `var1.y`,
  `var3`
FROM `d1`
FULL JOIN `d2`
  ON (`d1`.`KEY1` = `d2`.`KEY1` AND `d1`.`KEY2` = `d2`.`KEY2`)
```

#### Reproducible example
``` r
library(tidyverse)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = ":memory:")

set.seed(3)
d1 = tibble(
  KEY1 = c("A","A","B","B"),
  KEY2 = c(10, 11, 10, 11),
  VAR = c(1,2,1,2),
  vAr0 = rnorm(4),
  var1 = rnorm(4),
  var2 = rnorm(4)
)

d2 = tibble(
  KEY1 = c("A","A","B","B"),
  KEY2 = c(10, 11, 10, 11),
  VAR = c(1,2,1,3),
  vAr0 = rnorm(4),
  var1 = rnorm(4),
  var3 = rnorm(4)
)

copy_to(con, d1, "d1", temporary = FALSE, overwrite=TRUE)
copy_to(con, d2, "d2", temporary = FALSE, overwrite=TRUE)

# Join works with local data frames
full_join(d1, d2, by=c("KEY1","KEY2"))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 10
#>   KEY1   KEY2 VAR.x vAr0.x var1.x   var2 VAR.y vAr0.y var1.y   var3
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 A        10     1 -0.962 0.196  -1.22      1 -0.716 -0.953 -0.578
#> 2 A        11     2 -0.293 0.0301  1.27      2  0.253 -0.648 -0.942
#> 3 B        10     1  0.259 0.0854 -0.745     1  0.152  1.22  -0.204
#> 4 B        11     2 -1.15  1.12   -1.13      3 -0.308  0.200 -1.67

# Database query fails if any shared non-join_by column names have a capital letter
full_join(tbl(con, "d1"), tbl(con, "d2"), by=c("KEY1","KEY2"))
```

title: `if_any` needs surrounding parentheses
description:
When using `if_any` with dbplyr, logic inconsistent with dplyr is noted when the result is used as an operand in a larger expression.  This behavior can be addressed by surrounding the produced SQL with parentheses.

Consider:
``` r
dbplyr::tbl_lazy(starwars, dbplyr::simulate_odbc()) %>% 
  filter(
    if_any(matches('color'), ~. == 'brown') & species == 'Human'
    )
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> WHERE (`hair_color` = 'brown' OR `skin_color` = 'brown' OR `eye_color` = 'brown' AND `species` = 'Human')
```

Because `if_any` renders _inline_ to a chain of `X OR Y OR Z ...`, and because `AND` has higher precedence compared to `OR` (in all dialects I could identify), the backend evaluation of `WHERE` is equivalent to
```
#> WHERE (`hair_color` = 'brown' OR `skin_color` = 'brown' OR (`eye_color` = 'brown' AND `species` = 'Human'))
```
when in fact we need
```
#> WHERE ((`hair_color` = 'brown' OR `skin_color` = 'brown' OR `eye_color` = 'brown') AND `species` = 'Human')
```

Surrounding the SQL representation of `if_any` in parentheses in _all_ contexts would fix this issue at the expense of an occasionally unneeded pair of braces.  I believe this would be much easier than intelligently adding them when needed.

dbplyr version 2.3.0

title: `pivot_wider` handles NAs inconsistently with `tidyr`
description:
When there are NA's in the `names_from` variable `dbplyr` translates `pivot_wider` inconsistently.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(tidyr)

### need to setup your own SQL Server connection
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
x <- tibble(
  id = "id",
  x = 1:3,
  y = c("A", NA, "B")
)
copy_to(con, x, overwrite = T)
x2 <- tbl(con, "x")

# NA's work properly in-memory this returns 2
x %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = x) %>%
  pull(`NA`)

# with dbplyr this returns NA
x2 %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = x) %>%
  pull(`NA`)
```

title: Using `dplyr::dense_rank` without attaching `dplyr` causes the function replacement to fail
description:
Here is a strange edge case. Under the following conditions, `dplyr::dense_rank` is *not* converted to a `DENSE_RANK()` SQL function:
* `dplyr::dense_rank()` is inside a `dplyr::across()`
* `dplyr` is not attached via `library`
* The function is called via the namespace: `dplyr::dense_rank`

Here are some examples. Firstly, the failure case. Note how `vec_rank` (which is a `dplyr`, and not an SQL function) is used:
```r
> dbplyr::lazy_frame(a=5:1, b=1:5) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), dplyr::dense_rank)) |> dplyr::show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT
  vec_rank(`a`, 'dense' AS `ties`, 'na' AS `incomplete`) AS `a`,
  vec_rank(`b`, 'dense' AS `ties`, 'na' AS `incomplete`) AS `b`
FROM `df`
Warning messages:
1: Named arguments ignored for SQL vec_rank
2: Named arguments ignored for SQL vec_rank
```

However, if we simply remove the `dplyr::` namespace, it works fine:
```R
> dbplyr::lazy_frame(a=5:1, b=1:5) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), dense_rank)) |> dplyr::show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((`a` IS NULL))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((`a` IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `a`)
END AS `a`,
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((`b` IS NULL))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((`b` IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `b`)
END AS `b`
FROM `df`
```

Also, if we don't use `across()`:
```R
> dbplyr::lazy_frame(a=5:1, b=1:5) |> dplyr::mutate(a = dplyr::dense_rank(a)) |> dplyr::show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((`a` IS NULL))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((`a` IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `a`)
END AS `a`,
  `b`
FROM `df`
```

title: Add support for ntile() with window_order()
description:
This request is similar to #169. It seems that `dbplyr` will translate `ntile` when given a value for `order_by`, but not with `window_order()`. This seems to be a documentation issue, as many window functions are translated nicely with `window_order()`.

Ideally one could also do this:

```r
earthquakes %>%
  select(place, mag) %>%
  group_by(place) %>%
  window_order(mag) %>%
  mutate(ntile = ntile(4))
```

But only this form seems to work:

```r
earthquakes %>%
  select(place, mag) %>%
  group_by(place) %>%
  mutate(ntile = ntile(4, order_by = "mag"))
```

Note that there is a slight difference between `dplyr::ntile()` and `ntile()` in `dbplyr`.
The former is `ntile(x = row_number(), n)`, whereas the latter requires the `order_by` argument. 
The `dplyr` version of the above is something like:

```r
earthquakes %>%
  select(place, mag) %>%
  collect() %>%
  group_by(place) %>%
  arrange(mag) %>%              # No `window_order()` in dplyr; see #627
  mutate(ntile = ntile(n = 4))  # No order_by in dplyr version.
```

(Note that #627 was closed.)

This is a feature request and seems clear enough, so I have not included a reprex, but could do so if this helped.

As an aside, the "ideal" code above produces the error message below. Perhaps a clearer error message would be an alternative.

```
Error in `purrr::pmap()`:
ℹ In index: 3.
ℹ With name: ntile.
Caused by error in `UseMethod()`:
! no applicable method for 'as.sql' applied to an object of class "c('double', 'numeric')"
Backtrace:
  1. base (local) `<fn>`(x)
 30. dbplyr (local) ntile(4)
 31. dbplyr::win_over(...)
 32. dbplyr::as.sql(order, con = con)
```

title: Fix interface of `ntile()`
description: Somehow `ntile()` is defined as `ntile = function(order_by, n)` in the dbplyr backend instead of `ntile(x = row_number(), n)` like in dplyr.

title: Alias T for TRUE in case_when() not honored inside across()
description:
Alias T for logical value TRUE is no longer honored inside across function.
This alias works fine with other constructs.

Below is a reprex to exemplify the same.
- mpgspark is the spark table for mpg data as shown below.
- Running a simple transformation using dplyr across function on mpg works absolutely fine.
- Generating SQL query for the same transformation on mpgspark shows that alias T is interpreted as a column instead of logical value TRUE
- Execution of the same query on mpgspark results in a column not found error
- Execution of the same transformation on mpgspark using a construct other than across function works fine.

title: dplyr to SQL error
description:
I get incorrect SQL-code from dplyr tbl()-function.
Code that was working last year is no longer working (not sure what version of dplyr it was then but now I'm on v. 1.1.0).
What I'm trying to do is to connect to a database and join several tables of which some have to be handled as subquerys to get the right data. 
The database is in Microsoft SQL Server, and I'm using a odbc connection via the `DBI` and `odbc` package but these are not necessary for the reprex below where I use the `tbl_lazy()` method to simulate a dabase.

---

dplyr converts the code below to several SQL-querys that gets their own alias like '...1', '...2' and so on and refer to these for the joins. 
This is where something seems to goes wrong. In the generated SQL-code it is trying to connect the wrong tables; trying to connect a table later in piped the code with a table early in the piped code that doesn't have that key in it instead of connecting via a table in the middle that has the keys of both the earlier table and the later ones.

In the reprex below (**which only generates the faulty sql-code, not giving an error itself**) 'df3' will be aliased as '...3' and '...4' since it is being joined in twice.
'df4' which is the first table that includes the 'cID' is aliased as '...5'
'df5' and 'df6' should be joined via 'cID' to the '...5' subquery but it's trying to join it to the '...3' subquery like this: "ON (`...3`.`cID` = `...6`.`cID`)". There is no '...3.cID'.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

df1 <- data.frame(aID = c(1,2,3), year = c(1,1,2))
df2 <- data.frame(aID = c(1,2,3), bID = c(4,5,6))
df3 <- data.frame(bID = c(4,4,5,5,6,6), key = c(1,2,1,2,1,2), value = c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6"))
df4 <- data.frame(bID = c(4,5,6), cID = c(7,8,9))
df5 <- data.frame(cID = c(7,7,8,8,9,9), key = c(1,2,1,2,1,2), value = c("y1", "y2", "y3", "y4", "y5", "y6"))
df6 <- data.frame(cID = c(7,8,9), a_value = c("z1", "z2", "z3"))


tbl_lazy(df1, con = simulate_mssql()) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df2, con = simulate_mssql())) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df3, con = simulate_mssql()) %>% 
               filter(key == 1) %>% 
               select(bID,
                      variable1 = value)) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df3, con = simulate_mssql()) %>% 
               filter(key == 2) %>% 
               select(bID,
                      variable2 = value)) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df4, con = simulate_mssql())) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df5, con = simulate_mssql()) %>% 
               filter(key == 1) %>% 
               select(cID, variable3 = value)) %>% 
  inner_join(tbl_lazy(df6, con = simulate_mssql()))
```

title: fill() does not work for Presto
description:
Similar to #651, Presto/Trino expects `IGNORE NULLS` to be outside the closing parenthesis of the window function, e.g., `LAST_VALUE()`. Currently `fill()` throws an error like

```r
conn <- dbConnect(Presto(), catalog = "foo", schema = "default", user = "bar")
my_tbl <- tbl(conn, "my_tbl")
my_tbl |>
  window_order(x) |>
  fill(y)
#> Error in stop.with.error.message(content) : 
#>  Query abc123 failed: line 5:6: mismatched input 'IGNORE'. Expecting: ')', ',', 'ORDER'
```

A similar solution to #651 works here, too (with RPresto providing the driver).

```r
last_value_sql.PrestoConnection <- function(con, x) {
  build_sql("LAST_VALUE(", ident(as.character(x)), ") IGNORE NULLS", con = con)
}
```

Happy to submit a PR if helpful.

title: fill() does not work with Databricks ODBC driver
description:
This is similar to https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/651 and https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/1026, but for Databricks the server expects:

`LAST_VALUE(expr, true)`

instead of

`LAST_VALUE(expr) IGNORE NULLS`

The `true` there means _"yes, ignore nulls"_: https://docs.databricks.com/sql/language-manual/functions/last_value.html

I was able to make it work by running this prior to `fill()`:

```
`last_value_sql.Spark SQL` <- function(con, x) {
  dbplyr:::build_sql("LAST_VALUE(", ident(as.character(x)), ", true)", con = con)
}
```

Thanks to all involved for the awesome resource that is `dbplyr`.

title: Support `na_rm` argument for `nth()`, `first()`, and `last()`
Teradata distinct
description:
We are currently running Teradata 16.20.5329 so this issue may have been fixed for different versions, but thought I would bring it up.

x %>% distinct() works when simulating a teradata connection, sql_render, and show_query, however it tries to use TOP 11 when it is run in an actual teradata session. The tdplyr package from teradata overwrites the sql_query_select and the sql_clause but the code returns the same values in either package.
``` r
dsnName <- "tera_hc"
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql
library(tdplyr)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'tdplyr':
#>   method                     from  
#>   sql_query_select.Teradata  dbplyr
#>   sql_table_analyze.Teradata dbplyr
#>   sql_translation.Teradata   dbplyr

con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsnName, timeout = 10)

x <- data.frame(x = 1)
x_test <- x %>% copy_to(con, ., "x_test", temporary = TRUE)
x_test %>% distinct() %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT *
#> FROM "x_test"
x_test %>% distinct() %>% sql_render()
#> <SQL> SELECT DISTINCT *
#> FROM "x_test"
x_test %>% distinct()
#> Error: nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1655: HY000: [Teradata][ODBC Teradata Driver][Teradata Database](-6916)TOP N Syntax error: Top N option is not supported with DISTINCT option. 
#> <SQL> 'SELECT DISTINCT TOP 11 *
#> FROM "x_test"'
```
The issue seems to arise from the fact that the sql_clause_select statement always thinks that there is a value for top, so it always inserts the "TOP 11" statement, even though you cannot both have DISTINCT and TOP in the same teradata statement. The easiest fix I have found is to create a new sql_clause_select for Teradata and to add to the (!is.null(top)) a second statement of !distinct, which pulls out the TOP line. 

The easiest way for this to work would be to have sql_clause_select be a generic, and have teradata have its own class, but this might be overkill. Also if no one else has had this problem, it may just be our teradata version.

title: Allow extracting connections from `tbl_sql` objects
description:
Let's say we have a factory that creates database-backed data frames:

```r
make_tbl = function(){
     duckdb() |>
            dbConnect(drv = _, read_only = TRUE) |>
            tbl(db_path)
}
df = make_tbl()
```

This is a useful pattern, because it abstracts the connection details away from the user. However, the user no longer has a clear way to access the connection, either to close it, or to re-use it for some other operation.

Technically it is possible to use `df$src$con`, which returns the connection object, but this seems like exploiting an internal structure which doesn't feel stable. e.g. what happens if the table has a column called `src`?
```
DBI::dbDisconnect(harmonised$src$con)
```

I therefore wonder if we could add a method along the lines of `as.connection.tbl_sql` that returns a connection given a `tbl_sql` object.

As an added bonus, it would be cool to implement `DBI::dbDisconnect` *for* `tbl_sql` to automatically extract this connection and close it. This would simplify a common use case without adding anything extra to the namespace.

title: Issue with order of operations with DISTINCT
description:
## Brief description of the problem

I expect the same answer from all three queries below. The queries are the same except for the following

1. Using local data frame
2. Using SQL
3. Using SQL with `compute()` to force evaluation of `distinct()`

However, the second one gives a different answer. This is a new-ish issue, as code that worked previously is now broken.

I think the translated SQL should be something like

```sql
SELECT `name`, `id`,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY `name`) AS `n_distinct`
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT `name`, `id` FROM `df`) AS some_table
```

## Reprex

``` r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2023)

df <- 
  tibble(name = letters, id = 1:26) %>%
  mutate(rep = sample(list(1, 1:2, 1:3), 
                       size = nrow(.), replace = TRUE)) %>%
  unnest(rep) 

df
#> # A tibble: 45 × 3
#>    name     id   rep
#>    <chr> <int> <dbl>
#>  1 a         1     1
#>  2 b         2     1
#>  3 b         2     2
#>  4 b         2     3
#>  5 c         3     1
#>  6 d         4     1
#>  7 d         4     2
#>  8 d         4     3
#>  9 e         5     1
#> 10 e         5     2
#> # … with 35 more rows

# Query 1: dplyr
df %>%
  select(name, id) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(n_distinct = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_distinct > 1)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # … with 3 variables: name <chr>, id <int>, n_distinct <int>

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = ":memory:")

df_sql <- copy_to(con, df)

# Query 2: SQL
df_sql %>%
  select(name, id) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(n_distinct = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_distinct > 1)
#> # Source:   SQL [?? x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.40.1 [:memory:]
#>    name     id n_distinct
#>    <chr> <int>      <int>
#>  1 b         2          3
#>  2 d         4          3
#>  3 e         5          2
#>  4 f         6          2
#>  5 n        14          3
#>  6 o        15          2
#>  7 p        16          3
#>  8 q        17          3
#>  9 u        21          3
#> 10 w        23          2
#> # … with more rows

# SQL for problematic Query 2
df_sql %>%
  select(name, id) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(n_distinct = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT
#>   `name`,
#>   `id`,
#>   COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY `name`) AS `n_distinct`
#> FROM `df`

# Query 3: SQL with compute to force evaluation of distinct()
df_sql %>%
  select(name, id) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  compute() %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(n_distinct = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_distinct > 1)
#> # Source:   SQL [0 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.40.1 [:memory:]
#> # … with 3 variables: name <chr>, id <int>, n_distinct <lgl>
```

title: Trouble creating a DuckDB table with `dbplyr::sql`
description:
When attempting to use `dbplyr::sql` to create a `dplyr::tbl` using a `duckdb` connection, I receive the following error:

```
Error: Parser Error: syntax error at or near "SELECT"
LINE 2: FROM SELECT * FROM items AS q01
```

Please see reprex below.

```r
# Creating connection and data
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = ":memory:")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE items(item VARCHAR, value DECIMAL(10,2), count INTEGER)")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO items VALUES ('jeans', 20.0, 1), ('hammer', 42.2, 2)")

# Confirming data is in the db

# Works
dplyr::tbl(con, "items")

# Does not work
dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::sql(paste("SELECT * FROM items")))
```

The above, `dplyr::tbl(con, dbplyr::sql(paste("SELECT * FROM items")))`, currently works in other SQL dialects, including Snowflake, Postgres, and SQLite.

title: Restrict table alias length
description:
Databases have limits on the length of a table alias (e.g [Postgres has 63](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27865770/how-long-can-postgresql-table-names-be)). The table alias should therefore be shortened to not exceed this length but still be unique.

``` r
library(dplyr)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres())

nm1 <- strrep("a", 63)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, nm1, tibble(x = 1))
df1 <- tbl(con, nm1)

nm2 <- strrep("b", 63)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, nm2, tibble(x = 1))
df2 <- tbl(con, nm2)

left_join(df1, df1) |> show_query()
#> Joining, by = "x"
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS"."x" AS "x"
#> FROM "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" AS "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS"
#> LEFT JOIN "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" AS "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_RHS"
#>   ON ("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS"."x" = "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_RHS"."x")
left_join(df1, df1)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#> NOTICE:  identifier "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS" will be truncated to "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
#> 
#> NOTICE:  identifier "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS" will be truncated to "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
#> NOTICE:  identifier "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_RHS" will be truncated to "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
#> NOTICE:  identifier "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_LHS" will be truncated to "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
#> NOTICE:  identifier "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa_RHS" will be truncated to "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
#> Error in `collect()`:
#> ! Failed to collect lazy table.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Failed to prepare query: ERROR:  table name "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" specified more than once
```

title: Feature Request: Add Pipe-able version of sql_query_save
description:
Sometimes when building complex queries with `dbplyr` it is helpful to be able to save a table without collecting and pulling into memory like `copy_to`. `sql_query_save` can do this, but the interface is clearly not intended for handling `tbl` objects, so I once wrote a naive wrapper function along the lines of:

```r
# use this instead of copy_to so we don't pull data into memory
save_temp_table <- function(tbl, temp_name) {
  con <- tbl[[1]]$con
  dbExecute(con, glue(
    "IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..{temp_name}') IS NOT NULL
DROP TABLE {temp_name};\n",sql_query_save(con, db_sql_render(con, tbl), name = as.sql(temp_name, con))), immediate = TRUE)

  tbl(con, temp_name)
}
```
Ideally I wouldn't have to glue sql strings together and it would be better to have interface along lines of:

```{r}
my_remote_tbl %>% 
mutate() %>% 
filter() %>% 
save_into('new_table_name',  ...all same parameters as copy_to) %>% 
can_continue_doing_stuff_on_new_table()
```

title: Wrong `rows_upsert()` test
description:
With RSQLite >= 2.3.0, the ```"`rows_upsert()` works with `in_place = TRUE` and `returning`"``` test fails. I believe that the test is wrong.

With Postgres:

```sh
psql <<EOF
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE a(x int PRIMARY KEY, y int);
INSERT INTO a (x, y) VALUES (1, 11), (2, 12), (3, 13);
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE b(x int, y int);
INSERT INTO b (x, y) VALUES (2, 22), (3, 23), (4, 24);
INSERT INTO a (x, y) SELECT * FROM b WHERE true ON CONFLICT (x) DO UPDATE SET y = excluded.y RETURNING a.x, a.y;
EOF
```

```
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 x | y
---+----
 2 | 22
 3 | 23
 4 | 24
(3 rows)

INSERT 0 3
```

dbplyr version:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql
con <- RPostgres::postgresDefault()
x <- copy_to(con, tibble(x = 1:3, y = 11:13), name = "df_x", overwrite = TRUE, unique_indexes = "x")
y <- copy_to(con, tibble(x = 2:4, y = 22:24), name = "df_y", overwrite = TRUE)
df_upserted <- rows_upsert(
  x, y,
  by = "x",
  in_place = TRUE,
  returning = everything()
)
get_returned_rows(df_upserted)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2

#> 2     3    23
#> 3     4    24
```

title: expand() call is translated to LEFT JOIN
description:
Using `expand(column1, column2)` on a BigQuery table is translated to a LEFT JOIN statement and thus to the following error: 
"LEFT JOIN must have an immediately following ON or USING clause"

If I'm not mistaken, the expression should be translated to a CROSS JOIN. 

I suspect that the translation to a left join may have to do with the fact that the `by` attribute of the resulting structure is `character(0)` and not `NULL`. 

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(bigrquery)
library(dbplyr)
library(DBI)

project_id = ...
dataset_id = ...

con <-  dbConnect(bigquery(), project = project_id, billing = project_id, dataset = dataset_id, use_legacy_sql = FALSE)
table <- tbl(con, "TableName")
table %>% expand(column1, column2) # causes an error
```

title: SQL code for distinct() followed by mutate() swaps the order of operations?
description:
Firstly, thanks to all contributors very much for developing {dbplyr}.

Since the {dbplyr} update to v2.3.0, some of the {dm} tests were all of sudden failing on remote sources. 
During my efforts to track down the reasons, I saw that the SQL code produced for `distinct()` followed by `mutate()` seems to now execute `mutate()` before `distinct()`, which often enough might not affect the results.
However, here an example on duckdb -- it seems to happen across several DBMS -- where it does:
``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
  library(tibble)
  library(duckdb)
})
packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '2.3.0'
lcl_tbl <- tibble(
  a = c(1, 2, 1),
  e = c("c", "b", "c"),
  f = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
lcl_tbl %>% 
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(aef = row_number())
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>       a e     f       aef
#>   <dbl> <chr> <lgl> <int>
#> 1     1 c     TRUE      1
#> 2     2 b     FALSE     2

con_duckdb <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())

rmt_tbl <- copy_to(con_duckdb, lcl_tbl)
# expecting the same result as above
rmt_tbl %>% 
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(aef = row_number(a))
#> # Source:   SQL [3 x 4]
#> # Database: DuckDB 0.6.2-dev1166 [root@Darwin 22.2.0:R 4.2.2/:memory:]
#>       a e     f       aef
#>   <dbl> <chr> <lgl> <dbl>
#> 1     1 c     TRUE      1
#> 2     1 c     TRUE      2
#> 3     2 b     FALSE     3

# produced SQL-code:
rmt_tbl %>% 
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(aef = row_number()) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS aef
#> FROM lcl_tbl

# produced SQL-code for the inverse order is actually the same:
rmt_tbl %>% 
  mutate(aef = row_number()) %>% 
  distinct() %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS aef
#> FROM lcl_tbl
```

title: multiple joins with `rename()`-calls for y-table lead to SELECT statement with wrong column names

``` r
rmt_tbl_4_renamed <- rename(rmt_tbl_4, e_4 = e)

# expected the same result as locally, but column `e_4` changed:
```

title: rows_insert fails to populate duplicated entries to remote table with autoincrement ON
description:
The **rows_insert** function in the dplyr package is failing to populate duplicate entries in remote databases (SQLite and MSSQL) where a single column is designated as an auto-incrementing primary key. Although manual insertion of the duplicate rows works as expected, the **rows_insert** function is unable to properly insert the duplicates, leading to a discrepancy in the data stored in the remote database.


This might be either bug in the rows_insert source code of misuse of the function argument from my side.


dplyr version: 1.1.0

---

Brief description of the problem

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
  library(DBI)
  library(odbc)
})

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())


tbl <- "CREATE TABLE table1(
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        value int)" |> as.sql(con)

DBI::dbExecute(con, tbl)
#> [1] 0


table1 <- tbl(con, "table1")

# initializing inserted rows: I am not specifying id since it will be generated by autoincremente column
rows_to_insrt <- tibble(value = 1)

# initializing the first row: rows_insert will populate the row with autoincrement ON
dplyr::rows_insert(table1, rows_to_insrt, copy = TRUE, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
#> Matching, by = "value"


table1 |> select(everything())
#> # Source:   table<table1> [1 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 []
#>      id value
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1

# trying again: There should be additional row with id = 2 and value = 1
dplyr::rows_insert(table1, rows_to_insrt, copy = TRUE, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
#> Matching, by = "value"


table1 |> select(everything())
#> # Source:   table<table1> [1 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 []
#>      id value
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1

# this works as supposed
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO table1 (value) values(1)")
#> [1] 1

table1 |> select(everything())
#> # Source:   table<table1> [2 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 []
```

title: `compute` doesn't handle errors with DBI::Id tables
description:
Since version 2.3.0, handling errors in `compute` method doesn't work with DBI::Id tables in the "name" parameter. I work with Teradata, but it looks like it applies to all databases.

The reprex
```r
library(dplyr)
db <- DBI::dbConnect(<connection info>)
target_name <- DBI::Id(schema = "my_shema", table = "my_table")

DBI::dbCreateTable(db, name = "test_compute", fields = c(my_id = "INTEGER"), temporary = TRUE)
DBI::dbCreateTable(db, name = target_name, fields = c(my_id = "INTEGER"), temporary = TRUE)

# should fail because `target_name` already exists
tbl(db, "test_compute") %>%
  compute(
    name = target_name,
    indexes = list("my_id"),
    temporary = FALSE
)
```

The following error appears
```
Error in as.character.default(target_name) : 
  no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector
Called from: as.character.default(target_name)
```

With debugging, it comes from [db_save_query](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/b16399f4fb7d862f84ca7f12fb6d4502390a3e12/R/db-sql.R#L908). It seems it started with the use of `cli_abort`. DBI::Id tables cannot be converted to character directly. Maybe it applies somewhere else in the code ?

title: dbplyr >=  2.3.0 incorrectly combines distinct() and select(), giving wrong results
description:
Since dbplyr 2.3.0, combinations of select() and distinct() are combined to erronous sql-queries, giving incorrect results.

The queries `df |> select() |> distinct()` and `df |> distinct() |> select()` should produce different sql queries, instead they are the same. Both queries would result in output x=1:

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dbplyr'
#> Die folgenden Objekte sind maskiert von 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql
lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1:2) |> select(x) |> distinct() |> print()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `x`
#> FROM `df`
lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1:2) |> distinct() |> select(x) |> print()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `x`
#> FROM `df`
```

Before version 2.3.0, the correct output was as follows. The first query would result in x=1, the second query would result in x=c(1, 1)

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dbplyr'
#> Die folgenden Objekte sind maskiert von 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql
lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1:2) |> select(x) |> distinct() |> print()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `x`
#> FROM `df`
lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1:2) |> distinct() |> select(x) |> print()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT DISTINCT *
#>   FROM `df`
#> ) `q01`
```

I consider this issue to break the functionality of dbplyr

title: `mutate()` is incorrectly inlined after `distinct()`
description:
I just updated to dplyr v1.1.0 + dbplyr 2.3.0, and my code broke. Upon investigation it seems that now a wrong SQL query is generated. Namely, in my case, I have `distinct` prior to the `group_by` block.
``` r
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% count(y) %>% filter(y == "YYY") 
# Source:     SQL [1 x 2]
# Database:   postgres  [.../postgres]
# Ordered by: x, y
  y        n
  <chr>  <int64>
1 YYY       1
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% group_by(y) %>% tally() %>% ungroup() %>% filter(y == "YYY") 
# Source:     SQL [1 x 2]
# Database:   postgres  [.../postgres]
# Ordered by: x, y
  y        n
  <chr>  <int64>
1 YYY       1
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% group_by(y) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(y == "YYY") 
# Source:     SQL [1 x 3]
# Database:   postgres  [.../postgres]
# Ordered by: x, y
  x y        n
      <int64> <chr>  <int64>
1        XXX YYY       2
```

If I add `compute` between them, i.e. the result of `distinct` is actually computed and stored in a temporary table, `n()` returns values as expected.
``` r
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% compute() %>% group_by(y) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(y == "YYY") 
# Source:     SQL [1 x 3]
# Database:   postgres  [.../postgres]
# Ordered by: x, y
  x y        n
      <int64> <chr>  <int64>
1        XXX YYY       1
```

This is the SQL query generated by  dplyr v1.1.0 + dbplyr 2.3.0:
``` r
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% group_by(y) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(y == "YYY") %>% show_query() 
<SQL>
SELECT DISTINCT
  "x",
  "y",
  COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY "y") AS "n"
FROM "dbplyr_026"
WHERE ("y" = 'YYY')
```
Note how it extended `distinct` onto the subsequent query.

And this one is generated (as expected) by dplyr v1.0.10 + dbplyr 2.2.1:
``` r
> remote_table %>% distinct(x, y) %>% group_by(y) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(y == "YYY") %>% show_query() 
<SQL>
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY "y") AS "n"
  FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT "x", "y"
    FROM "dbplyr_026"
  ) "q01"
) "q02"
WHERE ("y" = 'YYY')
```

title: dbplyr:::get_col_types.PqConnection doesn't handle schemas
description:
In short, when using schemas (`dbplyr::in_schema`) & PostgreSQL, the table name parameter isn't properly built when calling underlying functions. In my case, I'm trying to use the new `dbplyr::rows_insert` suite of functions.

About as close to a reprex as I can produce:
```R
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  host = db$host,
  port = db$port,
  dbname = db$name,
  user = db$user,
  password = db$password
)
dplyr::copy_to(conn, mtcars[1:5,], dbplyr::in_schema(db$schema, "cars"), temporary = FALSE)
db_cars <- dplyr::tbl(conn, dbplyr::in_schema(db$schema, "cars"))
new_cars <- mtcars[6:10,]
db_new_cars <- dbplyr::copy_inline(conn, new_cars)
dplyr::rows_insert(db_cars, db_new_cars, conflict = "ignore")
```


The error I get is:
```R
Error: Expecting a single string value: [type=character; extent=2].
>traceback()
13: stop(structure(list(message = "Expecting a single string value: [type=character; extent=2].", 
        call = NULL, cppstack = NULL), class = c("Rcpp::not_compatible", 
    "C++Error", "error", "condition")))
12: result_create(conn@ptr, statement, immediate)
11: initialize(value, ...)
10: initialize(value, ...)
9: new("PqResult", conn = conn, ptr = result_create(conn@ptr, statement, 
       immediate), sql = statement, bigint = conn@bigint)
8: .local(conn, statement, ...)
7: DBI::dbSendQuery(con, paste0("SELECT * FROM ", name))
6: DBI::dbSendQuery(con, paste0("SELECT * FROM ", name))
5: get_col_types.PqConnection(remote_con(x), name, call)
4: get_col_types(remote_con(x), name, call)
3: rows_auto_copy(x, y, copy = copy)
2: rows_insert.tbl_lazy(db_cars, db_new_cars, conflict = "ignore")
1: dplyr:::rows_insert(db_cars, db_new_cars, conflict = "ignore")
```

In the function stack I have traced the issue to:
```R
# dbplyr:::get_col_types.PqConnection(remote_con(x), name, call)
function (con, name, call) 
{
    res <- DBI::dbSendQuery(con, paste0("SELECT * FROM ", name))
    on.exit(DBI::dbClearResult(res))
    DBI::dbFetch(res, n = 0)
    col_info_df <- DBI::dbColumnInfo(res)
    set_names(col_info_df[[".typname"]], col_info_df[["name"]])
}
```

Notice the `paste0` call, this effectively creates something akin to the following when a schema is used:
```R
> name <- dbplyr::in_schema("my_schema", "my_table")
> paste0("SELECT * FROM ", name)
[1] "SELECT * FROM my_schema" "SELECT * FROM my_table"
```

And naturally the error is produced:
```R
> DBI::dbSendQuery(conn, c("SELECT * FROM my_schema", "SELECT * FROM my_table"))
Error: Expecting a single string value: [type=character; extent=2].
```


I do not know at which point the schema'd name should be built, whether that should be earlier in the stack or not, but I'm fairly sure that it is the cause of the problem.

title: (Bug) Window Frame and Filter create unexpected SQL query (wrong order)
description:
**Context:** 
I am using `dbplyr::window_order` and `dbplyr::window_frame` to create windowed sums of a variable. For some rows I might not have enough data points for a full windowed sum, i.e., I am at the end of my data, but need data for the next few days. In this case the windowed sum would be NA or a partial sum, depending on what row you are (see example in reprex). Then, to remove these rows without a full window, I use `dplyr::filter`. 

**Problem:**
 Even though the windowed sum calculation comes before the use of `dplyr::filter`, the values are actually calculated as if the `dplyr::filter` was applied before the windowed calculations, yielding wrong summations. See the reprex below for a small example, and the expected vs actual SQL query generated.

**Example:**
```r
# Create the following table 
data <- tibble::tibble(
                 identification = c(1,1,1),
                 date = c(1,2,3),
                 value = c(1,1,1)
               )
# Write the data to a remote server before continuing
```
![Screenshot 2023-02-07 at 3 56 35 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/68299186/217363873-954b4910-3bbe-4767-b2a8-fea9313e0a67.png)

```r
# Calculate windowed sums
sums <- data %>%
    dplyr::group_by(identification) %>%
    dbplyr::window_order(identification, date) %>%
    dbplyr::window_frame(
              from = 1,
              to = 2
            ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
             summed = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)
           ) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup()
```
![Screenshot 2023-02-07 at 3 58 20 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/68299186/217364207-44bd78ad-80bb-440f-9640-b1d55d71e10a.png)

The problem happens here:
```r
# Remove the rows without a full window
dplyr::filter(sums, date <= 1)
```
Output:
![Screenshot 2023-02-07 at 4 00 41 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/68299186/217364623-1e9d4603-6f04-429d-9c90-ded12b93eada.png)
Expected:
![Screenshot 2023-02-07 at 4 00 41 PM copy](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/68299186/217364846-291478fe-91bb-463c-bd42-8a1b55c11d5e.png)

This is the query generated:
```r
SELECT
  *,
  SUM("value") OVER (PARTITION BY "identification" ORDER BY "identification", "date" ROWS BETWEEN 1 FOLLOWING AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS "summed"
FROM "vrvkvwtftvhrekibsploqvthpfjmzt"
WHERE ("date" <= 1.0)
```
Notice that the filter is added directly to the select statement, instead of being added to a second select statement after the windowed sum is calculated. This is the query I expected (since filtering comes after the creation of the windowed sums):
```r
SELECT
  *
FROM (
  SELECT
    *,
    SUM("value") OVER (PARTITION BY "identification" ORDER BY "identification", "date" ROWS BETWEEN 1 FOLLOWING AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS "summed"
  FROM "vrvkvwtftvhrekibsploqvthpfjmzt"
  WHERE ("date" <= 1.0)
  );
```

title: Issue with group_by() %>% summarise(quantile()) on SQL Server
description:
SQL code generated for `summarise(quantile())` for SQL Sever is invalid. 
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = F)

data <- tibble::tibble(ind = rep(1:3, 100),
                       value = runif(300))

# desired output of the further generated SQL queries
data %>% 
  group_by(ind) %>% 
  summarise(q05_value = quantile(value, 0.05))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>     ind q05_value
#>   <int>     <dbl>
#> 1     1    0.0240
#> 2     2    0.0667
#> 3     3    0.0625

# Translation to Postgres works:
df_postgres <- tbl_lazy(data, con = simulate_postgres())
df_postgres %>% 
  group_by(ind) %>%
  summarise(q05_value = quantile(value, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT
#>   `ind`,
#>   PERCENTILE_CONT(0.05) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY `value`) AS `q05_value`
#> FROM `df`
#> GROUP BY `ind`

# Translation to SQL Server doesn't work:
df_mssql <- tbl_lazy(data, con = simulate_mssql())
df_mssql %>% 
  group_by(ind) %>%
  summarise(q05_value = quantile(value, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT
#>   `ind`,
#>   PERCENTILE_CONT(0.05) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY `value`) OVER () AS `q05_value`
#> FROM `df`
#> GROUP BY `ind`
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-25 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Attempt to run generated SQL on SQL Server fails with the following error:
`Column 'tab.value' is invalid in the select list because it is not contained in either an aggregate function or the GROUP BY clause.`

SQL Server uses window function type of syntax for `PERCENTILE_CONT()` as opposed to Postgres which utilizes aggregate approach.

Working SQL for SQL Server for the demonstrated query would be the following:
```
SELECT DISTINCT
  ind, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.05) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY value) OVER (PARTITION BY ind) AS q05_value
  FROM tab;

```

title: dbplyr::sql_render() produces non-working SQL code when fields in dplyr::dense_rank() aren't inside quotes
description:
I am working with database tables (`tbl` objects) and have noticed that, when passing to `dplyr::dense_rank()` a vector of column names **not** inside quotes, the SQL query output from `dbplyr::sql_render()` carries over the `c()` function that contains the column names. Conversely, when the column names in the vector are inside quotes, the SQL query is correct.

Consider the following `tbl` object:

```
mtcars_db <- mtcars %>% 
  dbplyr::memdb_frame()
```

**The bad way**
Now, let's do a dense rank on a couple of columns. We pass the columns without quotes:

```
mtcars_db %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(yy = dplyr::dense_rank(c(cyl, am))) %>% 
  dbplyr::sql_render()
```

The SQL quote has the `c()` function in it in two places:

```sql
<SQL> SELECT
  *,
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((c("`cyl` IS NULL", "`am` IS NULL")))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((c("`cyl` IS NULL", "`am` IS NULL"))) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `cyl`, `am`)
END AS `yy`
FROM `dbplyr_004`
```

You can't run the above in SQL- it'll say that the `c()` function isn't registered.

**The good way**
Let's repeat the above, however by supplying the column names inside quotes:

```
mtcars_db %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(yy = dplyr::dense_rank(c('cyl', 'am'))) %>% 
  dbplyr::sql_render()
```

This time, the SQL query has no problems:

```sql
<SQL> SELECT
  *,
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((('cyl', 'am') IS NULL))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((('cyl', 'am') IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `cyl`, `am`)
END AS `yy`
FROM `dbplyr_004`
```

**Note**
When one of the column names is passed as a character vector object, the SQL code is also correct:

```
cyl_vector <- 'cyl'
mtcars_db %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(yy = dplyr::dense_rank(c(cyl_vector, 'am'))) %>% 
  dbplyr::sql_render()
```

```sql
<SQL> SELECT
  *,
  CASE
WHEN (NOT((('cyl', 'am') IS NULL))) THEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY (CASE WHEN ((('cyl', 'am') IS NULL)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY `cyl`, `am`)
END AS `yy`
FROM `dbplyr_004`
```

title: Cannot join 3+ tables with the same column name
description:
Hello!

Joining 2 tables results in sensible SQL, but any more results in the second table being used repeatedly:-

```r
> library(magrittr)
> library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
> library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
>
> packageVersion('dplyr')
[1] ‘1.1.0’
> packageVersion('dbplyr')
[1] ‘2.3.0’
>
> lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)
> lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2)
> lf3 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 3)
> lf4 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 4)
> lf5 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 5)
>
> left_join(lf, lf2, by = "x") %>%
+   left_join(lf3, by = "x") %>%
+   left_join(lf4, by = "x") %>%
+   left_join(lf5, by = "x")
<SQL>
SELECT
  `df...1`.*,
  `df...2`.`b` AS `b.x`,
  `df...3`.`b` AS `b.y`,
  `df...3`.`b` AS `b.x.x`,
  `df...3`.`b` AS `b.y.y`
FROM `df` AS `df...1`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
  ON (`df...1`.`x` = `df...2`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...3`
  ON (`df...1`.`x` = `df...3`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...4`
  ON (`df...1`.`x` = `df...4`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...5`
  ON (`df...1`.`x` = `df...5`.`x`)
```

Note the LEFT JOIN clauses are reasonable, but the SELECTs have got "stuck" on ``df...3``.

It seems highly likely that this is related to #865, the previous stack-of-subqueries SQL formulation as generated by dbplyr 2.2.1 could produce working queries for this sort of request.

FWIW in our actual use case we are rename()ing the joins first, to give the additional columns unique names, but that only affects the column aliases in the generated SQL, it still gets stuck on the second sub-select.

title: Implementation of Oracle's 'CONNECT BY' clause as dplyr verbs.
description:
Currently, I'm working with an Oracle database with tables containing hierarchies. I'm using SQL clauses `CONNECT BY` in combination with `PRIOR` to obtain the hierarchical information recursively. Using SQL directly (wrapped in `dbplyr::sql`) with `tbl` allows me to obtain the hierarchical info. However, dbplyr generates invalid SQL queries when I join the `tbl` with other `tbl`s obtained from the database using dplyr verbs.

I have noticed that `select_query` has support for `group_by` and `order_by`, but not for `connect_by`. Could this be implemented as feature? If not, what would be the preferred route to work around this?

It's hard to provide a proper reprex without a database, hopefully this is helpful. Consider this code:
```
## con is a connection to a specific Oracle database
tab <- dplyr::tbl(
  con, dplyr::sql(
    paste(
      "SELECT",
      "\"SPE_ID\",",
      "\"SSE_ID\" AS ROOT_ID,",
      "CONNECT_BY_ROOT \"ID\" \"ID_NEST\"",
      "FROM (TABLE_A) CONNECT BY PRIOR \"ID\" = \"SSE_ID\""))
)

## This works ok
tab

## When mixing with dplyr verbs I get into trouble
dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::tbl(con, "TABLE_B") %>% dplyr::filter(ID == 6448),
  tab,
  c(ID = "SPE_ID")
)
```
This generates the following faulty SQL:
```
<SQL>
SELECT "LHS".*, "ROOT_ID", "ID_NEST"
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM ("TABLE_B") 
  WHERE ("ID" = 6448.0)
) "LHS"
LEFT JOIN (SELECT "SPE_ID", "SSE_ID" AS ROOT_ID, CONNECT_BY_ROOT "ID" "ID_NEST" FROM (TABLE_A) CONNECT BY PRIOR "ID" = "SSE_ID") "SELECT ""SPE_ID"", ""SSE_ID"" AS ROOT_ID, CONNECT_BY_ROOT ""ID"" ""ID_NEST"" FROM (TABLE_A) CONNECT BY PRIOR ""ID"" = ""SSE_ID"""

```
and results in:

```
  Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error:
! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1655: HY000: [Oracle][ODBC][Ora]ORA-03001: unimplemented feature
```

title: Malfunctioning SQL generation with dbplyr 2.3.0
description:
Good day,

with dbplyr 2.3.0 I managed to construct a statement which does not correctly translate to SQL.

Consider the following example:
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

table1 <- tbl_lazy(tibble(key = 1), dbplyr::simulate_hana()) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("table1.", .))
table2 <- tbl_lazy(tibble(key = 2, parent = 3), dbplyr::simulate_hana()) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("table2.", .))
table3 <- tbl_lazy(tibble(key = 3, parent = 4), dbplyr::simulate_hana()) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("table3.", .))
table4 <- tbl_lazy(tibble(key = 4, parent = 5), dbplyr::simulate_hana()) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("table4.", .))

table1 %>%
  inner_join(table2, by = c("table1.key" = "table2.parent")) %>%
  inner_join(table3, by = c("table2.key" = "table3.parent")) %>%
  inner_join(table4, by = c("table3.key" = "table4.parent"))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT
#>   `df...1`.`key` AS `table1.key`,
#>   `df...2`.`key` AS `table2.key`,
#>   `df...3`.`key` AS `table3.key`,
#>   `df...3`.`key` AS `table4.key`
#> FROM `df` AS `df...1`
#> INNER JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
#>   ON (`df...1`.`key` = `df...2`.`parent`)
#> INNER JOIN `df` AS `df...3`
#>   ON (`df...2`.`key` = `df...3`.`parent`)
#> INNER JOIN `df` AS `df...4`
#>   ON (`df...3`.`key` = `df...4`.`parent`)
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-18 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Notice the fourth line after SELECT: `df...3.key AS table4.key`. I would expect it to read `df...4.key AS table4.key` (*4* instead of *3*), i.e. 
```r
#> SELECT
#>   `df...1`.`key` AS `table1.key`,
#>   `df...2`.`key` AS `table2.key`,
#>   `df...3`.`key` AS `table3.key`,
#>   `df...4`.`key` AS `table4.key`
#> FROM `df` AS `df...1`
```
Somehow the same column is selected twice with different names.
But I really want "table4.key" from "table4" to be selected.

Unfortunately this behavior seems to break some of my queries which were working before.

title: Across subquery produces wrong results when referring to another column of data
description:
Hello--it appears that across in dbplyr returns different results from dplyr when both these happen...

* a formula contains another variable from the data (e.g. `~ .x / mpg`)
* an early operation in across overrides the variable's name (e.g. result gets named `mpg`)

When this happens, operations on other selected variables use the overridden column, rather than the original (see [this dplyr test](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/main/tests/testthat/test-across.R#L423-L424), which I think would fail for dbplyr).

This is shown in the reprex below. It looks like the issue is a subquery is created during the across..

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

# dplyr ----
cars_small <- mtcars %>%
  select(mpg, cyl, gear) %>%
  head(2)

# all columns divided by original mpg
cars_small %>%
  mutate(across(c(mpg, cyl, gear), ~ .x / mpg))
#>               mpg       cyl      gear
#> Mazda RX4       1 0.2857143 0.1904762
#> Mazda RX4 Wag   1 0.2857143 0.1904762

# dbplyr ----
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = ":memory:")
copy_to(con, cars_small)

# mpg re-assigned in first operation, then used in later ones
q <- tbl(con, "cars_small") %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ .x / mpg))

q
#> # Source:   SQL [2 x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.38.5 [:memory:]
#>     mpg   cyl  gear
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     6     4
#> 2     1     6     4

show_query(q)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `mpg`, `cyl` / `mpg` AS `cyl`, `gear` / `mpg` AS `gear`
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT `mpg` / `mpg` AS `mpg`, `cyl`, `gear`
#>   FROM `cars_small`
#> )
```

title: Compute() with Oracle - missing keyword GLOBAL
description:
Hi,

First of all, thank you for your work. I think there's a bug with the command `compute()` when used with Oracle connection.

```r
library(ROracle)
library(dplyr)
drv <- dbDriver("Oracle")
conn <- dbConnect(drv, dbname = "DATABASE")
tbl(conn, "table") %>% compute
```
Returns this error 

```r
Error in .oci.SendQuery(conn, statement, data = data, prefetch = prefetch,  : 
ORA-14459: missing GLOBAL keyword
```

It's exactly the same that happens if you do `dbExecute(conn, 'CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE table_name(id NUMBER)')` instead of `dbExecute(conn, 'CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE table_name(id NUMBER)')` which works fine. [See other people concerned](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49635646/how-to-use-dbplyr-to-store-a-query-in-an-oracle-temporary-table-without-ever-sto).

title: slow `tbl(con, ...)` access to view, caused by db_query_fields.DBIConnection implementation
description:
## Situation

The `tbl(con, ...)` function to access tables on DB is very slow and costly when the target table is actually a `VIEW`. 

## Investigation 

I checked the implementation and DB logs and found that

```sql
SELECT * FROM `view_name` WHERE (0 = 1)
```

was executed to query the fields of the table. This statement is general and cheap for real tables, but for views, this is a disaster for some DBs, including the *Snowflake* I am currently using.

In the previous version of `dbplyr`, a solution is to overload the `dplyr::db_query_fields(con, sql, ...)` S3 method with your own function in a more suitable way. For example the `odbc::dbListFields` can be used in the customized implementation (e.g. `db_query_fields.OdbcConnection`) because it doesn't have problems with views when getting field names.

Since major version 2, a new function `dbplyr_query_fields` has been used to query the fields of table. This function is not an S3 method so it is not possible to overload it directly. But as far as I saw in the source code, it's only a wrapper for the original `db_query_fields.DBIConnection()` to serve some purposes, like downward compatibility. In the implementation of this new function, `dbplyr_query_fields`, `dbplyr_fallback` is called to indirectly handle the call of `db_query_fields.DBIConnection` and here is the problem. [This line](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/v2.2.1/R/db.R#L81),

> fun <- sym(paste0(.generic, ".DBIConnection"))

dictates that regardless of the type of the connection `con`, only the `db_query_fields.DBIConnection` shall be called.

Overloading `dplyr::db_query_fields` (in my case it's `db_query_fields.OdbcConnection`) won't work at present.


## Summary

I think this issue is more likely a feature request than a bug report.

1. Is there any way for the users to optimize the `db_query_fields` method without changing anything in `dbplyr` or other loaded libraries in this version?

2. If the answer to question 1 is no, then does the team have any plan to optimize `db_query_fields` in the following releases? Such as writing the optimized version of overlading S3 method for each backends?

3. If the answer to question 2 is no, then will the team consider giving back the freedom of overloading `db_query_fields` to the users?

Thanks in advance!

Have a nice day.


P.S. This is only a toy example...
```r
library(dbplyr)

# prepare DB and table/view
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dplyr::copy_to(con, mtcars, "remote_view")

# `tbl` can be very costly if it's remote view instead of real table
# considering the result earned at the cost is only field names...
# it's even more costly than it already was
remote_view <- dplyr::tbl(con, "remote_view")
```

title: Groupby and mutate (with SQL verb) fails to generate correct SQL translation

```r
mf <- memdb_frame(x = 1, y = 2)

mf |>
```

title: No TRUE literal in SQL Server, should `escape()` default to `list(clause = "SELECT")` ?
description:
MSSQL has no `TRUE` literal, but it's returned from translations: https://stackoverflow.com/a/7171264/946850.

dm uses a home-grown routine to insert records into MS SQL Server, via `dbplyr::escape()` . This breaks with dbplyr >= 2.2.0.

The reprex illustrates the problem. What's a good solution?

``` r
library(dbplyr)

con <- simulate_mssql()

# Buggy, no TRUE literal: https://stackoverflow.com/a/7171264/946850
escape(TRUE, con = con)
#> <SQL> TRUE

# This is what dm needs:
escape(c(TRUE, FALSE), parens = FALSE, collapse = NULL, con = con)
#> <SQL> TRUE
#> <SQL> FALSE

# Still buggy:
translate_sql_(list(TRUE), con = con)
#> <SQL> TRUE

# Correct, but how to achieve for a vector?
translate_sql_(list(TRUE), con = con, context = list(clause = "SELECT"))
#> <SQL> 1

# Useless for dm:
translate_sql_(list(c(TRUE, FALSE)), con = con, context = list(clause = "SELECT"))
#> <SQL> (1, 0)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-07-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

CC @TSchiefer.

title: HANA DB: SHORTTEXT casting not supported anymore?
description:
I updated the Hana driver recently, and I noticed that some previously working dbplyr queries are failing now.

In particular, a data type conversion using `as.character` seems to be failing with the SQL error message
```r
Error in `collect()`:
! Failed to collect lazy table.
Caused by error in `new_result()`:
! nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1412: 42000: [SAP AG][LIBODBCHDB DLL][HDBODBC] Syntax error or access violation;257 sql syntax error: incorrect syntax near "SHORTTEXT": line 1 col 27 (at pos 27) 
```

An explicit example which returns that error:
```r
some_lazy_table %>% select(some_number) %>% mutate(some_text = as.character(some_number))
```
which generates the SQL
```SQL
SELECT "some_number", CAST("some_number" AS SHORTTEXT) AS "some_text"
FROM "MYSCHEMA"."some_lazy_table"
```

When looking up the [specs for CAST](https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_HANA_PLATFORM/4fe29514fd584807ac9f2a04f6754767/20db6dd475191014aa7b978452f92bbd.html), SHORTTEXT is also not mentioned as allowed data type, so I wonder if it was ever supported in the first place.

title: Median is Translated wrongly for MSSQL in summarize
description:
Calculating the overall median does not yield valid `SQL`

```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
d <- lazy_frame(x = 1:10, con = simulate_mssql())
d %>% summarize(med = median(x, na.rm = TRUE))
# <SQL>
# SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY `x`) AS `med`
# FROM `df`
```
The proper `SQL` syntax would look like:

```sql
--- Set up
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #temp;
WITH rcte (x) AS (
  SELECT 1 AS x
   UNION ALL
  SELECT x + 1
    FROM rcte
   WHERE x <= 100
) 
SELECT x
  INTO #temp
  FROM rcte;

--- SQL should look like this
SELECT DISTINCT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) OVER () AS med
  FROM #temp;
```

Thus instead of
```sql
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY `x`) AS `med`
  FROM `df`;
```

we would expect
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY `x`) OVER() AS `med`
  FROM `df`;
```

title: Improve error messages
description:
## Missing Variables

The error message for missing variables is generated by the database. Therefore, the error message does not mention the verb where the issue is.

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- memdb_frame(x = 1)

df %>% 
  mutate(x = y + 1)
#> Error: no such column: y

df %>% 
  group_by(x = y + 1)
#> Error: no such column: y

df %>% 
  distinct(x = y + 1)
#> Error: no such column: y
```

<sup>Created on 2022-04-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## Functions without translation

The error message also does not mention the verb where the issue comes from:

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- memdb_frame(x = 1)

df %>% 
  mutate(x = y %/% 1)
#> Error: %/% is not available in this SQL variant
```

<sup>Created on 2022-04-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## `across()`

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- memdb_frame(x = 1)

df %>% 
  mutate(across(c(x), "a"))
#> Error: no such function: a
```

<sup>Created on 2022-04-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## How to improve

* translate to SQL directly when calling the verb
* do not translate unknown symbols
* Consider using `cli_abort()`

title: Multiple joins in one query
description:
In databases one often needs to join multiple tables. In dbplyr this produces rather many nested queries which one would more often write as a single query.

## Example

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2)
lf3 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, c = 3)

left_join(lf, lf2, by = "x") %>% 
  left_join(lf3, by = "x")
```

<sup>Created on 2022-05-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Currently produces

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`, `c`
FROM (
  SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
  FROM `df1` AS `LHS`
  LEFT JOIN `df2` AS `RHS`
    ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
) `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df3` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

It would be nicer if it could produce something like

```sql
SELECT `df`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`, `c`
FROM `df1`
LEFT JOIN `df2`
  ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df3`
  ON (`df1`.`x` = `df3`.`x`)
```

## Thoughts & Questions

* Is the result of joins in subqueries and multiple joins in one query necessarily the same?
* What about table aliases?
  * Now we have `x_as` and `y_as`. I think if they are not provided it might make more sense to not use a table alias.
  * If `x_as` is provided in a join which is not the first join, then maybe a subquery should be generated
  * If `y_as` is provided it can always be used
* A `FULL JOIN` can be tricky to combine with other joins:
  * SQLite does not directly support `FULL JOIN`
  * The columns joined by are `coalesce()`
* If `semi_join()` or `anti_join()` is followed by `left/right/inner/full_join()` they cannot be combined because `WHERE` is evaluated after `JOIN`

So, I think that
* a sequence of `left_join()` and `inner_join()` can be combined in one query
* a sequence of `semi_join()` and `anti_join()` might be combined (though nested queries might be more efficient)

title: Several related issues with `fill()`
description:
`fill()` doesn't work as expected, see reprex.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
mydb <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "")
mydata <- tibble(id = 1:3, val = c(NA, "hello", NA))
DBI::dbWriteTable(mydb, "mydata", mydata)

# The message is a bit cryptic, it's not obvious that `arrange()` will do some
# magic since id is already sorted
# also, typo "determinstic"
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "down")
#> Error in `tidyr::fill()`:
#> ✖ `.data` does not have explicit order.
#> ℹ Please use `arrange()` or `window_order()` to make determinstic.

# If I do use arrange, I get a warning that doesn't make sense for a R user
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  arrange(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "down")
#> Warning: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
#> ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead?
#> # Source:     SQL [3 x 2]
#> # Database:   sqlite 3.39.4 []
#> # Ordered by: id
#>      id val  
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     1 <NA> 
#> 2     2 hello
#> 3     3 hello

# window order doesn't exist, it's a {dbplyr} function, not obvious for {dplyr} user who never use {dbplyr} explicitly
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "up")
#> Error in window_order(., id): could not find function "window_order"

# this works perfectly
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  dbplyr::window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "down") 
#> # Source:     SQL [3 x 2]
#> # Database:   sqlite 3.39.4 []
#> # Ordered by: id
#>      id val  
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     1 <NA> 
#> 2     2 hello
#> 3     3 hello

# however if I fill "up" the order is reversed
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  dbplyr::window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "up") 
#> # Source:     SQL [3 x 2]
#> # Database:   sqlite 3.39.4 []
#> # Ordered by: id
#>      id val  
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     3 <NA> 
#> 2     2 hello
#> 3     1 hello

# and updown and downup are not supported
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  dbplyr::window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "updown") 
#> Error in `tidyr::fill()`:
#> ! `.direction` must be one of "down" or "up", not "updown".
#> ℹ Did you mean "down"?

dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  dbplyr::window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "downup") 
#> Error in `tidyr::fill()`:
#> ! `.direction` must be one of "down" or "up", not "downup".
#> ℹ Did you mean "down"?

# though it is achievable
dplyr::tbl(mydb, "mydata") %>% 
  dbplyr::window_order(id) %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "up") %>% 
  tidyr::fill(val, .direction = "down") 
#> # Source:     SQL [3 x 2]
#> # Database:   sqlite 3.39.4 []
#> # Ordered by: id
#>      id val  
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     1 hello
#> 2     2 hello
#> 3     3 hello
```

<sup>Created on 2022-11-30 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I think we need : 

* A better error message : ditch the reference to `arrange()`, something like : 

> Please use call `dbplyr::window_order()` before `fill()` to set an explicit row order.

* Fix row order after `.direction = "up"`
* Support "downup" and "updown" 
* A note in the tidyr doc, or a link to a help file for the tbl_lazy method, documenting the row order issue

title: Summarize across fails on Microsoft Azure SQL due to IIF statement

Bang Bang with named vector breaks filter
description:
When using `!!` to evaluate a variable in a `dbplyr` filter statement, the presence of a named value creates an invalid `AS` statement in the SQL

```r
library(dbplyr)
```

title: inserting a duplicated row to an auto incremented table does not work
description:
Inserting a duplicated row to an auto incremented table does not work. See the reprex below:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
  library(RSQLite)
  library(DBI)
})

con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE Info (
   id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
   number INTEGER
)")
#> [1] 0
info <- tbl(con, "Info")

# first insert is ok with duplicate rows
rows1 <- copy_inline(con, data.frame(number = c(1, 1)))
rows_insert(info, rows1, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE)
#> Matching, by = "number"
info
#> # Source:   table<Info> [2 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 [:memory:]
#>      id number
#>   <int>  <int>
#> 1     1      1
#> 2     2      1

# adding a non duplicated works
rows2 <- copy_inline(con, data.frame(number = 2))
info <- rows_insert(info, rows2, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE, returning = "id")
#> Matching, by = "number"
info
#> # Source:   table<Info> [3 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 [:memory:]
#>      id number
#>   <int>  <int>
#> 1     1      1
#> 2     2      1
#> 3     3      2
get_returned_rows(info)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>      id
#>   <int>
#> 1     3

# adding a duplicated row (when comparing to the existing table) does not work
# since the "where_not_exists" conflic clause in the select query does not 
# return anything that matches the existing table
rows3 <- copy_inline(con, data.frame(number = 1))
info <- rows_insert(info, rows3, conflict = "ignore", in_place = TRUE, returning = "id")
#> Matching, by = "number"
info
#> # Source:   table<Info> [3 x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.39.4 [:memory:]
#>      id number
#>   <int>  <int>
#> 1     1      1
#> 2     2      1
#> 3     3      2
get_returned_rows(info)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 1
#> # … with 1 variable: id <int>

dbplyr:::sql_query_insert.DBIConnection(
  con = dbplyr:::remote_con(info),
  x_name = dbplyr:::target_table_name(info, in_place = TRUE),
  y = rows3,
  by = dbplyr:::rows_check_by(by = NULL, rows3),
  conflict = "ignore",
  returning_cols = dbplyr:::rows_check_returning(info, "id", expr(id)),
  method = NULL
)
#> Matching, by = "number"
#> <SQL> INSERT INTO `Info` (`number`)
#> SELECT *
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT CAST(`number` AS REAL) AS `number`
#>   FROM (
#>     SELECT NULL AS `number`
#>     WHERE (0 = 1)
#>     UNION ALL
#>     VALUES (1.0)
#>   ) AS `values_table`
#> ) AS `...y`
#> WHERE NOT EXISTS (
#>   SELECT 1 FROM `Info`
#>   WHERE (`Info`.`number` = `...y`.`number`)
#> )
#> RETURNING `Info`.`id`
```
<sup>Created on 2022-11-04 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


A potential fix could be to add the autoincremented column to the WHERE NOT EXISTS clause:
```sql
INSERT INTO `Info` (`number`)
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT CAST(`number` AS REAL) AS `number`
  FROM (
    SELECT NULL AS `number`
    WHERE (0 = 1)
    UNION ALL
    VALUES (1.0)
  ) AS `values_table`
) AS `...y`
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM `Info`
  WHERE 
      (`Info`.`id` = NULL) AND -- the autoincrement/identity column
      (`Info`.`number` = `...y`.`number`)
)
RETURNING `Info`.`id`
```
The identification of this column could be done via a new `auto_increment` argument in `rows_insert()` that is optional and if defined, is passed to `dbplyr:::sql_query_insert.*()`

description:

title: names() method for tbl_* objects?
description:
Copying from the dbplyr vignette:

```r
library(dplyr)
```


I would have expected `names()` to give the column names (which `colnames()` does). Maybe I am not understanding the `tbl_*` class for remote connections, but `src/lazy_query` seem implementation detail-y to me.

Should we add a `names.tbl_lazy` (or other class) method to match my instinct here?

title: Redshift varchar character length not respected by dplyr::rows_*()
description:
Thank you for this amazing package! I hope this is the right place for this issue. I know that dplyr::rows_*() are experimental.

When writing a text value to a Redshift table whose column is varchar(anything larger than 256), using dplyr::rows_append() or dplyr::rows_update() seems to cast the text to varchar(256) before writing to the database. Longer texts will then fail to write even though the table should be able to accommodate them.

To reproduce the issue:
- Create a Redshift table with columns id and txt (I haven't run into this with Postgres connections but it might happen there too).
- Make the datatype of the txt column varchar(max, or anything larger than 256)
- Connect to the table using a privileged user. I use RPostgres::Redshift() (but this isn't the issue).
- This will work successfully.
```r
dplyr::rows_append(x = dplyr::tbl(src = redshift_conn, DBI::Id(schema = schema, table = table)), y = tibble(id = 1, txt = paste(rep('a', 256), collapse = '')), copy = TRUE, in_place = TRUE)
```
- This will fail with `Error: Failed to fetch row: ERROR:  value too long for type character varying(256).`
```r
dplyr::rows_append(x = dplyr::tbl(src = redshift_conn, DBI::Id(schema = schema, table = table)), y = tibble(id = 2, txt = paste(rep('a', 257), collapse = '')), copy = TRUE, in_place = TRUE)
```
- But using RPostgres::dbAppendTable() works with the same data that failed with dplyr::rows_append().
```r
RPostgres::dbAppendTable(conn = redshift_conn, name = DBI::Id(schema = schema, table = table), value = tibble(id = 2, txt = paste(rep('a', 257), collapse = '')), row.names = NULL)
```

Somewhere along the line the text value is cast from varchar(65535) to varchar(256) for rows_append() and rows_update(), and I haven't figured out where.

title: dense_rank() ignores NAs in data frames, counts them in database tables
description:
The documentation of function `dense_rank` currently does not mention that `NA` values won't be accounted for when working with data frames, but _will_ be counted in when working with DB tables. Note the value of column `dr` in the two examples below.


Data frame:
```
mtcars$vs[1] <- NA
mtcars$vs[3] <- NA
mtcars %>% 
    dplyr::slice(1:5) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(dr = dplyr::dense_rank(vs)) %>% 
    dplyr::arrange(dr)

# Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4  1
# Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2  1
# Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1 NA    3    1  2
# Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46 NA NA    4    4 NA
# Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61 NA  1    4    1 NA
```

DB table:
