title: compute.tbl_sql calls as.sql without passing in the con argument
description:
I want to use `compute` to transform a dplyr query into a persistent table in a sql server database. I get the following error.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                      Driver   = "ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server",
                      Server   = Sys.getenv("CDM5_SQL_SERVER_SERVER"),
                      Database = Sys.getenv("CDM5_SQL_SERVER_CDM_DATABASE"),
                      UID      = Sys.getenv("CDM5_SQL_SERVER_USER"),
                      PWD      = Sys.getenv("CDM5_SQL_SERVER_PASSWORD"),
                      TrustServerCertificate = "yes",
                      Port     = 1433)

concept <- tbl(con, dbplyr::in_catalog("cdmv5", "dbo", "concept"))

db <- concept %>% 
  filter(concept_id == 0) %>% 
  select(starts_with("concept")) %>% 
  compute(name = DBI::Id(catalog = "tempdb", schema = "dbo", table = "temp_example9"), temporary = FALSE)
#> Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)): error in evaluating the argument 'conn' in selecting a method for function 'dbQuoteIdentifier': argument "con" is missing, with no default

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-24 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


When I step through the code the table is created as expected. The error is caused by a call to `as.sql(name)` without passing in the connection. The method being called is `as.sql.Id`.

**compute.tbl_sql**
```
function (x, name = unique_table_name(), temporary = TRUE, unique_indexes = list(), 
  indexes = list(), analyze = TRUE, ..., cte = FALSE) 
{
  name <- unname(name)
  vars <- op_vars(x)
  assert_that(all(unlist(indexes) %in% vars))
  assert_that(all(unlist(unique_indexes) %in% vars))
  x_aliased <- select(x, !!!syms(vars))
  sql <- db_sql_render(x$src$con, x_aliased$lazy_query, cte = cte)
  name <- db_compute(x$src$con, name, sql, temporary = temporary, 
    unique_indexes = unique_indexes, indexes = indexes, 
    analyze = analyze, ...)
  tbl_src_dbi(x$src, as.sql(name), colnames(x)) %>% group_by(!!!syms(op_grps(x))) %>% 
    window_order(!!!op_sort(x))
}
```

Changing 
`tbl_src_dbi(x$src, as.sql(name), colnames(x)) %>% group_by(!!!syms(op_grps(x))) %>% 
    window_order(!!!op_sort(x))`

to 
`tbl_src_dbi(x$src, as.sql(name, x$src$con), colnames(x)) %>% group_by(!!!syms(op_grps(x))) %>% 
    window_order(!!!op_sort(x))`

fixes the problem since `as.sql.Id` requires both the name and connection arguments.
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/e4f909a4a019bafe48ed24bd80132aef9fbc81e9/R/schema.R#L82

If this is a suitable solution I can make the PR for this change.

title: Redshift shouldn't support window clause
description:
Currently, `supports_window_clause()` returns `TRUE` for Redshift connections, because the Redshift backend inherits from the Postgres backend, and Postgres _does_ support window clauses.

However, Redshift does _not_ currently support window clauses - at least, they are not mentioned anywhere in the AWS Redshift docs, and attempting to use a named window in a Redshift query in the same way as in a Postgres query, results in a syntax error.

Fixable by adding `supports_window_clause()` S3 methods for Redshift connections in `backend-redshift.R`.

title: Redshift `round()` can't return decimal places
description:
Redshift's `numeric` (== `decimal`) type has a default scale (number of decimal places) of 0, so naively casting values to `numeric` can lead to surprising results.

The Redshift backend already guards against this, by instead casting to `float`:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/f4cef2360088c39620bd85f474ec2e888a520dcc/R/backend-redshift.R#L40

However the Postgres backend, which the Redshift backend inherits from, uses a [custom function](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/ec2374f22debcd98a05cd2905273aa1f63cf6809/R/backend-postgres.R#L62) for its translation of `round()`, which contains an explicit cast to `numeric`:
```r
postgres_round <- function(x, digits = 0L) {
  digits <- as.integer(digits)
  sql_expr(round(((!!x)) %::% numeric, !!digits))
}
```

This means we end up with the following SQL translation:
```r
translate_sql(round(1.234, 1), con = simulate_redshift())
#> <SQL> ROUND((1.234) :: numeric, 1)
```

This _always:_
* Implicitly rounds to 0 decimal places, via the cast to `numeric`
* Then, explicitly rounds the result to the specified number of decimal places, meaning we end up with at best 0dp

Hopefully an easy fix by overriding `round` in the Redshift translator with a small `round_redshift()` function - I'll add a pull request shortly!

title: Nested queries versus no results
description:
Dear @mgirlich,

I am facing a situation where I either have short SQL queries but no results or a long SQL query that gives results. I am probably doing something wrong (the short version has less aliases but doesn't pick the desired LHS). I looked into #728 and #726 but was not able to find a solution.

When I execute the following code (that has too many aliases), I get results:

```
s <- memdb_frame("col1" = 1:10,"col2" = 2:11,"col9" = 9:18)
t <- memdb_frame("col10" = 10:19,"col11" = 11:20)
c <- memdb_frame("col1" = 1:10,"col12" = 12:21,"col13" = 13:22)
a <- memdb_frame("col14" = 14:23,"col15" = 15:24,"col16" = 16:25)
p <- memdb_frame("col23" = 23:32,"col24" = 24:33,"col25" = 25:34,"col5" = 5:14)

left_join(s,t, 
          by = c("col1" = "col10"), 
          suffix = c("s","t"),
          x_as = "s",
          y_as = "t") %>%
  left_join(c, by = c("col9" = "col1"),
            suffix = c("s","c"),
            x_as = "s",
            y_as = "c") %>% 
  left_join(a, by = c("col11" = "col14"),
            suffix = c("t","a"),
           x_as = "t",
            y_as = "a")%>%
  left_join(p, by = c("col15" = "col23"),
            suffix = c("a","p"),
            x_as = "a",
            y_as = "p") %>% head(5)
```

And `show_query()` prints out:

```
SELECT `a`.*, `col24`, `col25`, `col5`
FROM (
  SELECT `t`.*, `col15`, `col16`
  FROM (
    SELECT `s`.*, `col11`, `col12`, `col13`
    FROM `dbplyr_016` AS `s`
    LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_017` AS `t`
      ON (`s`.`col1` = `t`.`col10`)
    LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_018` AS `c`
      ON (`s`.`col9` = `c`.`col1`)
  ) AS `t`
  LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_019` AS `a`
    ON (`t`.`col11` = `a`.`col14`)
) AS `a`
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_020` AS `p`
  ON (`a`.`col15` = `p`.`col23`)
```
which is not optimized for the Azure set-up I've been assigned.
So, in order to simplify the query, I pulled away the aliases on LHS from join 2 to 4:

```
left_join(s,t, 
          by = c("col1" = "col10"), 
          suffix = c("s","t"),
          x_as = "s",
          y_as = "t") %>%
  left_join(c, by = c("col9" = "col1"),
            suffix = c("s","c"),
            #x_as = "s",
            y_as = "c") %>% 
  left_join(a, by = c("col11" = "col14"),
            suffix = c("t","a"),
          #x_as = "t",
            y_as = "a")%>%
  left_join(p, by = c("col15" = "col23"),
            suffix = c("a","p"),
            #x_as = "a",
            y_as = "p") %>% show_query()
```

which produces the following SQL query:

```
SELECT
  `s`.*,  `col11`,  `col12`,  `col13`,  `col15`,  `col16`,  `col24`,  `col25`,  `col5`
FROM `dbplyr_016` AS `s`
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_017` AS `t`
  ON (`s`.`col1` = `t`.`col10`)
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_018` AS `c`
  ON (`s`.`col9` = `c`.`col1`)
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_019` AS `a`
  ON (`s`.`col11` = `a`.`col14`)
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_020` AS `p`
  ON (`s`.`col15` = `p`.`col23`)
```
`collect()`returns: `Error in collect(): ! Failed to collect lazy table. Caused by error: ! no such column: s.col11`.
And indeed, the column `col11` comes from `t` and not `s`. So how can I ensure to have the right LHS picked while having a short SQL query?

In advance, thanks a lot for your answer!

Best,
D.

title: ORACLE RANDOM Synonym
description:
I am working with a sample in a Oracle ODBC.

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  drv = odbc::odbc(), 
  dsn = "oracle_dsn"
)

my_table <- tbl(con, in_schema("my_schema", "my_table"))

n <- 100
my_table  %>% slice_sample(n = n) %>% show_query()

```

Showing this query

```sql
SELECT
  "column 1",
  "column 2",
   ....
FROM (
  SELECT
      "column 1",
     "column 2",
       ....,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY **RANDOM()**) AS "q02"
  FROM ("my_schema"."my_table") 
) "q01"
WHERE ("q02" <= 100)
```

But ORACLE does not recognize RANDOM without the package prefix dbms_random (that statement works replacing RANDOM() by dbms_random.RANDOM()).

I do not have privileges to make that synonym in my Oracle database, but I thought should do not assume a synonym.

Could you add the prefix or show me how to? Thanks.

title: Piped left joins get no results
description:
Dear all,

I'm currently working on an Azure database. I wrote piped left joins in order to gather data from different tables and nothing ever comes back. In comparison to my code, a colleague wrote an SQL query with the same purpose and it did work. Nonetheless, I would like to keep on working with dbplyr's verbs (otherwise I feel I'd have to work only with SQL) which is why I need some support.

Here's my reprex:

```
s <- memdb_frame("col1" = 1:10,"col2" = 2:11,"col3" = 3:12,"col4" = 4:13,"col5" = 5:14,"col6" = 6:15,"col7" = 7:16,"col8" = 8:17,"col9" = 9:18)
t <- memdb_frame("col10" = 10:19,"col11" = 11:20)
c <- memdb_frame("col1" = 1:10,"col12" = 12:21,"col13" = 13:22)
a <- memdb_frame("col14" = 14:23,"col15" = 15:24,"col16" = 16:25,"col17" = 17:26,"col18" = 18:27,"col19" = 19:28,"col20" = 20:29,"col21" = 21:30,"col8" = 8:17,"col22" = 22:31)
p <- memdb_frame("col23" = 23:32,"col24" = 24:33,"col25" = 25:34,"col5" = 5:14,"col26" = 26:35,"col27" = 27:36,"col28" = 28:37,"col29" = 29:38)

 left_join(s,t, 
          by = c("col1" = "col10"), 
          suffix = c("s","t"),
          x_as = "s",
          y_as = "t") %>%
  left_join(c, by = c("col9" = "col1"),
            suffix = c("s","c"),
            x_as = "s",
            y_as = "c") %>% 
  left_join(a, by = c("col11" = "col14"),
            suffix = c("t","a"),
            x_as = "t",
            y_as = "a")%>%
  left_join(p, by = c("col15" = "col23"),
            suffix = c("a","p"),
            x_as = "a",
            y_as = "p") %>% 
show_query()
```

which returns:

```
<SQL>
SELECT
  `col1`, `col2`,  `col3`,  `col4`,
  `a`.`col5` AS `col5a`,
  `col6`,  `col7`,`col8t`,`col9`,  `col11`,  `col12`,  `col13`,  `col15`,  `col16`,  `col17`,  `col18`,  `col19`,  `col20`,  `col21`,  `col8a`,  `col22`,  `col24`,  `col25`,
  `p`.`col5` AS `col5p`,
  `col26`,  `col27`,  `col28`,  `col29`
FROM (
  SELECT
    `col1`,    `col2`,`col3`,`col4`,`col5`, `col6`,`col7`,
    `t`.`col8` AS `col8t`,
    `col9`,    `col11`,`col12`,`col13`,`col15`,`col16`,`col17`,`col18`,`col19`,`col20`,`col21`,
    `a`.`col8` AS `col8a`,    `col22`
  FROM (
    SELECT
      `s`.`col1` AS `col1`,     
 `col2`,`col3`,`col4`,`col5`,`col6`,`col7`,`col8`,`col9`,`col11`,`col12`,`col13`
    FROM (
      SELECT
        `col1`,`col2`,`col3`,`col4`,`col5`,`col6`,`col7`,`col8`,`col9`,`col11`
      FROM `dbplyr_016` AS `s`
      LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_017` AS `t`
        ON (`s`.`col1` = `t`.`col10`)
    ) AS `s`
    LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_018` AS `c`
      ON (`s`.`col9` = `c`.`col1`)
  ) AS `t`
  LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_019` AS `a`
    ON (`t`.`col11` = `a`.`col14`)
) AS `a`
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_020` AS `p`
  ON (`a`.`col15` = `p`.`col23`)
```

In comparison, the SQL query I received is:

```
SELECT s.col1,s.col2,s.col3,s.col4,s.col5,s.col6,s.col7,s.col8,s.col9,
t.col10,t.col11,
c.col1,c.col12,c.col13,
a.col14,a.col15,a.col16,a.col17,a.col18,a.col19,a.col20,a.col21,a.col22,a.col8,
p.col23,p.col24,p.col25,p.col26,p.col27,p.col28,p.col29,p.col5
FROM s as s
left join t as t
on s.col1= t.col10
left join c as c
on s.col9 = c.col1
left join a as a
on t.11 = a.14
left join p as p
on a.col15 = p.col23
```

Would you be able to tell me what could I improve to have dbplyr's creating more or less the same SQL query?

In advance, thanks a lot for your support.

Best regards,
D.

title: Support for drop_na
description:
It would be nice to have support for `drop_na` from `dplyr`.

It can be implemented as a filter with `!is.na(column)`, but this would make code more reusable, and it would be easier to call for multiple columns.

I was wondering if this has already been considered? I see some solutions suggested here: https://stackoverflow.com/a/66812251/435093 — but `paste0("!is.na(",colnames,")")` and `filter(!!!parse_exprs(conditions))` look like something that `dbplyr` won't do …

title: fill() not working with tbl_MoJAthenaConnection object
description:
Hi,

I am having trouble running verb `tidyr::fill` with `dbplyr`. I am working with sensitive data, so apologies for lack of a reprex.

Consider that `df` is a `tbl_MoJAthenaConnection` object. Columns ID, B & C are, respectively, numeric, character and character.

```
df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(ID, B) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(C, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
    tidyr::fill(C, .direction = 'down') %>%
    dplyr::ungroup()

Error: InvalidRequestException (HTTP 400). line 82:34: mismatched input 'IGNORE'. Expecting: ',', <expression>
```

I looked for hints in the SQL code using `dbplyr::sql_render(df)` and found that this bit:

```
LAST_VALUE("C" IGNORE NULLS) OVER (PARTITION BY "ID", "B" ORDER BY "ID", "B", "C") AS "C"
```

may need to be rewritten as

```
LAST_VALUE("C") IGNORE NULLS OVER (PARTITION BY "ID", "B" ORDER BY "ID", "B", "C") AS "C"
```

(i.e. move `IGNORE NULLS` outside the parentheses). Could you check?

Thanks

title: grepl on Snowflake needs parentheses surrounding pattern
description:
On Snowflake, patterns like `a|b` do not work properly, because they translate to
```r
REGEXP ('.*' || ('a|b') || '.*)
```
Which is equivalent (due to implicit anchoring on both ends) to
```r
REGEXP ('(.*a$)|(^b.*)')
```

Patterns like `a|b` should instead translate to
```r
REGEXP ('.*' || '(a|b)' || '.*)
```
(parens inside string)

This is addressed by #989 .

The blow code works fine with `dbplyr` v. 2.1.1.9000 for a `tbl` object named `re`:

```

re %>%
    dplyr::distinct() %>%
    dplyr::group_by(
      dplyr::across(
        dplyr::all_of(groups)

    ) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(n = dplyr::n())
```

title: copy_inline() not working on oracle backends
description:
This is basically a repeat of the issues listed in https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/950, but for Oracle backends.

```
copy_inline(con, tibble(a=c(1,1), b=c(2,3)))
```
> Error in .oci.SendQuery(conn, statement, data = data, prefetch = prefetch,  : 
>  ORA-00903: invalid table name

As for the Hana DB it seems the `values` command does not yield the desired result and you need use `union all ` in combination with selecting from `dual` in the query. So instead of the previous query this works:

```
SELECT CAST("a" AS NUMBER) AS "a", CAST("b" AS NUMBER) AS "b"
FROM (
  (
    SELECT NULL AS "a", NULL AS "b"
    FROM dual 
    WHERE (0 = 1)
  )
  UNION ALL
  (select 1.0, 2.0 from dual union all select 1.0, 3.0 from dual)
) "values_table"

```

title: How to handle other column types in `rows_append()` and `rows_insert()`?
description:
Inserting in a `jsonb` column is not that easy

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres())

if (DBI::dbExistsTable(con, "..json_test")) {
  DBI::dbRemoveTable(con, "..json_test")
}

DBI::dbExecute(
  con,
  'CREATE TABLE "..json_test" (
    id integer NOT NULL,
    json_field jsonb
  )'
)
#> [1] 0

data.frame(id = 1, json_field = "[1, 2, 3]") %>% 
  rows_append(
    x = tbl(con, "..json_test"),
    copy = TRUE,
    in_place = TRUE
  )
#> Error: Failed to fetch row: ERROR:  column "json_field" is of type jsonb but expression is of type text
#> LINE 2: SELECT *
#>                ^
#> HINT:  You will need to rewrite or cast the expression.
DBI::dbReadTable(con, "..json_test")
#> [1] id         json_field
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

# need to explicitly copy and cast beforehand
copy_inline(con, data.frame(id = 1, json_field = "[1, 2, 3]")) %>% 
  mutate(json_field = sql("json_field::jsonb")) %>% 
  rows_append(
    x = tbl(con, "..json_test"),
    in_place = TRUE
  )
DBI::dbReadTable(con, "..json_test")
#>   id json_field
#> 1  1  [1, 2, 3]
```

Maybe we can add explicit casts. Otherwise, we should add an example how to deal with this yourself

title: Joins and set operations queries not reused in CTEs
description:
``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf1 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, .name = "lf1")
lf <- lf1 %>% 
  filter(x == 1)

# the CTE for `lf` is reused
union_all(
  lf,
  lf
) %>% 
  show_query(cte = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> WITH `q01` AS (
#>   SELECT *
#>   FROM `lf1`
#>   WHERE (`x` = 1.0)
#> )
#> (
#>   SELECT *
#>   FROM `q01`
#> )
#> UNION ALL
#> (
#>   SELECT *
#>   FROM `q01`
#> )

# the CTE for `lf` is not reused
lf <- lf1 %>% 
  inner_join(lf1, by = "x")
union_all(
  lf,
  lf
) %>% 
  show_query(cte = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> WITH `q01` AS (
#>   SELECT `lf1_LHS`.`x` AS `x`
#>   FROM `lf1` AS `lf1_LHS`
#>   INNER JOIN `lf1` AS `lf1_RHS`
#>     ON (`lf1_LHS`.`x` = `lf1_RHS`.`x`)

#>   INNER JOIN `lf1` AS `lf1_RHS`
#>     ON (`lf1_LHS`.`x` = `lf1_RHS`.`x`)
#> )
#> (
#>   SELECT *
#>   FROM `q01`
#> )
```

title: Omit aliases in joins?
description:
It just occurred to me that in this query:

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf1 <- lazy_frame(a = 1, b = 2, c = 1, .name = "lf1")
lf2 <- lazy_frame(a = 1, b = 2, z = 1, .name = "lf2")

#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `LHS`.*, `z`
#> FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
#> LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS`
#>   ON (`LHS`.`a` = `RHS`.`a` AND `LHS`.`b` = `RHS`.`b`)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Since the LHS and the RHS of the join are simple tables, we could drop the aliases, and write:

```R
#> <SQL>

#> FROM `lf1`
#> LEFT JOIN `lf2`
#>   ON (`lf1`.`a` = `lf2`.`a` AND `lf1`.`b` = `lf2`.`b`)
```

title: Translate `window_order` to `arrange` for local data frames
description:
Feature request: Add `window_order` to `dplyr` for local data frames. 

Following on from tidyverse/dplyr#2874, it seems that using `arrange()` to produce windows using SQL sources yields a warning like this:

```
## Warning: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
## ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead?
```

This is fine, as either I can just swap out `arrange` for `window_order` and the code runs or I can select `warning=FALSE` in the code chunk options.

There are two downsides to the former approach:

1. Because `window_order` lives in `dbplyr`, its use requires either `dbplyr::window_order` or `library(dbplyr)`.
2. The code becomes adapted to SQL sources, as it will no longer work with local data frames. (I find myself often inserting or removing a `collect()` call as I mess around with data, as **if one is careful and uses standard `dplyr` verbs**, code works in either place. This is a really nice feature.)

If `window_order` existed for local data frames, then both problems would be solved. And it seems it has a well-defined meaning in that new context.

title: Combine `*_join()` + `select()` in one query
description:
A `*_join()` followed by `select()` currently produces an unnecessary subquery. This can easily be combined in a single query.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2)

left_join(lf, lf2, by = "x") %>% 
  select(x, b)
```

Currently

```sql
SELECT `x`, `b`
FROM (
  SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
  FROM `df` AS `LHS`
  LEFT JOIN `df` AS `RHS`
    ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
) `q01`
```

Should be

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `b`
FROM `df` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

```r
semi_join(lf, lf2, by = "x") %>% 
  select(x)
```

Currently

```sql
SELECT `x`
FROM (
  SELECT * FROM `df` AS `LHS`
  WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM `df` AS `RHS`
    WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
  )
) `q01`
```

Should be

```sql
SELECT x FROM `df` AS `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM `df` AS `RHS`
  WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
)
```

title: Bug: can use `distinct()` on removed variable
description:
The issue exists in the CRAN and the dev version of `dbplyr`.

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1) %>% 
  select(-x) %>% 
  distinct(x)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `x`
#> FROM `df`
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

The issue is in `partial_eval_sym()`:

```r
partial_eval_sym <- function(sym, data, env) {
  vars <- op_vars(data)
  name <- as_string(sym)
  if (name %in% vars) {
    sym
  } else if (env_has(env, name, inherit = TRUE)) {
    eval_bare(sym, env)
  } else { # this else clause is the issue
    sym
  }
}
```

Currently, this is needed in three places:

* `across()`: this calls `partial_eval_call()` where we might use `.x` or function arguments.
* `mutate()` with references to previously created variables (this won't be necessary after merging #802).
* one test for `partial_eval()` where this behaviour is explicitly tested ("existing non-variables get inlined"). But this test was only added recently when aligning `partial_eval()` with `dtplyr`, so I think it can be removed.

So, overall I think this can be removed and the evaluation can be made a bit safer.

title: count() does not group transiently
description:
As per the help page, I would expect count() to act like summarise(n = n()) and tally() and only drop the last level of grouping (like .groups = "drop_last"). In practice, count() drops all levels of grouping (like .groups = "drop").
In addition, when using count() on a remote SQL database, count() behaves as expected, dropping only the last level of grouping. This makes the two applications of count() inconsistent with each other.

```r
# Reprex
library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                 .connection_string = "driver={SQL Server Native Client 10.0};
                 server=#######################;
                 database=###########;
                 Trusted_Connection=yes", 
                 timeout = 10)

# First local -------------------------------------------------------------

as_tibble(mtcars) %>% 
  count(gear, am)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#> gear    am     n

as_tibble(mtcars) %>% 
  group_by(gear, am) %>% 
  summarise(n = n())
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'gear'. You can override using the `.groups` argument.
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#> # Groups:   gear [3]
#> gear    am     n

as_tibble(mtcars) %>% 
  group_by(gear, am) %>% 
  tally()
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#> # Groups:   gear [3]
#> gear    am     n

# Now remote --------------------------------------------------------------

as_tibble(mtcars) %>% 
  copy_to(con, ., name = "#mtcars")

tbl(con, "#mtcars") %>% 
  count(gear, am)
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 3]
#> # Database: Microsoft SQL Server 15.00.4198[########################################]
#> # Groups:   gear
#> gear    am     n

tbl(con, "#mtcars") %>% 
  group_by(gear, am) %>% 
  summarise(n = n())
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'gear'. You can override using the `.groups` argument.
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 3]
#> # Database: Microsoft SQL Server 15.00.4198[########################################]
#> # Groups:   gear
#> gear    am     n

tbl(con, "#mtcars") %>% 
  group_by(gear, am) %>% 
  tally()
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 3]
#> # Database: Microsoft SQL Server 15.00.4198[########################################]
#> # Groups:   gear
#> gear    am     n
```

I am using R version 4.0.2, RStudio version 1.3.1073, tidyverse version 1.3.1 and DBI version 1.1.1.

title: Error when including `stringr` (`str_to_title` and such) in a filter
description:
When including one of `stringr::str_to_title()`, `stringr::str_to_lower()`, `stringr::str_to_upper()`, or `str_c()` in a filter relying on `dbplyr`, I get an error.

See reprex below for details. 

This [issue has been previously reported on `pool`](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/issues/132), but it appears to be a `dbplyr` issue.

As [mentioned in a comment there](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/issues/132#issuecomment-1164779807), it appears that the solution is simply to "force the `str_to_title()` computation to happen locally."

Indeed, this is the workaround I used myself. 

I still thought it was worth reporting, as this all worked as expected before the `dbplyr 2.2.0` update, and the change broke a number of scripts I had, as well as a CRAN package I maintain (I fixed this on my side, so not any more an issue at this stage). 



``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
months <- data.frame(
  abb = head(month.abb),
  name = head(month.name)
)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "months", months)

months_db <- tbl(con, "months")

months_db |>
  filter(abb %in% stringr::str_to_title(c("feb", "apr")))
#> Error: no such table: INITCAP

months_db |>
  filter(abb %in% stringr::str_to_title(c("feb", "apr"))) |>
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `months`
#> WHERE (`abb` IN INITCAP(('feb', 'apr')))
```

title: Failure to handle column renaming before grouping
description:
Hi, this is my first issue so hopefully I have provided enough of a reprex to work with - please let me know if I can provide additional information.

**Brief description of the problem**

Rendering a query for Oracle from `dplyr`, I rename columns in a SELECT statement before doing a GROUP BY. The SELECT is tricky because I rename my grouping column to take the name of one of the non-grouping columns (which is also renamed). This appears to confuse `dbplyr`: it groups on what should be the non-grouping column and drops my intended grouping column.

**Expected output**

I would expect the SQL for `dbplyr` to handle the renaming _before_ the grouping, and thus to group by (and retain when summarizing) the just-renamed column. This is the behavior observed in the non-remote `dplyr` example on `mtcars` below.

Please note that as far as I can tell, the query ran as expected with version 2.1.1 of `dbplyr`.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(odbc)
library(DBI)
library(dbplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     ident, sql
library(dplyr)

packageVersion("tidyverse")
#> [1] '1.3.1'
packageVersion("odbc")
#> [1] '1.3.2'
packageVersion("DBI")
#> [1] '1.1.1'
packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '2.2.1'
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.9'

# Query run on Oracle DB

con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(),
                      Driver = "Oracle in OraClient64_home1",
                      DBQ   = *redacted*,
                      UID    = *redacted*,
                      PWD    = *redacted*)

licsfull <- tbl(con, in_schema("GLBL_MAIN", "G_MATL_LIC")) %>%
  select(MATL_ID = REF_MATL_ID, JOIN_ID = MATL_ID, VALID_TO_DT) %>%
  group_by(MATL_ID) %>%
  summarise(JOIN_ID = max(JOIN_ID, na.rm = TRUE),
            VALID_TO_DT = max(VALID_TO_DT, na.rm = TRUE))

# The generated SQL drops the desired grouping column and joins on a different column

licsfull %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT MAX("JOIN_ID") AS "JOIN_ID", MAX("VALID_TO_DT") AS "VALID_TO_DT"
```

title: compute() breaks schemas in dbplyr 2.2.0
description:
The addition of an unconditional call to `unname()` in `compute.tbl_sql()` added in #793 breaks use of schemas and catalogs, since both `dbplyr::in_schema()` and `dbplyr::in_catalog()` rely on names to identify the parts of the table identifier.  Once the names are removed, a schema-qualified table name always renders as "NULL.NULL" (and similarly for catalog-schema-qualified tables).

```r
require(dplyr)
require(RSQLite)
db <- DBI::dbConnect(SQLite(), ':memory:')
schematized <- dbplyr::in_schema('test', 'this')
# Create a table to select and compute
mtcars %>% slice_head(n = 5) %>% copy_to(db, ., name = 'this')
thistbl <- tbl(db, 'this')
#Bang
thistbl %>% compute(name = schematized)
```
yields `Error: near "NULL": syntax error`

A minimal fix would be to preserve names in cases we know they'll be needed:

```
 if (!any(class(name) %in% c('dbplyr_schema', 'dbplyr_catalog'))) name <- unname(name)
```

title: Error with group_by and across in version 2.2.1
description:
In version 2.2.1, using across after a group_by expression gives the following error : 

```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)

mf <- memdb_frame(ID = 1:5, b = 1:5, c = 10:6)

mf %>% 
  group_by(ID) %>% 
  summarise(across(-ID,  ~ min(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
```
> Error in `chr_as_locations()`:
> ! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
> ✖ Column `ID` doesn't exist.
> Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

I believe this is related to what is mentioned in the across help page : 
> Because across() is used within functions like summarise() and mutate(), you can't select or compute upon grouping variables.  

But the previous code worked in version 2.1.0.
I think the error message should be more expressive.

title: dbplyr - Oracle -
description:
Thank you so much for developing `dbplyr` - it is awesome to use `dplyr` directly on databases.

I am working with `dbplyr` on a connection created with `ROracle` (not using `odbc` because of [this](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/issues/206) unfortunate issue).

I create a table with   `akv <- tbl(con, in_schema("myschema","BILAN"))`   and can access the data.

The functions `group_by()`, `summarise()`, `n()`, `is.na()` work perfectly well. However, `mutate()` returns an Error:
```
> akv %>% filter(DATBILAN==201905) %>% select(DATBILAN, RENTE) %>%  mutate(R1 = RENTE>0)  
Error in .oci.SendQuery(conn, statement, data = data, prefetch = prefetch,  : 
  ORA-00923: FROM keyword not found where expected
```

The SQL query behind this is:

```
> show_query({  akv %>% filter(DATBILAN==201905) %>% select(DATBILAN, RENTE) %>%  mutate(R1 = RENTE>0)   })
<SQL>
SELECT "DATBILAN", "RENTE", "RENTE" > 0.0 AS "R1"
FROM (AOO_AKV.T_AKV_PREST_BILAN) 
WHERE ("DATBILAN" = 201905.0)

```
whereas it should be something like this:

```
SELECT DATBILAN, RENTE, CASE WHEN RENTE > 0.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
FROM AOO_AKV.T_AKV_PREST_BILAN 
WHERE DATBILAN = 201905
```

(which works with `dbGetQuery()`)

Hope you can include this in the next version :)

title: The new version is not compatible with Oracle
description:
Hello,

The modification in this commit https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/commit/8dd7639cc84759b6c30c88f5661e97a225a2637f  is very interesting, however in the case of Oracle it is not fully functional.

In Oracle, if I want to select all the columns and add a new one, I must write the query in the following way
SELECT q01.*, COLUM_1+COLUM_2 AS VALUE FROM TEST q01;

And not as dbplyr is currently doing, which is this way.

SELECT *, COLUM_1+COLUM_2 AS VALUE FROM TEST q01;

The big difference is that the * is preceded by the name that the table is being called, which in this case is q01

Thank you.

title: bug report
description:
We use dbplyr through sparklyr.
When we moved to dbplyr version 2.2.0 we got a failure during execution of a code which previously worked fine, while getting the following error message: 
"Error in dbi_ensure_no_backtick(x) : Can't escape back tick from string"
It happens when we sprarklyr::collect a spark data frame after some dplyr::anti_join operation.
We workaround it by applying sprarklyr::collect to each of the two data frames and then do the dplyr::anti_join on the resulted R data frames, instead of anti_join the original spark data frames.

title: Improve readability of subqueries
description:
`dbplyr` generated SQL would be much easier to understand if one could add custom subquery names or even create CTE ("with" clause). For example

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

tbl_lazy(nycflights13::flights) %>% 
  group_by(dest) %>% 
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  filter(delay, count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```

produces (I added some indentation to improve readability already a bit)

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `df`
  GROUP BY `dest`
) `q01`
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))
```

This would be a bit easier with a custom name for the subquery

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `df`
  GROUP BY `dest`
) `destination_summary`
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))
```

and even better with a CTE

```sql
WITH `destination_summary` AS (
  SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `df`
  GROUP BY `dest`
)
```

title: Feature Request: Force use of indices in query
description:
Hey there,

I'm sure the particular use case I'm going to describe here is relatively rare, but I still feel like adding additional customizability could further improve `dbplyr`. I'm running an absolutely gigantic disk-based SQLite DB in a sandbox for data analysis and to get literally anything done, I have to rely pretty heavily on indexes. Most of my other `dpblyr` work typically does not rely heavily on indices so I haven't seen any native patterns for forcing their use before. I've appreciated the ability to create indexes in `copy_to`, but wish there was a way to force a query generated by `dbplyr` to use provided indices. For example, suppose we have a common join column, `join_col` in two datasets, `x` and `y`. 

I have indexed column `join_col` in both `x` and `y`, but it appears that the query optimizer occasionally doesn't use these two indexes when joining the datasets. In SQL, there are typically ways to enforce usage of indices, so a similar `dbplyr` pattern would be the goal.

Feature request: add an optional argument, similar to `copy`, to `*_join` and maybe (?) `filter` that one can provide names of indices to
```r
left_join(x, y, by = 'join_col', copy = TRUE, indexes = list('x_join_col_index', 'y_join_col_index')) 

```

title: `sd()` should accept `na.rm` argument
description:
For consistency with the other aggregation functions.

I think we could also consider warning about `na.rm` once per session for all aggregation functions, rather than once per session for each aggregation function. And that way we could take advantage of `warn()`'s `frequency` and `frequency_id` arguments, rather than hand rolling it.

title: Simplify `copy_inline()` using column aliases
description:
eg. 
```sql
SELECT CAST(`x` AS INTEGER) AS `x`, CAST(`y` AS TEXT) AS `y`
FROM 
  (VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c'), (4, 'd'), (5, 'e')) AS inline(x, y)
```

At least duckdb and postgresl support this (although SQLite does not). Postgres calls it a "column alias list", the [SQL standard](http://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~shadow/sql/sql1992.txt) calls it "derived column list".

title: `collapse()` and `compute()` do not use `tbl()` dispatch anymore
description: PR #668 was actually a breaking change. Previously, `compute()`, `collapse()` and `copy_to()` used the generic `tbl()`. Now, they use `tbl_src_dbi()` which is not a generic. The sparklyr package has defined its own method for `tbl()`. So, this change broke their `compute()` function.

title: Keep `ON` on same line as `JOIN`?
description:
In #875 I noticed that `ON` starts a new line:

```sql
SELECT `a` AS `a2`, `x1` AS `x`, `b`
FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x1` = `RHS`.`x2`)
```

I think ideally it'd remain on the same line as the join:

```sql
SELECT `a` AS `a2`, `x1` AS `x`, `b`
FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS` ON (`LHS`.`x1` = `RHS`.`x2`)
```

``` r
mytable |>
```

title: [FR] Allow database name in `in_schema`
description:
When connecting to an MSSQL Server, we can have several databases from which we can pull data. To get the quoting straight, one has to add an additional `sql` call to `in_schema` to be able to get the data in a particular database, which is not that clear:


```r
library(dbplyr)

(s1 <- in_schema("mydatabase.myschema", "mytable"))
## <SCHEMA> `mydatabase.myschema`.`mytable`
(s2 <- in_schema(sql("mydatabase.myschema"), "mytable"))
## <SCHEMA> mydatabase.myschema.`mytable`
# library(dplyr)
# con <-  dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), "mydatabase_server")
# tbl(con, s1) ## will not work
# tbl(con, s2) ## will work
```

Admittedly, my knowledge of standard SQL is mediocre at best, so there may be very good reasons for not adding a `catalog/database` parameter to `in_schema`, but at least the proper way of addressing a table in a schema in a catalog / database should be documented somewhere. w/o  [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71410349/store-new-permanent-table-in-schema-using-compute) I would yet not have any idea of how to pull data with the fully qualified name. 

Thus, either we add that to the docs or even add a new parameter to `in_schema`.

```
show_query(testr_mtcars_left)
```

title: Incorrect translation of dplyr verbs involving use of across() inside filter()
description:
Here's an interesting one. When `dplyr::across()` is used inside `dplyr::filter()`, it seems like `dbplyr` (v. 2.1.1) gets somehow confused and assigns a name to the filtering operation in the translated SQL script.

I have prepared an example below. I'm sorry that it's not reproducible, but I'm working with databases on a private server.

**Incorrect translation:**
```
some_table_field <- 'field1'

dplyr::show_query(
    some_tbl_object %>% 
        dplyr::filter(
            dplyr::across(
                dplyr::all_of(some_table_field),
                ~ !is.na(.)
            )
        )
)
```

The above returns an SQL script where the last line is a filtering combination that is assigned the name of the field:

```
<SQL>
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *
FROM "some_database"."some_table") "q01"
WHERE (NOT((("offender_id") IS NULL)) AS "offender_id")
```

However, if we manually specify the field we want to filter by in `dplyr::filter()`, the translation is correct.

Unsurprisingly, running

```
some_tbl_object %>% 
        dplyr::filter(
            dplyr::across(
                dplyr::all_of(some_table_field),
                ~ !is.na(.)
            )
        )
```

returns this error:

```
Error: InvalidRequestException (HTTP 400). line 4:39: mismatched input 'AS'. Expecting: <expression>
```

**Correct translation:**

```
dplyr::show_query(
    some_tbl_object %>% 
        dplyr::filter(!is.na('field1'))
)

#<SQL>
#SELECT *
#FROM (SELECT *
#FROM "some_database"."some_table") "q01"
#WHERE (NOT((('offender_id') IS NULL)))
```

title: quantile() ignores ordering in window_order
description:
Hi,

When using quantile() in an ordered window the ordering seems to be ignored when it's translated to SQL. 

`mf <- memdb_frame(
  tibble(
    grp = c(rep('a',4), rep('b', 5)),
    order = seq(1,9),
    val = seq(11,19)
  )
)

mf %>%
  window_order(order) %>%
  window_frame(-2,0) %>%
  mutate(
    roll_quantile = quantile(val,0.95),
    roll_sum= sum(val)
  ) %>%
  show_query()`


Output is:
`SELECT grp, order, val,
PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY val) OVER (ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS roll_quantile,
SUM(val) OVER (ORDER BY order ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS roll_sum
FROM dbplyr_001 ` 

Output should be:
`SELECT grp, order, val,
PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY val) OVER (ORDER BY order ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS roll_quantile,
SUM(val) OVER (ORDER BY order ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS roll_sum
FROM dbplyr_001`


I think this bug is related to https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/700

Regards

title: Add support for DuckDB
description:
Most things should already work but e.g. `fill()` needs to be supported via

```r
dbplyr_fill0.duckdb_connection <- dbplyr_fill0.SQLiteConnection
```

Update 2022-02-04:
DuckDB itself is currently integrating `dbplyr` support with many more function translations: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/2926

They agreed that it makes more sense for now, at least until DuckDB has reached version 1.0

> To note, some discussion related to this PR can be found from the DuckDB Discord R-channel. In short, it is probably better to have the backend bundled with DuckDB instead of putting it as a part of dbplyr at this point (at least before version 1.0) as it will be easier to update the backend in case of changes or additions in DuckDB.

title: Running the same tests against multiple backends
description:
Should we implement a wrapper around `test_that()` that would run the tests with all (registered) backends?

```r
test_that_db(except = "mysql", "some test on the database", {
  df <- memdb_frame(a = 1)
  ...
})
```

This code would run the tests once for each backend, except `"mysql"`, and append the backend to the test description. Calls to `src_memdb()` would return a connection to the test database, `memdb_frame()` should work by extension. In conjunction with #827 we would get snapshots for all supported backends at once.

I see that we can do a lot of testing with lazy frames, these would be "integration tests" that test the generated SQL against the real database.

title: Ordering in a subquery is gone
description:
Apparently `arrange(desc())` is not translated when used in a subquery.

I commented the reprex below.

``` r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))

# create in-memory database
con_mem <- RSQLite::SQLite() %>% DBI::dbConnect(":memory:")

# create table
con_mem %>% DBI::dbWriteTable("mtcars", mtcars)

# read table
con_mtcars <- con_mem %>% tbl("mtcars")

# get 3 highest carb values
top_3_carb <- con_mtcars %>%
    distinct(carb) %>%
    arrange(desc(carb)) %>%
    head(3)

top_3_carb %>% collect()
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>    carb
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     8
#> 2     6
#> 3     4

# "ORDER BY `carb` DESC" is included in SQL
top_3_carb %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT DISTINCT `carb`
#> FROM `mtcars`
#> ORDER BY `carb` DESC
#> LIMIT 3

# use it to filter mtcars
top_3_carb_mtcars_dbplyr <- top_3_carb %>%
    left_join(con_mtcars, by = "carb")

# "ORDER BY `carb` DESC" is gone
top_3_carb_mtcars_dbplyr %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `LHS`.`carb` AS `carb`, `mpg`, `cyl`, `disp`, `hp`, `drat`, `wt`, `qsec`, `vs`, `am`, `gear`
#> FROM (SELECT DISTINCT `carb`
#> FROM `mtcars`
#> LIMIT 3) AS `LHS`
#> LEFT JOIN `mtcars` AS `RHS`
#> ON (`LHS`.`carb` = `RHS`.`carb`)

# dbplyr is getting it wrong
top_3_carb_mtcars_dbplyr %>% distinct(carb) %>% collect()
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>    carb
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     4
#> 2     1
#> 3     2

identical(
    top_3_carb %>% collect(),
    top_3_carb_mtcars_dbplyr %>% distinct(carb) %>% collect()
)
#> [1] FALSE

# add "ORDER BY `carb` DESC" manually
top_3_carb_mtcars_sql <- "
SELECT `LHS`.`carb` AS `carb`, `mpg`, `cyl`, `disp`, `hp`, `drat`, `wt`, `qsec`, `vs`, `am`, `gear`
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT `carb`
FROM `mtcars`
ORDER BY `carb` DESC
LIMIT 3) AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `mtcars` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`carb` = `RHS`.`carb`)
"

# use modified SQL query directly
top_3_carb_mtcars_sqlite <- con_mem %>%
    DBI::dbGetQuery(top_3_carb_mtcars_sql) %>%
    as_tibble()

# SQL working properly
top_3_carb_mtcars_sqlite %>% distinct(carb)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>    carb
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     8
#> 2     6
#> 3     4

identical(
    top_3_carb %>% collect(),
    top_3_carb_mtcars_sqlite %>% distinct(carb)
)
```

title: Implement grepl using %like%
description:
:wave: Thanks for this amazing package. It really is such a joy.

I am wondering what if would take to implement `grepl` for other SQL variants other than [Postgresql](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/54/files). dbplyr already supports `LIKE` so that could be leveraged into a `grepl` function. Here is a quick stab at this:

```r
grepl_sql = function(pattern, x, ignore.case = FALSE, perl = FALSE, fixed = FALSE, useBytes = FALSE) {
  if (any(c(perl, fixed, useBytes))) {
    stop("perl, fixed and useBytes parameters are unsupported")
  }
  if (ignore.case) {
    build_sql("LOWER(", !!x, ") LIKE LOWER('%", !!pattern, "%')")
  } else {
    build_sql("", !!x, " LIKE '%", !!pattern, "%'")
  }
}
```

This would mimic dplyr behaviour like this:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(DBI)
```

title: feature to rename sql tables using tbl() function
description:
There should be a feature in the `tbl` function where one could rename the table.
```SQL
SELECT * FROM test_tbl_1 as t1
INNER JOIN test_tbl_2 as t2 ON t1.a = t2.a
```
Reprex
```R
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

# Hack solution
test_tbl_1 <- memdb_frame(a = 1:4, b = 11:14, .name = "test_tbl_1")
test_tbl_2 <- memdb_frame(a = 1:4, c = 21:24, .name = "test_tbl_2")
lazy_tbl <- test_tbl_1 %>% 
  rename_all(function(x) paste0("t1.", x)) %>% 
  inner_join(
    test_tbl_2 %>% rename_all(function(x) paste0("t2.", x)), 
    by = c("t1.a" = "t2.a")
  )
lazy_tbl
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 3]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.30.1 [:memory:]
#>    t1.a  t1.b  t2.c
#>   <int> <int> <int>
#> 1     1    11    21
#> 2     2    12    22
#> 3     3    13    23
#> 4     4    14    24
lazy_tbl %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `LHS`.`t1.a` AS `t1.a`, `LHS`.`t1.b` AS `t1.b`, `RHS`.`t2.c` AS `t2.c`
#> FROM (SELECT `a` AS `t1.a`, `b` AS `t1.b`
#> FROM `test_tbl_1`) AS `LHS`
#> INNER JOIN (SELECT `a` AS `t2.a`, `c` AS `t2.c`
#> FROM `test_tbl_2`) AS `RHS`
#> ON (`LHS`.`t1.a` = `RHS`.`t2.a`)

# Elegant solution -> tbl function has argument `as`
tryCatch(
  tbl(src_memdb(), "test_tbl_1", as = "t1") %>%
    inner_join(tbl(src_memdb(), "test_tbl_2", as = "t2"), by = c("t1.a" = "t2.a")) %>% show_query(),
  error = function(e) {
    build_sql("
SELECT t1.a, t1.b, t2.c FROM test_tbl_1 as t1
INNER JOIN test_tbl_2 as t2 ON t1.a = t2.a", con = simulate_mssql())
  }
)
#> <SQL> 
#> SELECT t1.a, t1.b, t2.c FROM test_tbl_1 as t1
#> INNER JOIN test_tbl_2 as t2 ON t1.a = t2.a
```

title: Only select necessary columns in nested queries
description:
Currently when you instantiate a table with tbl(conn,'table_name') it creates a select a, b, c from table_name with all columns referenced.

With a columnar database pulling fewer columns make for a faster query. It would be great both from that perspective and from a clean query perspective, for dbplyr to be able to drop unused columns from the query.

For example: 
table = tbl(conn,'poes')
table %>% 
group_by(id) %>% 
summarise(a = max(username, na.rm=T)) %>% 
sql_render()

<SQL> SELECT "id", MAX("username") AS "a"
FROM (SELECT "tickerexchange", "tickervalue", "confidence", "createddate", "updateddate", "deleted", "username", "fund", "tickernoteid", "currencycode", "createdby", "tickervalueloc", "systemcreateddate", "systemupdateddate", "subfund", "confidenceoverride", "lastfileupdateddate", "islatestrecord", "id", "overridestatus", "convictionoverridereason", "initial_ticker", "system_created_datetime", "client_created_datetime"
FROM quant.dbo.poes) "dbplyr_002"
GROUP BY "id"


Ideally this query should instead look like:
<SQL> SELECT "id", MAX("username") AS "a"
FROM (SELECT "username", "id"
FROM quant.dbo.poes) "dbplyr_002"
GROUP BY "id"

title: Add support for week function on PostgreSQL backend
description:
Add support for `week` function to be translated in PostgreSQL backend. This should be fairly easy to do since PostgreSQL has a native implementation of this.

As specified in [Postgres documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.1/functions-datetime.html), we can extract the week from a Date column with the following:

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(WEEK FROM TIMESTAMP '2001-02-16 20:38:40');
Result: 7
```

We can easily implement this directly into the backend.

title: Default translation of unions to Hive does not work
description:
Hi there,

Again, I don't know if this is an issue of the specific version of Hive (2.1.1-cdh6.2.1) or a general one.
The default translation of unions puts the two `SELECT` statements on both sides of `UNION` into parantheses.
This is no problem in Impala, but in Hive I get a syntax error about an unexpected string near UNION `(`. 

```r
df <- tibble(x = 1:10,
            group = c(rep("a", 3), rep("b", 4), rep("c", 3))
            )

df_a <- lazy_frame(df = df, con = simulate_hive()) %>% 
  filter(group == "a")

df_b <- lazy_frame(df = df, con = simulate_hive()) %>% 
  filter(group == "b")

union_all(df_a, df_b) %>% 
  show_query()
```

The query generated will be 

```sql
(SELECT *
FROM `df`
WHERE (`group` = 'a'))
UNION ALL
(SELECT *
FROM `df`
WHERE (`group` = 'b')) 
```

I tried a similar simple query with an actual database in HUE and the parantheses seemed to have caused the issue. At least without them it worked.

The ideal translation would be thus:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM `df`
WHERE (`group` = 'a')
UNION ALL
SELECT *
FROM `df`
WHERE (`group` = 'b') 
```

In my real-life application the query is much more complex and dbplyr works with naming intermediate queries `q01` et cetera. This is fine, but also the outer ones, i.e. the two sides of the UNION ALL are named like this via placing the SELECT queries in parentheses and this should be avoided.

Looking forward to hearing your views/experiences and possible fixes!
Best,
Alex

title: Translate conditional sums in Hive differently
description:
Translate conditional sums in Hive differently
---

Hi everyone,

I don't know if this is a specific issue of the Hive version in my company (2.1.1-cdh6.2.1) or a general one, but it seems that it does not like to sum up Booleans.
I had experimented doing some calculations with Impala first where these operations worked, but for some specific calculations (approximate percentiles) it made more sense to move everything to Hive. In both Impala and Hive these conditional sums in R `sum(var == specific_value)` are translated the same, but only work in Impala.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
df <- tibble(x = 1:10,
            group = c(rep("a", 3), rep("b", 4), rep("c", 3))
            )

lazy_frame(df = df, con = simulate_impala()) %>% 
  summarise(n_a = sum(group == "a"),
            n_b = sum(group == "b"),
            n_c = sum(group == "c")) %>% 
  show_query()

lazy_frame(df = df, con = simulate_hive()) %>% 
  summarise(n_a = sum(group == "a"),
            n_b = sum(group == "b"),
            n_c = sum(group == "c")) %>% 
  show_query()
```

```sql
SELECT SUM(`group` = 'a') AS `n_a`, SUM(`group` = 'b') AS `n_b`, SUM(`group` = 'c') AS `n_c`
FROM `df`
````

Would it be useful in Hive connections to translate conditions in a sum by default into an `IF(group = 'a', 1, 0)`, as also described [on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25130681/how-hive-ql-do-query-with-multiple-count-function-and-make-a-divides-methon-with)? I tested this within HUE and it worked fine.

For now I will probably just solve my issue by explicitly changing the condition in the R code, that should do the trick. 
This conditional sum was the better way to do this as I had other calculations that were not done at this grouping. The alternative way of doing those other calculations separately, then grouping by the group, counting, pivoting and joining everything together seemed more cumbersome in this context.

Looking forward to hearing your feedback on this!

In the same context I also noticed that there were problems translating unions into a Hive query while they were fine for Impala, but those queries were quite complex and will require some digging on Monday... I will just open a different issue for that.

Best,
Alex

title: support for cut() function in dbplyr (snowflake)
description:
Hi, 

I'm using dbplyr to interface with Snowflake, and a very common task is to group numeric columns by bands to summarise output. With classic dplyr one would do group_by(cut(factor, c(1, 2, 3))) and it works wonders, but dbplyr does not appear to support it (at least in snowflake). 

So this is a post of two halves:
1) Could we please build in support for cut() function in SQL translations?
2) In the mean time, what would be the best workaround for this? 

e.g. i can build a function that creates an appropriate sql phrase, but how do I get it to be evaluated properly?

```
db_cut <- function(fact, bins) {
  k = length(bins)
  string = paste0("CASE WHEN ", fact, " < ", bins[1], " THEN '<", bins[1], "' ")   
  for (i in 2:k) {
    string = paste(string,
                   paste0("WHEN ", fact, " < ", bins[i], " THEN '[",
                          bins[i-1], "-", bins[i], ")' "))}
  string = paste0(string, " END")
  return(string)
}

this does not work...:
data %>%
  mutate(bands = db_cut(column_name, c(1, 2, 3))) %>%
  group_by(bands) %>%
  summarise(n()) 

```

am I missing something simple, or going down the wrong path?

Thanks!

title: Pagination with LIMIT and OFFSET
description:
Feature Request.

I'm working on a plumber API and am looking to add pagination to one of my endpoints with LIMIT and OFFSET as described [here](https://www.petefreitag.com/item/451.cfm). 

My database is mysql driven and I connect using a pool.

I expected to be able to build a query that translated to:

```sql

SELECT * FROM iris ORDER BY index LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1

```
I'm unable to build the functionality with current dbplyr functions without building the query with string manipulation. My entire code base uses dbplyr constructed queries and I'd like to maintain that consistency.

```r
library(odbc)
library(DBI)
library(pool)

library(tidyverse) 
library(dbplyr)

con <- pool::dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), host = ":memory:")

iris$index = seq(nrow(iris))
dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)
iris2 <- tbl(con, "iris")

iris2 %>% 
  select(index, Sepal.Length) %>%
  arrange(index) %>%
  head(n = 2) %>% # expected to add an offset here
  show_query() %>%
  collect() # or expected to add an offset here
```

My work around involved creating a row_number column which I then filter by to get the selected entries.

```r
start = 2
end = 3

iris2 %>% 
  select(index, Sepal.Length) %>%
  arrange(index) %>%
  mutate(row_number = row_number()) %>%
  filter(row_number >= start & row_number <= end) %>%
  select(-row_number) %>%
  show_query()

```
This gives the required output in this case by chance, but ignores the `ORDER BY` part of the query due to the additional `SELECT`. I want my users to be able to collect the pages of entries with a specific order given, hence I can't move the arrange to the end of the pipeline to prevent this.

I also tried a solution described [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57651458/how-to-read-data-from-a-database-by-chunk-in-r). But as I'm using pool I cannot use `sql_render` to easily append to the query, I could checkout a connection but really like the pool handling of my database connections.

This functionality would really help enable R in a production setting I feel. 

Thanks

title: as.wkb() / as.wkt() support for dbplyr
description:
It is currently challenging to use `dbplyr` with spatial columns. There seems to be work going on to improve various database backends to support recognition of spatial types (e.g., https://github.com/r-dbi/RPostgres/issues/114, https://github.com/r-dbi/DBI/issues/225). I'm wondering if there is a simpler solution in the meantime: develop interfaces for `as.wkb()` and `as.wkt()` that implement a [SQL translation](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/sql-translation.html). For example, for a MS SQL Server  database:

```r
tbl(conn, "some_table") %>%
  transmute(WKB = as.wkb(Shape)) %>%
  show_query()

# <SQL>
# SELECT Shape.STAsBinary() AS WKB
# FROM "dbo"."vwBathymetryGrid
```

And then it's up to the user to deal with the WKB/WKT, e.g., using `package:wk`.

title: Extra arguments in explain() do not reach backend specific sql_query_explain -method
description:
Postgres-backend includes a format argument to the [`sql_query_explain` -method](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/27dec37db0187328ba9080e56603bacc4ec708f9/R/backend-postgres.R#L224-L233). However, that argument never survives to the function, and default value is always used. This is very restrictive for the backends that would benefit for passing arguments to the method.

To demonstrate the issue, the following reprex changes the `sql_query_explain` -method of SQLiteConnection so that the value of the argument becomes visible.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# Adding format argument (from Postgres explain) to SQLite explain
sql_query_explain.SQLiteConnection <- function(con, sql, format = "text", ...) {
  dbplyr:::cat_line("Parameter 'format' with value: ", format)
  build_sql("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN ", sql, con = con)
}
assignInNamespace("sql_query_explain.SQLiteConnection", sql_query_explain.SQLiteConnection, ns = "dbplyr")

con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
df <- copy_to(con, tibble(x=1))
df %>% explain(format="json") # Value below should be: json
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `tibble(x = 1)`
#> 
#> <PLAN>
#> Parameter 'format' with value: text
#>   id parent notused             detail
#> 1  2      0       0 SCAN tibble(x = 1)
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: Create nicer SQL
description:
The SQL queries generated by `dbplyr` are not very readable. Of course one can use one of the many available online SQL formatters but it would be still be very nice if the query itself would be more readable.

For example turn this

```SQL
SELECT `x.x`, `x.y`, `y`
FROM (SELECT `x.x`, `x.y`, `y`, AVG(`x.x`) OVER (PARTITION BY `y`) AS `q01`
FROM (SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x.x`, `RHS`.`x` AS `x.y`, `y`
FROM `dbplyr_001` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_002` AS `RHS`
ON (LHS.x < RHS.x)
))
WHERE (`q01` > 1.0)
```

into something like this

```SQL
SELECT `x.x`,
       `x.y`,
       `y`
FROM
  (SELECT `x.x`,
          `x.y`,
          `y`,
          AVG(`x.x`) OVER (PARTITION BY `y`) AS `q01`
   FROM
     (SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x.x`,
             `RHS`.`x` AS `x.y`,
             `y`
      FROM `dbplyr_001` AS `LHS`
      LEFT JOIN `dbplyr_002` AS `RHS` ON (LHS.x < RHS.x)))
WHERE (`q01` > 1.0)
```

I looked around a little for existing R packages providing an SQL formatter but there seems to hardly any. I found [sqlparseR](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/sqlparseR/index.html) which has quite a lot of extra Python dependencies.

`dbplyr` could directly generate pretty SQL code but this would probably require quite a bit of work and maintenance. So, it might be easier to create a wrapper around an existing SQL formatter.

title: add SQL translation for weighted.mean
description:
I often encounter the need to perform weighted average calculations. R has a neat functionality to perform this with `weighted.mean`. It's even more useful when there are missing values, in which I can provide `na.rm = TRUE`. 

I think it's worthwhile providing a `weighted.mean` translation for dbplyr. Mainly because, the method in which we produce weighted average calculations is verbose:

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(babynames)
library(dbplyr)
baby_db <- tbl_memdb(babynames)

## R and dplyr
babynames %>% 
  summarize(wavg_prop = weighted.mean(prop, n))
## dbplyr
baby_db %>% 
  summarize(wavg_prop = sum(prop * n) / sum(n))
```
This becomes a little more verbose and repetitive when missing values are apparent:

```r
set.seed(1337)
babynames_missing <- babynames
babynames_missing[sample(1:nrow(babynames), 1e5, replace = F), "prop"] <- NA
baby_missing_db <- tbl_memdb(babynames_missing)

babynames_missing %>% 
  summarize(wavg_prop = weighted.mean(prop, n, na.rm = TRUE))
baby_missing_db %>% 
  summarize(
    wavg_prop = sum(prop * n) / sum(if_else(! is.na(prop), n, 0)),
    wavg_prop2 = sum(prop * n) / sum(n)
  )
```

Note the difference in between `wavg_prop` and `wavg_prop2` when missing values are apparent. 

I wrote code in `backend-.R` to supply a translator. If you think it's worthwhile, I can add that on for a pull request.

title: add_count returns grouped dataframe
description:
According to the [dplyr docs](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/count.html), `add_count()` is supposed to:

> group transiently, so the output has the same groups as the input.

Although this is true for the dplyr version, I discovered that the dbplyr version does change the groups.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

df <- tribble(
  ~name,    ~gender,   ~runs,
  "Max",    "male",       10,
  "Sandra", "female",      1,
  "Susan",  "female",      4
)

# ungrouped output
df %>% add_count(gender, wt = runs)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   name   gender  runs     n
#>   <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Max    male      10    10
#> 2 Sandra female     1     5
#> 3 Susan  female     4     5

# grouped output
memdb_frame(df) %>% add_count(gender, wt = runs)
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 4]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.34.1 [:memory:]
#> # Groups:   gender
#>   name   gender  runs     n
#>   <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Sandra female     1     5
#> 2 Susan  female     4     5
```

title: dbplyr does not translate base R integer division %/%
description:
*@emilyriederer commented on Aug 27, 2017, 7:16 PM UTC:*

Base R integer division (%/%) is translated to normal division (/) in SQL.

Apologies for non-reprex. I couldn't think of a way to get around the fact that a user must establish a connection to get this to run. When run connected to a AWS Redshift DB, data$z contains values 0, 1, and 2 while data_db$z contains floating point values.

The cause is that %/% is translated as / without accounting for integer-format. One correct SQL translation (at least for Redshift) would be CAST("x"/5 AS INTEGER) or FLOOR("x"/5)

```r
library(dplyr)

data <- data.frame(x=as.integer(1:10))
data_db <- copy_to(con, data, "data_db", temporary = FALSE)

data <- mutate(data, z = x %/% 5)
data_db <- mutate(data_db, z = x %/% 5)

data
collect(data_db)

show_query(data_db)
```

title: Wrong SQL query generated for left_join() in sparklyr when column names same but case
description:
I encountered a bug when two tables have same joining column names that differ only in case (e.g. "x" and "X").
When they are the same the query is correct:
```
library(tidyverse)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

temp_tibble1 <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = 11:15) %>% copy_to(sc, ., name = "temp_tibble1", overwrite = TRUE)
temp_tibble2 <- tibble(x = 1:5, z = 111:115) %>% copy_to(sc, ., "temp_tibble2", overwrite = TRUE)

temp_tibble1 %>%
  left_join(temp_tibble2, by = c("x" = "x")) %>% show_query()
```
giving
```
<SQL>
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `z`
FROM `temp_tibble1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `temp_tibble2` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```
but
```
temp_tibble1 <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = 11:15) %>% copy_to(sc, ., name = "temp_tibble1", overwrite = TRUE)
temp_tibble2 <- tibble(X = 1:5, z = 111:115) %>% copy_to(sc, ., "temp_tibble2", overwrite = TRUE)

temp_tibble1 %>%
  left_join(temp_tibble2, by = c("x" = "X")) %>% show_query()
```
gives
```
<SQL>
SELECT `x`, `y`, `z`
FROM `temp_tibble1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `temp_tibble2` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`X`)
```
which fails with

> Error : org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: Reference 'x' is ambiguous, could be: LHS.x, RHS.x.; line 1 pos 7

*I originally reported that issue to the sparklyr team (#3219) but I suppose it belongs here.*

title: MariaDB - Issue when joining two tables on a column with the same name but different case
description:
When `dplyr` or `dbplyr` joins data frames or tables, the column names are case sensitive, so two columns with the same name but different case are considered different.  When generating the SQL, table aliases are only prefixed to column names in the select clause when they are not unique column names.  However, since the case of column names in a SQL statement is not considered, at least not in MariaDB, it results in an error as seen below.

```r
library(odbc)
library(dbplyr)

conn <- dbConnect(drv = odbc::odbc(),
                  Driver = "MySQL")

# create a simple table called test_table1 with one column called COL_1 (all caps)
dbExecute(conn, "create table test_table1 as
                 select 1 as `COL_1`
                 union select 2 as `COL_1`
                 union select 3 as `COL_1`")

# create another table called test_table2 with the same structure of test_table1 but with the column called col_1 (lowercase)
dbExecute(conn, "create table test_table2 as
                 select 1 as `col_1`
                 union select 2 as `col_1`
                 union select 3 as `col_1`")

# join the two tables and collect results
tbl(conn, "test_table1") %>%
  left_join(tbl(conn, "test_table2"), by = c("COL_1" = "col_1")) %>%
  collect()
# Error in new_result(connection@ptr, statement, immediate) : 
#   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1412: 00000: [RStudio][MySQL] Column 'COL_1' in field list is ambiguous 

# The query being executed
tbl(conn, "test_table1") %>%
  left_join(tbl(conn, "test_table2"), by = c("COL_1" = "col_1")) %>%
  show_query()
# <SQL>
# SELECT `COL_1`
# FROM `test_table1` AS `LHS`
# LEFT JOIN `test_table2` AS `RHS`
# ON (`LHS`.`COL_1` = `RHS`.`col_1`)
```
The error occurs because both tables have a column named `col_1` and case is not considered when deciding which one to select.  If the table alias was included in the select clause, it would have worked.

When the column names are identical, there's no issue.

```r
# create test_table3 which is identical to test_table1
dbExecute(conn, "create table test_table3 as
                 select 1 as `COL_1`
                 union select 2 as `COL_1`
                 union select 3 as `COL_1`")

# join the two tables and collect results
tbl(conn, "test_table1") %>%
  left_join(tbl(conn, "test_table3"), by = "COL_1") %>%
  collect()

## A tibble: 3 × 1
#  COL_1
#  <int>
#1     1
#2     2
#3     3

# The query being executed
tbl(conn, "test_table1") %>%
  left_join(tbl(conn, "test_table3"), by = "COL_1") %>%
  show_query()
# <SQL>
# SELECT `LHS`.`COL_1` AS `COL_1`
# FROM `test_table1` AS `LHS`
# LEFT JOIN `test_table3` AS `RHS`
# ON (`LHS`.`COL_1` = `RHS`.`COL_1`)
```
Now there's no issue because the column name is prefixed with the table alias in the select clause.

This doesn't work as expected due to the case differences:
```r
tbl(conn, "test_table1") %>%
  left_join(tbl(conn, "test_table2"), by = "COL_1") %>%
  collect()
# Error: `by` can't contain join column `COL_1` which is missing from RHS.
```

It would be useful if column names were always prefixed with the table alias, or if there was the option to allow this.

title: confusing output after multiple `arrange()` calls
description:
For example,

```
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

df <- memdb_frame(a = 1, b = 2)

df %>% arrange(a) %>% arrange(b) %>% print()
```

will output

```
# Source:     table<dbplyr_001> [?? x 2]
# Database:   sqlite 3.35.5 [:memory:]
# Ordered by: a, b
      a     b
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     2
```

even though its generated query is

```
df %>% arrange(a) %>% arrange(b) %>% remote_query() %>% print()
```

```
<SQL> SELECT *
FROM `dbplyr_001`
ORDER BY `b`
```
(as expected)

So, the generated query is what I expected, but the "Ordered by: a, b" from the first print() output was confusing.

Similarly,

```
df %>% arrange(a, b) %>% print()
```

will also output "Ordered by: a, b", even though it will generate "ORDER BY `a`, `b`" instead of "ORDER BY `b`" as the SQL query.

Similar confusion happens for

```
df %>% arrange(a) %>% arrange(b) %>% arrange(a) %>% print()
```

as well (generated query will say "ORDER BY `b`" as expected but the print() output will say "Ordered by: a, b, a").

Anyhow, this seems to have caused some confusion and panicking for folks who probably mostly relied on REPL for debugging their SQL queries (e.g., see https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/issues/1847) but hopefully it's something that's easy to fix.

I've recently had to pull a random sample of a fairly large (>1.5M row) database that's stored in a MariaDB instance. I wrote a fairly basic dbplyr filter:

```r
# pseudocode: <set up database connection>

   db_tbl %>%
   slice_sample( n=5000 ) %>%
```

I assume that this may be a limitation in functions internally provided by MariaDB, but I'm also unsure from searching around whether this is something I can fix (by implementing tablename.random directly on the DB side?) or if I'm just missing something obvious.

As an aside, I'm in a lucky position here where we're about to move this whole dataset and collection across to a new system, so I have the option to move database servers. Is there a recommended database implementation that's most compatible for dbplyr?

title: Postgres function identifiers should be quoted
description:
Postgres allows the definition of functions that contain special characters, e.g.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION "is.finite"(x float) RETURNS bool AS '' LANGUAGE plr;
```

I can call the function by quoting its name:

```sql
SELECT "is.finite"('NaN'::float);
```

However, `dbplyr` does not quote function names when constructing queries, so the function is not recognized:

```r
tbl(con, 'iris') %>% mutate(z = is.finite(Sepal.Width))

```

title: Making dbplyr work with RJDBC to MS SQL Server
description:
I have a JDBC connection to a SQL Server Managed Instance on Azure with a pre-connect token using RJDBC and DBI.  I then want to use that connection with DBPLYR.  
The first issue I ran into was that DBPLYR was adding "LIMIT 10" to the end of all queries because it didn't recognize the JDBC connection as SQL Server.  To solve this, I added the following to my code:

```r

sql_translation.JDBCConnection <- dbplyr:::`sql_translation.Microsoft SQL Server`
sql_select.JDBCConnection <- dbplyr:::`sql_query_select.Microsoft SQL Server`

```
That allowed me to successfully run code like the following:

```r

tbl(con, "mytable") %>% head() %>% collect()

```

However, using a different verb, leads to an error implying that dbplyr is looking for the mssql version:

```r
tbl(con, "mytable") %>% filter(mycol == "myvalue")
```

**Error in if (mssql_version(con) >= "11.0") { : argument is of length zero**

Based on my interpretation of the backend_sqlserver code, I've tried to set the following:

```r
attr(con, "version") = "17"
attributes(con)$info$db.version = "17"
attributes(con)$info$driver.version = "17"
```
All to no avail.  That is, the attributes are set on the JDBCConnection but, it doesn't resolve the error.  I think there may be a simple fix for this that I'm just missing.  Any help is much appreciated!

title: Proper way to define custom sql functions
description:
In order to improve code readibility and robustness, I want to define some custom SQL scalar functions. For now what I am doing is create a new SQL variant. To do that I have to change the class of the connexion object:

```r
setClass("my_connexion", contains = "PostgreSQLConnection")

postgres_env <- dplyr::sql_translate_env(dbplyr::simulate_postgres())

sql_translate_env.my_connexion <- function(x) {
  sql_variant(
    scalar = sql_translator(
      .parent = postgres_env$scalar,
      weibull_surv = function(t, model) {
        par <- model$par
        translate_sql(exp(-(!!t) ^ (!!par$k) / (!!par$l)) * ifelse(!!t == 0,!!par$adj0, 1),
                      con = x)
      }
    ),
    aggregate = sql_translator(.parent = postgres_env$aggregate),
    window = sql_translator(.parent = postgres_env$window)
  )
}

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgreSQL::PostgreSQL(), ...)
class(con) <- "my_connexion"
tbl(con, "my_table") %>% mutate(pred = weibull_surv (seniority, model))
```
Is there a better way to achieve the same result?

title: NA int values for expected integer64 column in BigQuery table (despite working with dbGetQuery)
description:
When attempting to use `dbplyr` along with `dbConnect` to access a table in BigQuery, I cannot find a way to preserve `bit::integer64` type on a particular column. This is despite that type support appearing successfully in base dbConnect().

## Connection supports bit64::integer64 column without `dbplyr`
The following dbConnect() code uses the `bit64::integer64` implementation + `bigrquery()` to successfully return query results with `integer64` column:

```
# bq_auth and project_id config

con <- dbConnect(
  bigrquery::bigquery(),
  project = project_id,
  dataset = "test_data",
  billing = project_id,
  bigint = "integer64"
)

dbGetQuery(con,'
  select * from test_data.table limit 10') %>%
  glimpse()

```

as expected, `column_one` shows `<int64>`. However..



## No `integer64` with `tbl`, `glimpse()`, `collect()`, etc.

When attempting to form the connection the following way:

```{r}
note_info <- tbl(con, "test_data.table")

note_info %>%
   glimpse()
```
outputs that `column_one` is `<int>` type. 

```
note_info %>% 
  select(column_one, column_two, column_three) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  collect()

```
outputs `column_one` with `<int>` types and NA values for all observations.

## Other attempts 

The behaviors above persist no matter what I specify for the `bigint` paramter for `dbConnect()` (`character`, `integer`, not setting an explicit parameter).

I also attempted to coerce in the query itself via:

```
note_info %>% 
  select(column_one, column_two, column_three) %>%
  mutate(column_one = as.integer64(column_one)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  collect()

note_summary
```

but throws :
```
x Type not found: BIGINT at [1:26] [invalidQuery]
```
Which may imply an upstream issue with the the `tbl` method not seeing the `integer64` column type.

Any ideas? Thank you! (My apologies for not writing a true `reprex` -- I was unsure how to do so when relying on BigQuery specifically. I can look into mocking/other approaches if preferable!)

title: Dates in MS Access aren't escaped properly.
Computing query results causes attributes to be dropped
description:
Let's consider a simple example

```r
sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(master = "local")
mtcars_spark <- dplyr::copy_to(dest = sc, df = mtcars)

blah <- dplyr::select(mtcars_spark, mpg)                                                                                                                          
attr(blah, "testAttr") <- "hello"                                                                                                                                 
attributes(blah)                                                                                                                                                  
# $names
# [1] "src" "ops"
# $class
# [1] "tbl_spark" "tbl_sql"   "tbl_lazy"  "tbl"      
# $testAttr
# [1] "hello"

blah <- dplyr::compute(blah)                                                                                                                                      
attributes(blah)                                                                                                                                                  
# $names
# [1] "src" "ops"
# $class
# [1] "tbl_spark" "tbl_sql"   "tbl_lazy"  "tbl"
```

When using `dplyr::compute()` on a `tbl_spark` object, for example, it will dispatch to `dbplyr:::compute.tbl_sql()`. I feel like this should maybe have some similar method to `dplyr::dplyr_reconstruct()` to ensure that attributes are not dropped. This seems to be a recent problem as we've experienced this since upgrading to the latest dbplyr from 1.4.2.

title: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT is shown too often and often when it doesn't make sense
description:
Ever since upgrading to the latest version of dbplyr, our code output has been riddled with the warning

```
1: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
```

A simple, reproducible example would be:

```
r$> sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(master = "local")
r$> mtcars_spark <- dplyr::copy_to(dest = sc, df = mtcars)
r$> mtcars_spark %>% dplyr::distinct(am)                                                                                                                        
# Source: spark<?> [?? x 1]
     am
  <dbl>
1     1
2     0
Warning messages:
1: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
2: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
3: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
4: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead? 
5: ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT
ℹ Do you need to move arrange() later in the pipeline or use window_order() instead?
```

But we see these warnings in order of 50+ warnings for most of our functionality now. We purposefully avoid use of `arrange()` in our code due to old dbplyr behaviour where you couldn't un-arrange and so any code we have which needs an order, we make use of `dplyr::mutate(dbplyr::win_over())` and specify the ordering in there. One might thing this is the cause of the problem but it doesn't always make sense to use an order in here, you might just want to perform some logic over groups, for example. Coupled with the example above, I think this warning may need reviewing?

Looking at the query that this generates, it seems a little more complex than is needed? I am not so sure about all other backends but in Spark, it is enough to do

```r
sparklyr::sdf_sql(sc = sc, "SELECT DISTINCT(mpg) from mtcars")
```
