title: Non standard handling of iso-date strings in PrestoDB/AWS Athena
description:
[Will repost this under dplyr, as the active discussion seems to happen there also on dbplyr-related issues.]

Most databases are able to interpret iso-date strings as dates in, e.g., where caluses, such as

`select * from table where date_column = '2019-01-01'`

This is not the case with PrestoDB/AWS Athena however. Instead the strings need to be cast as dates first like:
`select * from table where date_column = date('2019-01-01')`,
`select * from table where date_column = date'2019-01-01'` or
`select * from table where date_column = cast('2019-01-01' as date)`

However, when a date variable is used as a parameter id dplyr/dbplyr, is is translated to a iso-date string in the generated sql, so a command such as:

```r
today <- Sys.Date()
tbl(AthenaCon, "table") %>% filter(date_column <= today)
```

produces and error, as the generated sql does not have the explicit cast to date of the iso-date string. One needs to manually cast the date variable as a date as in
`... %>% filter(date_column <= as.Date(today)`, but this feels unnecessary, as R knows today is a date already.


A DBI backend for AWS Athena is being developed at https://github.com/DyfanJones/RAthena, and I'm asking for some guidance on how to address this issue there.


My question is: is there a method for overiding the default behavior of dbplyr, where dates are translated to quoted strings and instead have them translated to, e.g., "date'2019-01-01'"?

I'm sorry if this seems like a trivial question, but I'm drawing a blank from reading the database specific source files and packages. All I can come up with is to use assignInNameSpace to replace the escape.Date -method, but this seemss pretty brutal.

title: Surprisingly case-sensitive name lookup behavior
description:
Perhaps this is intended behavior but I found it unintuitive. When using remote tbls with uppercase column names I frequently refer to the columns by their lowercase name so I don't feel like I'm yelling at my computer. However, this doesn't work if the lowercase name has a direct match in the local environment. It seems like the name lookup behavior is:

1. Look for a case-sensitive match in the remote tbl
2. Look for a case-sensitive match in the local env
3. Look for a case-insensitive match in the remote tbl

I personally expected it to do both types of lookups in the remote tbl before checking the local environment. Is this intended?

reprex:
```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

# SQL is not case sensitive, so this will work
memdb_frame(FOO = 1:10) %>% summarize(n_distinct(foo))

I use filter function inside of a function which used to work as expected before, but it stopped working since yesterday and i can't understand why.  I simplified my function to only filter a col in a dataset:
```r
d1 <- data.frame(new_id = rep(1:2, each = 5),
                 v1 = c(NA, 2, 4, NA, 6, 1, 3, NA, NA, NA),
                 v2 = seq(1,10),
                 v3 = c(0, runif(9, -5, 5)),
                 v4 = c('a','b', NA, 'd', 'e',NA,'g', 'h','i',NA),
                 scorecard = rep(c("mb0","mb1"), 5))

sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")
d1 <- copy_to(sc, d1, "datanew_sdf", overwrite = T)
test_func= function(.data, filter_value, filter_var){
 
  .data <- .data %>% dplyr::filter(!!enquo(filter_var) == filter_value)
    return(.data)
}

test_func(.data = d1, filter_value = "mb1", filter_var = scorecard) 

```
I expect to get a the rows that have scorecard equal to mb1 in the output, but when I run it in Rstudio I get empty output, and in databricks I get this error: 
```r
Error in call[[1]] : object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable.
```
I'm not sure what has changed in dplyr to cause this change.

title: filter with SQL infix function in a package: undefined global function
description:
I am using `dbplyr` in a function in an R package that queries a database. This works fine, but upon checking the package with Build - Check, the following note is printed:

````
> checking R code for possible problems ... NOTE
  my_query: no visible global function definition for '%LIKE%'
  Undefined global functions or variables:
    %LIKE%
````

Here's a reprex of the function:

```r
#' my function to query a database using dbplyr
#' 
#' @param mf
#' @param pattern
#' 
#' @importFrom rlang .data
#' @importFrom dplyr 
#' filter
#' collect
#' %>%
#' 
#' @example
#' library(dbplyr)
#' mf <- memdb_frame(x = c("abc", "def", "ghif"))
#' my_query(mf = mf)

my_query <- function(mf, pattern = "de%") {
  mf %>%
    filter(.data$x %LIKE% pattern) %>%
    collect
}

```

What should I do to get rid of this note?

title: pipe chain using !! results in error "object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable"
description:
This is a cross post from ove[r in the Studio Community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/dbplyr-local-eval-unexpected-behavior/32617) because I was not sure where to park this comment/issue. 

----

So I got bit by a breaking change in dbplyr. In 1.4.0 there was a breaking change that impacts where eval happens in dbplyr (local vs on the server).

This code used to work in 1.3 but now breaks:
```
library(tidyverse)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggplot2':
#>   method         from 
#>   [.quosures     rlang
#>   c.quosures     rlang
#>   print.quosures rlang
testfun <- function(tab, tst_input){
  en_tst <- dplyr::enquo(tst_input)
  tab %>%
    filter(!!en_tst > 15) -> out
  return(out)
}

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(con, mtcars)

mtcars2 <- tbl(con, "mtcars")
testfun(tab = mtcars2, tst_input = mpg)
#> Error in call[[1]]: object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable

```

but that's easy enough to fix by replacing
`filter(!!en_tst > 15)`

with

`filter(local(!!en_tst) > 15)`

Not a huge deal, but it was really tricky for me to debug. And while I'm not super well versed in tidy development, I'm typically reasonably competent. So I was a little surprised how hard this was to figure out.

In the release notes there's mention of changes that break subsetting:

> Subsetting ( [[ , $ , and [ ) functions are no longer evaluated locally.

So what changed that makes using !! in dbplyr problematic? Is it the subsetting change mentioned above or is it something else altogether?

FWIW, after the change I mention above, the code works great like this:

```
library(tidyverse)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggplot2':
#>   method         from 
#>   [.quosures     rlang
#>   c.quosures     rlang
#>   print.quosures rlang
testfun <- function(tab, tst_input){
  en_tst <- dplyr::enquo(tst_input)
  tab %>%
    filter(local(!!en_tst) > 15) -> out
  return(out)
}

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(con, mtcars)

mtcars2 <- tbl(con, "mtcars")

testfun(tab = mtcars2, tst_input = mpg)

title: Un-ideal NSE behavior when using `%in%` with `$` referenced columns in a secondary data frame
description:
Via https://twitter.com/dataandme/status/1124032580221906944?s=20

I'll work up a real reprex if you are willing to spend money in Amazon Athena to reproduce and have access to their default logs DB.

I have this line of code from an earlier set of analysis code:

```r
filter(db, location__country_code3 %in% !!apac_countries$iso3c)
```

where `apac_countries` is:

```r
Observations: 44
Variables: 3
$ country_name <chr> "American Samoa", "Australia", "Bhutan", "Brunei Darussalam", "China", "Taiwan", "Hong…
$ iso2c        <chr> "AS", "AU", "BT", "BN", "CN", "TW", "HK", "CX", "CC", "CK", "FJ", "PF", "GU", "ID", "J…
$ iso3c        <chr> "ASM", "AUS", "BTN", "BRN", "CHN", "TWN", "HKG", "CXR", "CCK", "COK", "FJI", "PYF", "G…
```
 and `db` is created by code like:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), …)
db <- tbl(con, "seekrit_db_name")
```

The error I get is:

```r
## Error in UseMethod("escape") : 
##  no applicable method for 'escape' applied to an object of class "c('spec_tbl_df', 'tbl_df', 'tbl', 'data.frame')"
```

However it works if the `$`-referenced dataframe column is prefixed with `!!` (e.g. `!!apac_countries$iso3c`).

I am going to strongly posit that it should not require the `!!` to work since one would _kinda_ expect R code to work like R code should (and, it used to work).

title: filter_at() translation issue
description:
**dbplyr 1.4.0** appears to translate  `filter_at()` calls incorrectly, translating the variable name themselves, rather than their values. See following example:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(con, mtcars)

mtcars2 <- tbl(con, "mtcars")
cols <- c("vs", "am", "gear", "carb")
nums <- c(4, 5)
num <- 1

test <- mtcars2 %>%
  filter(gear %in% nums, 
         gear == num) %>%
  filter_at(cols, any_vars(. %in% nums)) %>%
  filter_at(cols, any_vars(. == num))

show_query(test)
```

In **dbplyr 1.3.0** this gives the following SQL query:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *
FROM `mtcars`
WHERE ((`gear` IN (4.0, 5.0)) AND (`gear` = 1.0)))
WHERE (`vs` IN (4.0, 5.0) OR `am` IN (4.0, 5.0) OR `gear` IN (4.0, 5.0) OR `carb` IN (4.0, 5.0)))
WHERE (`vs` = 1.0 OR `am` = 1.0 OR `gear` = 1.0 OR `carb` = 1.0)
```

but in **dbplyr 1.4.0** the variables are translated literally as "num" and "nums" in the SQL translation of the `filter_at()` function, although they are translated as expected from the `filter()` function.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *
FROM `mtcars`
WHERE ((`gear` IN (4.0, 5.0)) AND (`gear` = 1.0)))
WHERE (`vs` IN `nums` OR `am` IN `nums` OR `gear` IN `nums` OR `carb` IN `nums`))
WHERE (`vs` = `num` OR `am` = `num` OR `gear` = `num` OR `carb` = `num`)
```

This then leads to an error when querying the database via `collect()` as there are no `num` or `nums` variables on the database end.

title: Can't use [[ with scoped mutate
description:
I want to dynamically extract one or more keys from a map column using the new remote evaluation of `[[`. I would expect each of the cases in the reprex below to give equivalent output.

ID | map column name | map column quoted | verb | works as expected
--- | --- | --- | --- | ---
1 | `x` | no | `mutate()` | yes
2 | `x` | no | `mutate_at()` | no
3 | `x` | yes | `mutate()` | no
4 | `x` | yes | `mutate_at()` | no
5 | `x` | no | `extract_keys()` | no
6 | `dim` | no | `extract_keys()` | yes

My best guess is that there is some interaction among `[[`, `mutate_at()`, and quasiquotation. The target DB is [Presto](https://prestodb.github.io/docs/current/functions/map.html), but this issue doesn't appear specific to Presto. Also, I suspect this is related to other recent issues, e.g., #305.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(purrr)
library(rlang, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

build_extractor <- function(map, key) {
  key_chr <- rlang::as_name(dplyr::enquo(key))
  map_quo <- rlang::enquo(map)
  rlang::list2(!!key_chr := ~ `[[`(!!map_quo, !!key_chr))
}

extract_keys <- function(.data, map, ...) {
  map_quo <- rlang::enquo(map)
  keys <- rlang::enquos(...)

  extractors <-
    keys %>%
    purrr::map(build_extractor, map = !!map_quo) %>%
    purrr::reduce(c)

  .data %>%
    dplyr::mutate_at(dplyr::vars(!!map_quo), extractors)
}

df <- tibble(x = list(c(a = 1, b = 2), c(a = 3, b = 4)))
df_dbi <- tbl_lazy(df)
map_var <- dplyr::quo(x)

df_dbi %>% mutate(a = x[["a"]], b = x[["b"]])
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `x`.`a` AS `a`, `x`.`b` AS `b`
#> FROM `df`

df_dbi %>% mutate_at(vars(x), list(a = ~`[[`(., "a"), b = ~`[[`(., "b")))
#> Error in as.pairlist(list(...)): object 'x' not found

df_dbi %>% mutate(a = !!map_var[["a"]], b = !!map_var[["b"]])
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`
#> FROM `df`

df_dbi %>% mutate_at(vars(!!map_var), list(a = ~`[[`(., "a"), b = ~`[[`(., "b")))
#> Error in as.pairlist(list(...)): object 'x' not found

df_dbi %>% extract_keys(x, a, b)
#> Error in as.pairlist(list(...)): object 'x' not found

df_dbi %>% rename(dim = x) %>% extract_keys(dim, a, b)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `dim`, `dim`.`a` AS `a`, `dim`.`b` AS `b`
#> FROM (SELECT `x` AS `dim`
#> FROM `df`) `dbplyr_001`
```

title: mutate_at fails to identify columns specified by .vars parameter
description:
Some code we have as part of a function in an internal R package started failing tests that previously worked as of a few weeks ago (the last time I ran our unit tests). I narrowed the issue down to mutate_at failing to identify variables specified in the .vars argument. 

Here is a toy example with the same behavior. Here I am simply trying to replace NA values in the specified columns with 0:

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

mf <- memdb_frame(A = c(NA, 1, NA, 2, 2), 
                  B = c(1, 2, 3, NA, NA),
                  C = c(NA, NA, 3, 2, 1),
                  D = c(NA, 4, NA, 2, 1))

replace_func <- function(val, replace) {
  ifelse(is.na(val), replace, val)
}

mf %>% 
  mutate_at(c("A", "B"), replace_func, replace = 0)
#> Error in ifelse(is.na(val), replace, val): object 'A' not found
```

title: Support ORDER BY in subqueries for MSSQL
description:
MSSQL is sensitive to subqueries that have an `ORDER BY` clause -- they are not allowed. A [suggested workaround](https://stackoverflow.com/a/985953/946850) is to use `TOP 100 PERCENT`~~, but I believe we can also solve this by more accurate optimization~~.

This is an actual problem if window functions are involved, in this case it's not easy to move the `arrange()` as noted in https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/94#issuecomment-460789909.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)

df <- lazy_frame(x = 1:4, g = rep(c(1, 2), each = 2), con = simulate_mssql())

df %>%
  group_by(g) %>%
  arrange(x) %>%
  mutate(r = cumsum(x))
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `g`, SUM(`x`) OVER (PARTITION BY `g` ORDER BY `x` ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS `r`
#> FROM (SELECT *
#> FROM `df`
#> ORDER BY `x`) `dbplyr_001`
```

<sup>Created on 2019-04-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

title: na.omit.tbl_lazy ?
description:
could we have a `tbl_lazy` for `na.omit` ? it's an *S3 generic*

I'm not sure how to translate it conveniently without it, as the following doesn't work.

```
tbl(con, "my_table") %>%
  filter_all(~!is.na(.))
```

so I end up repeating `... %>% filter(!is.na(var1), !is.na(var2), ...)` which seems suboptimal.

Moreover, `na.omit` doesn't fail on `tbl_lazy` objects, it just returns the input  unchanged ( as `tbl(con, "foo")` is a list without `NA`) , which might be unexpected by the user.

I guess it would imply building methods for and `na.fail` `na.exclude` as well. `na.pass` is not an `S3` generic but doesn't need a method as it's basically the `identity` function.

title: Presto Support
description:

    SELECT evs.device_ids['google_advertising_id'] AS device_id, count(*) AS evs_count
    FROM hive.aleph.impressions_daily AS imps
    JOIN hive.aleph.events_daily AS evs ON evs.trans_id = imps.trans_id

title: Unable to use quantile() in mutate()

library(DBI)

library(RPostgres)

db <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres())

copy_to(db, mtcars)

  mutate(wt = pmin(wt, quantile(wt, 0.99))) 

cars_query %>% show_query()

car_data <- cars_query %>% collect()

db_drop_table(db, 'mtcars')
dbDisconnect(db)
```
`cars_query` looks like this:

SELECT "mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "drat", LEAST("wt", PERCENTILE_CONT(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY "wt") OVER ()) AS "wt", "qsec", "vs", "am", "gear", "carb"

title: dbplyr 1.4.0 breaks filters with subsetted variables using SQLite
description:
The last two filters below fail, the first returns no results and the second throws `Error in result_create(conn@ptr, statement) : near "AS": syntax error`. I had similar code to this in a production shiny app that was working under the previous version and broke once we upgrade to dbplyr 1.4.0.

```r
library(dplyr)

test = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(test, iris)

iris_db = tbl(test, "iris")

key_vec = c(species = "setosa")
key_list = list(species = "setosa")

filter(iris_db, Species == key_vec)
filter(iris_db, Species == key_vec["species"])
filter(iris_db, Species == key_list["species"])
```

title: collect() tbl_df from Access connection, result_fetch() failed with Incomplete multibyte sequence
description:
I have an Access database with multibyte characters (Chinese) in it. It looks quite normal in Access and I can successfully read it into R using `RODBC::sqlQuery()`. But when I run the following codes, it failed with warning "Error in result_fetch(res@ptr, n, ...) : Incomplete multibyte sequence".

```r
library(dplyr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
    odbc::odbc(), 
    .connection_string=paste0("Driver={Microsoft Access Driver (*.mdb, *.accdb)};
                               Dbq=<a .accdb file>"), 
    encoding="CP936")
tbl(con, "Table1") %>% select(Place) %>% collect 
```

Then I changed the connection encoding to "UTF-8",

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
    odbc::odbc(), 
    .connection_string=paste0("Driver={Microsoft Access Driver (*.mdb, *.accdb)};
                               Dbq=<a .accdb file>"), 
    encoding="UTF-8")
tbl(con, "Table1") %>% select(Place) %>% collect 
```

```
# A tibble: 3 x 1

description:

Let me know if issue reports for development reports should be generated elsewhere.

In the reprex below, unfortunately I don't think we can reproduce with the `simulate_mssql()` method. 

``` r
devtools::dev_mode(on = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)

con_prodeng = DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), Driver = "SQL Server", Server = "ServerName", Database = "DBName")

df = tribble(

title: Add support for quantile()
description:
Would it be possible to add support for the [`quantile()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.5.1/topics/quantile) function?

Quite a few databases support `PERCENTILE_CONT` and `PERCENTILE_DISC`, which I think could make this possible (e.g. Google BigQuery, PostgreSQL, and Redshift).

I'd be willing to help of course, but would need some pointers on where to start.

title: types vs. field.types in db_write_table.`Microsoft SQL Server`
str_detect always treats pattern as fixed string
description:
When `str_detect` is used in a call to `filter` on a `tbl`, I expect `pattern` to be treated as a regular expression. Instead, it seems that it is treated as a fixed pattern:

```
> MASTER %>% filter(str_detect(FOO, "pen$")) %>% show_query
<SQL>
SELECT *
FROM "MASTER"
WHERE (INSTR("FOO", 'pen$') > 0)
```

The SQL `INSTR` function performs a case-insensitive search, and does not treat its second argument as a regex.

title: MSSQL translator should convert as.logical into CAST AS BIT instead of CAST AS BOOLEAN
description:
In MS SQL Server, `as.logical` translates to `CAST AS BOOLEAN`.  However, in SQL Server, it looks like BOOLEAN doesn't exist.  It seems to use [BIT instead of BOOLEAN](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1777257/how-do-you-create-a-yes-no-boolean-field-in-sql-server).  

It seems like this might be a simple fix.  A small example follows.  Let me know if there's anything I can do to help fix, if this is of interest.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  driver = "{SQL Server}",
  database = "AdventureWorks2012",
  uid = "sqlfamily",
  pwd = "sqlf@m1ly",
  server = "mhknbn2kdz.database.windows.net",
  port = 1433
)

# Fails
con %>% 
  tbl(in_schema("Production", "WorkOrder")) %>% 
  transmute(large_order = as.logical(if_else(OrderQty < 5, 0L, 1L)))
# Error: <SQL> 'SELECT  TOP 10 "large_order" AS "large_order"
# FROM (SELECT "WorkOrderID", "ProductID", "OrderQty", "StockedQty", "ScrappedQty", "StartDate", "EndDate", "DueDate", "ScrapReasonID", "ModifiedDate", CAST(CASE WHEN ("OrderQty" < 5.0) THEN (0) # ELSE (1) END AS BOOLEAN) AS "large_order"
# FROM Production.WorkOrder) "zvtstdmghk"'
#   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [Microsoft][ODBC SQL Server Driver][SQL Server]Type BOOLEAN is not a defined system type. 

# Works
con %>% 
  tbl(sql('SELECT CAST(CASE WHEN ("OrderQty" < 5.0) THEN (0) ELSE (1) END AS BIT) AS "large_order"
           FROM Production.WorkOrder'))
# # Source:   SQL [?? x 1]
# # Database: Microsoft SQL Server 12.00.1100[sqlfamily@mhknbn2kdz/AdventureWorks2012]
#    large_order
#          <lgl>
#  1        TRUE
#  2        TRUE
#  3        TRUE
#  4        TRUE
#  5        TRUE
#  6        TRUE
#  7       FALSE
#  8        TRUE
#  9       FALSE
# 10       FALSE
# # ... with more rows
```

title: Documentation clarification regarding `compute()`
description:
I struggle to understand the current documentation of the `compute()` function. Some clarification would we helpful.

[The `compute()` documentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dplyr/versions/0.7.8/topics/compute):
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/bbcfe99e29fe737d456b0d7adc33d3c445a32d9d/R/compute-collect.r#L1-L7

Particularly, the description above could say more on how `compute()` and `collect()` differ. Which types of objects do the functions return? Will changes to the returned objects change the original remote table or leave it unchanged? Can the functions be considered interchangeable, except for X? When should you use one over the other? When should you not? Does `compute()` retrieve data, and if so is the data stored in memory or stored remotely? Etc.

Including some of the descriptions from [the `src_dbi()` documentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dplyr/versions/0.7.8/topics/src_dbi) would help:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/bbcfe99e29fe737d456b0d7adc33d3c445a32d9d/R/src_dbi.R#L14-L25

I understand (or misunderstood) the functions as follows:
```r
data -> src_sqlite(...) %>% tbl(...) 
# Returns a `tbl_dbi` object.

local -> data %>% ... %>% collect() 
# Returns a `tbl_df` or `grouped_df` object.

cache -> data %>% ... %>% compute() 
# Returns a new `tbl_dbi` object, which temporarily is created in the database 
# (discarded once connection closes/session ends).
```

Thanks in advance.

title: Mutate creates single quote SELECT statement and code fails
description:
### Problem Description
When we're joining using the "by" argument and left and right 'by' are different column names, only 1 of those remains. For my code to work, I need both, so I use mutate() to re-create the lost column (which holds the exact same values of the one that's already there).
Now, when this happens once, the mutate will do a T-SQL Translation of `'ForeignKeyName' AS "PrimaryKeyName"` and the T-SQL code will still work, it doesn't crash.
However, when I do a second join using that tbl(), something is lost in the translation and a `, ""` is added to the T-SQL code, which now completely breaks the code and the tbl() shows an error instead of a table.

So, let's reproduce this bug:
__Unfortunately this reprex will be longer than my usual reprexes due to the nature of SQL translations and SQL tables needed__

### 1) Create a SQL Server Database (and possible populate it. It probably does the same since we're working with SCHEMA, but I suggest we populate it as well)
> Run this T-SQL code to create the database: https://github.com/N1h1l1sT/dbautojoinr/blob/master/SQL/Database%20Creation.sql
> Run this T-SQL code to populate it:
https://github.com/N1h1l1sT/dbautojoinr/blob/master/SQL/Data%20Population.sql

This dataset is created:
![ER Diagramme](https://github.com/N1h1l1sT/dbautojoinr/blob/master/SQL/dbautojoinr-er-diagramme.png?raw=true)

![Dataset](https://github.com/N1h1l1sT/dbautojoinr/blob/master/SQL/dbautojoinr-sql-database.png?raw=true)

### 2) Run this R code
```r
#My code uses variables that hold the column names to join so that consecutive joins can be automated, so let's simulate this too: 
RightSideColsNames <- NULL
RightSideColsNames[[2]] <- "Site_ID"
leftByCol <- "Employee_SiteID"
j <- 2

#Please create a connection to the SQL Database 'dbautojoinr' that was just created and name it con
main <- tbl(con, "DIM_Employee")
site <- tbl(con, "DIM_Site")
a <- left_join(main, site, by=(c("Employee_SiteID" = "Site_ID")), copy = FALSE)
```
So far so good. Everything's perfect until the next statement.
You see, we have now lost "Site_ID", so I'll use mutate() to recreate it.

### 3) The bug is recreated, i.e. there's a select using single quotes
```r
a %>% mutate(!!RightSideColsNames[j] := leftByCol) %>% explain
```

This yields the following SQL Code which selects a column using single quotes `'` which will not immediately make the code fail, but causes a catastrophic failure in any future attempts to join.

```sql
SELECT "Employee_ID", "Employee_FirstName", "Employee_LastName", "Employee_SiteID", "Employee_EntryOn", "Employee_EntryBy", "Site_RegionID", "Site_Name", "Site_Useless1", "Site_Useless2", "Site_Useless3", "Site_EntryOn", "Site_EntryBy", 'Employee_SiteID' AS "Site_ID"
FROM (SELECT "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_ID" AS "Employee_ID", "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_FirstName" AS "Employee_FirstName", "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_LastName" AS "Employee_LastName", "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_SiteID" AS "Employee_SiteID", "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_EntryOn" AS "Employee_EntryOn", "TBL_LEFT"."Employee_EntryBy" AS "Employee_EntryBy", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_RegionID" AS "Site_RegionID", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_Name" AS "Site_Name", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_Useless1" AS "Site_Useless1", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_Useless2" AS "Site_Useless2", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_Useless3" AS "Site_Useless3", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_EntryOn" AS "Site_EntryOn", "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_EntryBy" AS "Site_EntryBy"
  FROM "DIM_Employee" AS "TBL_LEFT"
  LEFT JOIN "DIM_Site" AS "TBL_RIGHT"
  ON ("TBL_LEFT"."Employee_SiteID" = "TBL_RIGHT"."Site_ID")
) "cgmyummsji"
```
_It's hard to see it, but search for `'Employee_SiteID'` to see what's going on_

#### My suggestion: Mutate should follow the double quotes `"` SELECT convention that the rest of the dbplyr functions follow

title: Support BigQuery column naming conventions
description:
In BigQuery, `.` are not allowed in column names. The default `dplyr` join behavior is to distinguish identical column names with the `.x` and `.y` suffix. This breaks `dplyr` joins in BigQuery.

The user could certainly update the `suffix` argument to join calls so that joins work (for example, `suffix = c("_x", "_y")` works). However, it would be nice if `dbplyr` contained a translation layer for BigQuery that took care of this.

BigQuery ODBC connections have class `BigQuery`

title: Package namespace conflicts (package::function)
description: Has there been any discussion of using `package::function` in the dbplyr quoting mechanism? I find this preferable in many cases to be clear about namespacing, but dbplyr does not understand the convention, which could cause issues if packages with conflicting namespaces both define dbplyr translations. On one hand, it would potentially create a _lot_ of redundancy... on the other, it could protect against some nasty / confusing behavior.

description:

When `summarise_at` uses a variable in `.vars` that it also uses in `.funs`, the result is different in dplyr and dbplyr, and I think the dbplyr result is the right one -- though there's a case for just making it an error.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(MonetDBLite)
library(DBI)
mydb <- dbConnect(MonetDBLite::MonetDBLite())
DBI::dbWriteTable(mydb, "mtcarsdb", mtcars)

mtcars %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl * mpg)))
## right
mtcars.db %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl * mpg)))
## also right
mtcars %>% mutate(cyl1=cyl) %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl1 * mpg)))

# intended result
with(mtcars, cbind(cyl * cyl * mpg,
                     disp * cyl * mpg,
                     hp * cyl * mpg,
                     drat * cyl * mpg) %>% colSums())
```

title: `dplyr::arrange()` with the `.by_group=TRUE` parameter set produces SQL with an error
description:
*@CerebralMastication commented on Apr 15, 2018, 1:56 PM UTC:*

This is a cross post from the RStats Community, where I initially posted it: [https://community.rstudio.com/t/dplyr-arrange-by-group-true-fails-with-sql-backend/7232](https://community.rstudio.com/t/dplyr-arrange-by-group-true-fails-with-sql-backend/7232)

I've either got a misunderstanding or a bug... I _think_ it's a bug.

It seems that `dplyr::arrange()` with the `.by_group=TRUE` parameter set produces SQL with an error. Here's how to reprex it:

On the DB (Redshift in my case) set up a dummy table:

```
drop TABLE sandbox.testorder; 

CREATE TABLE sandbox.testorder (
    grp varchar(255),
    n  DOUBLE PRECISION
);

INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('a',3.3);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('a',1.1);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('b',2.2);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('b',4.4);

```

Then from `R` (presuming a connection to the DB called `con` and already loaded `dbplyr`

```
testorder  <- tbl(con, "testorder")

testorder %>%
  group_by( grp ) %>%
  arrange( n, .by_group=TRUE) ->
out_test

show_query(out_test)

```

which generates the following SQL:

```
SELECT *
FROM "testorder"
ORDER BY "n", TRUE

```

which fails if I try to `collect(out_test)` with the following error:

```
Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) : 
  RS-DBI driver: (could not Retrieve the result : ERROR:  non-integer constant in ORDER BY

```

the rub seems to be the `,TRUE` there at the end. If I remove it, I get the followable runnable SQL:

```
SELECT *
FROM "testorder"
ORDER BY "n"

```

My guess is that the routine that generates the SQL has a glitch. Looks like it's just passing `, TRUE` instead of adding in the `group by` variables.

title: Explore poor query performance
description:
*@hadley commented on Sep 8, 2017, 9:19 PM UTC:*

```r
library(dplyr)
library(RPostgreSQL) 
myRedshift <- src_postgres(Sys.getenv("DBNAME"), 
                           host = Sys.getenv("JDBCURL"),
                           port = Sys.getenv("PORT"),
                           user = Sys.getenv("USER"),

experiment_id <- '455145790a164522d1f4f47f2df40c76728c84dd'  
date_start <- '2017-06-08'  
date_end <- '2017-06-15' 
experiment_data <- tbl(myRedshift, sql("SELECT *, DATE_TRUNC('day', ts)::date AS dt FROM p_experiments WHERE name LIKE '%variation::select%'")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(experimentid == experiment_id &
                  ts >= date_start &
                  ts < date_end &
                  !is.na(userid) &
                  variation != 'unknown')
cohorts <- experiment_data %>%
  group_by(userid, variation) %>%
  summarise(enrolment_date = min(dt))
reading_time <- tbl(myRedshift, "etl_reading") %>%
  dplyr::filter(createdate >= date_start &
                  createdate < date_end &
                  time_spent >= 0) %>%
  inner_join(cohorts, by = "userid") %>%
  dplyr::filter(createdate >= enrolment_date) %>%
  group_by(variation, userid) %>%
  summarise(rt = sum(time_spent)) %>%
  ungroup()
reading_time_all_allocated <- cohorts %>%
  left_join(reading_time, by = c("userid", "variation")) %>%
  collect(n = Inf)
```

produces this SQL (via explain()):

```sql
SELECT "TBL_LEFT"."userid" AS "userid", "TBL_LEFT"."variation" AS "variation", "TBL_LEFT"."enrolment_date" AS "enrolment_date", "TBL_RIGHT"."rt" AS "rt"
  FROM (SELECT "userid", "variation", MIN("dt") AS "enrolment_date"
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *, DATE_TRUNC('day', ts)::date AS dt FROM p_experiments WHERE name LIKE '%variation::select%') "ihznadkpcf"
WHERE ("experimentid" = '455145790a164522d1f4f47f2df40c76728c84dd' AND "ts" >= '2017-06-08' AND "ts" < '2017-06-15' AND NOT((("userid") IS NULL)) AND "variation" != 'unknown')) "biptkfpowo"
GROUP BY "userid", "variation") "TBL_LEFT"
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT "variation", "userid", SUM("time_spent") AS "rt"
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT "TBL_LEFT"."platform" AS "platform", "TBL_LEFT"."uuid" AS "uuid", "TBL_LEFT"."userid" AS "userid", "TBL_LEFT"."storyid" AS "storyid", "TBL_LEFT"."partid" AS "partid", "TBL_LEFT"."createdate" AS "createdate", "TBL_LEFT"."read_percent" AS "read_percent", "TBL_LEFT"."time_spent" AS "time_spent", "TBL_RIGHT"."variation" AS "variation", "TBL_RIGHT"."enrolment_date" AS "enrolment_date"
  FROM (SELECT *
FROM "etl_reading"
WHERE ("createdate" >= '2017-06-08' AND "createdate" < '2017-06-15' AND "time_spent" >= 0.0)) "TBL_LEFT"
  INNER JOIN (SELECT "userid", "variation", MIN("dt") AS "enrolment_date"
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT *, DATE_TRUNC('day', ts)::date AS dt FROM p_experiments WHERE name LIKE '%variation::select%') "bvqcfsxath"
WHERE ("experimentid" = '455145790a164522d1f4f47f2df40c76728c84dd' AND "ts" >= '2017-06-08' AND "ts" < '2017-06-15' AND NOT((("userid") IS NULL)) AND "variation" != 'unknown')) "nnwriawvlp"
GROUP BY "userid", "variation") "TBL_RIGHT"
  ON ("TBL_LEFT"."userid" = "TBL_RIGHT"."userid")
) "xmtbxcquyw"
WHERE ("createdate" >= "enrolment_date")) "ostngvabdq"
GROUP BY "variation", "userid") "TBL_RIGHT"
  ON ("TBL_LEFT"."userid" = "TBL_RIGHT"."userid" AND "TBL_LEFT"."variation" = "TBL_RIGHT"."variation")
```

Comparing this to the actual SQL I'd write to get these results:

```sql
reading_time_all_allocated <- dbGetQuery(con, glue(
"WITH cohorts AS (
  SELECT 
    p.variation, 
    p.userid,
    DATE(MIN(p.ts)) AS enrolment_date
  FROM p_experiments p
  WHERE 
    p.experimentid = '{experiment_id}' 
    AND p.name LIKE '%variation::select%'
    AND p.userid IS NOT NULL 
    AND p.ts BETWEEN '{date_start}' AND '{date_end}'
    AND p.variation != 'unknown'
  GROUP BY p.variation, p.userid),
reading_time AS (
  SELECT 
    c.userid, 
    c.variation,
    COALESCE(SUM(er.time_spent), 0) AS rt
  FROM etl_reading er
  JOIN cohorts c ON er.userid = c.userid
  WHERE 
    er.createdate >= c.enrolment_date
    AND er.createdate BETWEEN '{date_start}' AND ('{date_end}' - INTEGER '1')
    AND er.time_spent >= 0
  GROUP BY c.userid, c.variation)
SELECT 
  c.userid, 
  c.variation, 
  COALESCE(r.rt, 0) AS rt 
FROM cohorts c
  LEFT OUTER JOIN reading_time r ON c.userid = r.userid AND c.variation = r.variation",
    experiment_id = experiment_id,
    date_start = date_start,
    date_end = date_end))
```

Probably because of the extra subqueries inside the joins.

title: Cleaning up tables created by join(..., copy=TRUE)
description:
When using `dplyr` with an external database, performing joins with `copy=TRUE` results in a table being created in my database with a randomly assigned name.  I realize that do to lazy evaluation, this table cannot just be deleted once the call completes, or even after we first call `collect()`.  Still, it would be nice to have some ability / helper function to clean up these auto-created tables, otherwise running an analysis with `copy=TRUE` can create a very large number of table copies.  

Reproducible example:

```r
library(nycflights13)
library(MonetDBLite)
library(dplyr)

db <- DBI::dbConnect(MonetDBLite::MonetDBLite(), "test")

DBI::dbWriteTable(db, "flights", flights)
DBI::dbListTables(db)
x <- semi_join(tbl(db, "flights"), airlines, copy = TRUE)

## Look, now we have a randomly generated table name, ick:
DBI::dbListTables(db)

```

### Context

So why am I calling this potentially expensive operation so many times to begin with? In my use case, the table already in the database, table `x`, is quite large (i.e. too big for available RAM), and I wish to perform a filtering join.  Table `y` is not tiny but easily fits in memory.  Using MonetDBLite, a filtering join, even with copying in table `y`, runs about **200x faster** than a call to `filter`.  This filtering join is part of a function in package (for taxonomic name look-ups) that could be run many times, and I don't want to pollute the user's workspace with lots of copies of temporary tables.   I'm not sure what the best way to clean up said tables would be (e.g. the random names created do not look easy to distinguish from potentially real tables using simple regex patterns).  

Or maybe I'm going about this all wrong and I should really be avoiding `copy` whenever possible, but in this context performance seems to favor it.  Any suggestions?  I think a clean-up function or at least a way to set the name of the copied table before it is created would be great.  Apologies if I've overlooked a way in which that can already be done.

description:
Big picture: from Windows, the ODBC for SQL Server is sensitive to the selected order of "long data" (poorly quantified) columns. (The [best documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/develop-app/getting-long-data?view=sql-server-2017) I've found suggests that it *might* be greater than 255 bytes.)

Reproducible, using docker on windows with [microsoft/mssql-server-linux](https://hub.docker.com/r/microsoft/mssql-server-linux/) (and postgres for comparison).

<details><summary>(create/populate a test table)</summary>

```r
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

conss <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), driver="ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server", ...)
conpg <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), driver="PostgreSQL ANSI(x64)", ...)

DBI::dbExecute(conpg, "drop table if exists quux")
DBI::dbExecute(conss, "drop table if exists quux")

DBI::dbExecute(conpg, "
  CREATE TABLE quux (
    id              UUID DEFAULT uuid_generate_v1mc() PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL ,
    someint         INT4 NOT NULL ,
    notes           TEXT NULL ,
    createddatetime TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP )")
DBI::dbExecute(conss, "
  CREATE TABLE quux (
    id              UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID() PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL ,
    someint         INT NOT NULL ,
    notes           NVARCHAR(MAX) NULL ,
    createddatetime DATETIMEOFFSET NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSDATETIMEOFFSET() )")

DBI::dbWriteTable(conss, "quux", data.frame(someint=1L), append=TRUE)
DBI::dbWriteTable(conpg, "quux", data.frame(someint=1L), append=TRUE)
```

</details>

The underlying problem is not unique to `dbplyr` or even `odbc`, the problem is ODBC.

```r
### (with connections: conss, conpg)
DBI::dbGetQuery(conpg, "select * from quux")
#                                     id someint notes     createddatetime
# 1 7767DDF6-19A7-11E9-ABD7-138C23179576       1  <NA> 2019-01-16 15:57:46
DBI::dbGetQuery(conss, "select * from quux")
# Error in result_fetch(res@ptr, n, ...) : 
#   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:2894: 07009: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server]Invalid Descriptor Index 
# Warning in dbClearResult(rs) : Result already cleared
```

The workaround (after reopening the connection, since `conss` is now trashed):

```r
# postgres works unabated
tbl(conpg, "quux")

# avoid the "longish" fields
tbl(conss, "quux") %>% select(-notes)
# reorder the "longish" fields
tbl(conss, "quux") %>% select(-notes, everything(), notes)
```

This feels a little hacky, but I think it starts to break down when you don't know a priori what constitutes "longish", though after several attempts, one can break down and ask for the original schema to determine what is what; and it starts getting cumbersome when the number of misplaced "longish" fields increases.

With single tables, one easy-enough workaround might be to define a view that reorders the columns. Unfortunately, with joins the order of columns is no longer as-desired.

I know that this is ultimately a problem with the ODBC driver, not the `odbc` package or anything in R, as it affects other languages too.

**My question is this**: is there a better way to deal with this than the `select(-..., everything(), ...)` pattern? It doesn't need to be solved with `dbplyr` functions, but as it is particular to DBMS access, it might do well (in function or at least documentation) within `dbplyr`.

title: Case sensitivity when translating to SQL
description:
Some SQL functions may be case-sensitive, for instance spatial methods in MSSQL. The syntax is a bit weird, e.g. `colname.STBuffer(1)` for [`STBuffer()`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/spatial-geometry/stbuffer-geometry-data-type?view=sql-server-2017), the call `COLNAME.STBUFFER(1)` fails.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)
memdb_frame(a = 1) %>%
  mutate(x = a.STBuffer(1)) %>%
  sql_render()
#> <SQL> SELECT `a`, A.STBUFFER(1.0) AS `x`
#> FROM `opozhizxky`
```

<sup>Created on 2018-11-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

(This example works identically with MSSQL, using SQLite for the reprex.)

What's the reason for converting all function calls to uppercase?

title: Custom translation for transmute
description:
To avoid additional layer of querying — transmutes feel more common in SQL because for good performance you want to reduct query size as quickly as possible.

```R
library(dplyr)

dbplyr::memdb_frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5) %>% 
  transmute(z = x + y) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `z`
#> FROM (SELECT `x`, `y`, `x` + `y` AS `z`
#> FROM `iqfjdmzdxu`)
```

dbplyr: n_distinct translation does not handle na.rm
description:
*@colearendt commented on Jul 20, 2018, 10:33 AM UTC:*

Definition of `n_distinct`:

```r
function (..., na.rm = FALSE) 
{
    n_distinct_multi(list(...), na.rm)
}
<environment: namespace:dplyr>
```

And the translation:

```r
  n_distinct = function(...) {
    vars <- sql_vector(list(...), parens = FALSE, collapse = ", ")
    build_sql("COUNT(DISTINCT ", vars, ")")
  }
```

[https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/79d2a0377561ad57f67a65b914ce3195d10de0be/R/translate-sql-base.r#L199-L203](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/79d2a0377561ad57f67a65b914ce3195d10de0be/R/translate-sql-base.r#L199-L203)

[https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/79d2a0377561ad57f67a65b914ce3195d10de0be/R/translate-sql-base.r#L272-L275](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/79d2a0377561ad57f67a65b914ce3195d10de0be/R/translate-sql-base.r#L272-L275)

Which results in:

```r
pd %>% summarise(n_distinct(fld_integer, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% show_query()
#<SQL>
#SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT "fld_integer", TRUE AS "na.rm") AS "n_distinct(fld_integer, na.rm = TRUE)"
#FROM "testdata"
```

`na.rm` should not be included in the splicing.

title: .data pronoun does not work
description:
*@sverchkov commented on Jul 20, 2018, 7:10 PM UTC:*

Using the .data pronoun in filter, mutate, and transmute does not work with database tables

```r
library(dplyr)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
copy_to(con, mtcars)
mtcars2 <- tbl(con, "mtcars")

### Using mutate

# works
mutate(mtcars, foo = .data$cyl)

# also works
mutate(mtcars2, foo = cyl)

# doesn't
mutate(mtcars2, foo = .data$cyl)
# Error: Column `cyl` not found in `.data`

### Using transmute

# works
transmute(mtcars, blah = .data$cyl)

# also works
transmute(mtcars, blah = cyl)

# doesn't
transmute(mtcars2, blah = .data$cyl)
# Error: Column `cyl` not found in `.data`

### Using transmute to select

# works
transmute(mtcars, .data$cyl)

# also works
transmute(mtcars2, cyl)

# doesn't
transmute(mtcars2, .data$cyl)
# Error: Column `cyl` not found in `.data`

# select doesn't have this issue, this works
select( mtcars2, .data$cyl )

### Using filter

# works
filter( mtcars, .data$cyl > 4 )

# also works
filter( mtcars2, cyl > 4 )

# doesn't
filter( mtcars2, .data$cyl > 4 )
# Error: Column `cyl` not found in `.data`
```

(I actually ran into this when running code with a Postgres database, so it isn't DB-specific)

This is different from [issue#3370](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3370), since everything works without the .data pronoun, but might be somehow related.

*This issue was moved by [krlmlr](https://github.com/krlmlr) from [tidyverse/dplyr#3722](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3722).*

title: pmin and pmax fail in mutate connected to SQL Server
description:
*@jnolis commented on Nov 28, 2017, 6:36 PM UTC:*

Occasionally, I will need to use pmin or pmax to replace values above or below a threshold, for instance:

```r
require(dplyr)
data_frame(X = 1:10) %>%
  mutate(Y = pmax(X,5))
```

However, when I use dbplyr to try and do this using a SQL Server table, I get the following error:

```r
tbl(con,"OrderInfo") %>%
  mutate(Test = pmax(Revenue,0))
```

```
Error: <SQL> 'SELECT  TOP 10 "CustomerId", "OrderId", "ClientOrderId", "Channel", "OrderDate", "Revenue", "Cost", MAX("Revenue", 0.0) AS "Test"
FROM "OrderInfo"'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server][SQL Server]The MAX function requires 1 argument(s). 

```

As you can see, the SQL code generator assumes that I want to do a pairwise MAX, however SQL Server does not support that (only taking the maximum over a single column).

A cursory Stack Overflow search suggests that to do this operation a [case statement could be used](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6585160/i-want-to-set-negative-numbers-in-a-view-to-zero-and-any-positive-should-remain). I think either the SQL code generator should either be updated to do this, or an error should be generated at the time of calling the mutate.

*This issue was moved by [krlmlr](https://github.com/krlmlr) from tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3227.*

title: Reconsider local evaluation
description:
Currently `partial_eval()` locally evaluates calls of the form `pkg::bar()` (where pkg is not dplyr), and `x$y` (which will block #158). It's probably worth reconsidering in the light of unquoting as I think this would make the interface more consistent.

At the same time, we could deprecate `local()` (since it's basically equivalent to `!!`). `remote()` needs to stay in case we have override an SQL function with the same name but a different meaning.

title: check_na_rm() should warn with untranslated function names
description:
`check_na_rm()` warns like this, but apparently we cannot use `AVG(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; I believe it should be `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`.

But, I don't know how to pass the original name to `check_na_rm()`...

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

result <- memdb_frame(x = 1) %>% 
  summarise(x = mean(x)) %>%
  collect()
#> Warning: Missing values are always removed in SQL.

title: as.integer64 compability for SQL SERVER
description:
*@jnolis commented on Jan 16, 2018, 10:22 PM UTC:*

Currently, when converting from R to a SQL Server query, d[b]plyr incorrectly handles "as.integer64" This is the function I would expect to use if I want to cast as a bigint within SQL Server. What ends up happening is dplyr uses "AS.INTEGER64" as a SQL Command

1.  In SQL SERVER create an example table

```sql
CREATE TABLE Example (Number int)
```

2.  In R using dbplyr, try and query the table after casting Number as an integer64

```r
tbl(con,"Example") %>%
  mutate(Number64 = as.integer64(Number))
```

3.  This yields:

```
Error: <SQL> 'SELECT  TOP 10 "Number", AS.INTEGER64("Number") AS "Number64"
FROM "Example"'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'AS'.

```

Which wouldn't happen if the SQL Query was the correct:

```
SELECT TOP 10 Number, CAST(Number AS BIGINT) AS NUMBER64
FROM EXAMPLE

```

*This issue was moved by [krlmlr](https://github.com/krlmlr) from tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3305.*

title: Inconsistency between ifelse and case_when using dbplyr
description:
*@simon-anasta commented on Aug 27, 2018, 2:14 AM UTC:*

Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form. Instead, ask on [https://stackoverflow.com/](https://stackoverflow.com/) or [https://community.rstudio.com/](https://community.rstudio.com/).

Please include a minimal reproducible example (AKA a reprex). If you've never heard of a [reprex](http://reprex.tidyverse.org/) before, start by reading [https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex](https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex).

* * *

When writing queries using `dbplyr` for SQL server, `ifelse` and `case_when` produce different SQL code. The SQL code from `case_when` results in an exception. See also [this question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51978084/combining-dbplyr-and-case-when-in-sql-server)

Sorry the below is not a perfect reprex. Security restrictions prevent me from including business specific details in my example.

```r
# libraries
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

# establish connection to database table
connection_string = "database.specific.string"
# mine looks something like "DRIVER=...; Trusted_Connection=...; DATABASE=...' SERVER=..."
db_connection = dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string = connection_string)
my_table = tbl(db_connection, from = my_table_name)

# attempted query
tmp = my_table %>%
    mutate(new_col = case_when(col1 == col2 ~ "a",
                               TRUE ~ "b"))

# check SQL code for query
show_query(tmp)

# compared to
tmp = my_table %>%
    mutate(new_col = ifelse(col1 == col2, "a", "b"))

# check SQL code for query
show_query(tmp)
```

The resulting SQL query from the `case_when` command takes the form:

```sql
SELECT 
    col1, col2,
    CASE
       WHEN CONVERT(BIT, IIF(col1 = col2, 1.0, 0.0))) THEN ('a')
       WHEN (TRUE) THEN ('b')
    END AS new_col
FROM my_database.my_table_name
```

This produces an exception: "An expression of non-boolean type specified in a context where a condition is expected, near 'THEN'"

The resulting SQL query from the `ifelse` command takes the form:

```sql
SELECT 
    col1, col2,
    CASE
       WHEN (CONVERT(BIT, IIF(col1 = col2, 1.0, 0.0)))) = TRUE THEN ('a')
       WHEN (CONVERT(BIT, IIF(col1 = col2, 1.0, 0.0)))) = FALSE THEN ('b')
    END AS new_col
FROM my_database.my_table_name
```

This works as expected.

As best I can determine, this is a bug. I suspect the SQL syntax from `case_when` should be more similar to the SQL syntax from `ifelse`. In particular I suspect the additional brackets and the "= TRUE" in the `ifelse` version should also appear in the `case_when` version.

*This issue was moved by [romainfrancois](https://github.com/romainfrancois) from [tidyverse/dplyr#3774](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3774).*

description:

When collecting the results of an SQL query with duplicated column names, it would be nice if you got the warning as soon as possible so you don't waste time having to rerun long queries after fixing the column names.

INNER JOIN consumers others ON others.id = main.id") %>%

  collect(n = Inf)
```

It would be nice to have dplyr warn the user, automatically assign column names (phone_v1, phone_v2) and collected the results into a tibble, or in lieu of that immediately warn the user upon executing the command if possible.

title: Not handling '&' properly in ifelse statements containing %in% in MS SQL
description:
Here is a reproducible example:

This works:
```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%
  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) == 29 & month(TransactionDate) == 2, 'Y', 'N'))
```
However, when we replace one or more of the `==` expressions with `%in%`, it breaks:
```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%

  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) %in% c(29) & month(TransactionDate) == 2, 'Y', 'N'))

```
or
```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%

  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) == 29 & month(TransactionDate) %in% c(2), 'Y', 'N'))

```
or
```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%

  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) %in% c(29) & month(TransactionDate) %in% c(2), 'Y', 'N'))

```
Obviously in this example, you can get away with using `==` for both statements, but in the real world you may need to use an `&` and an `%in%` together.

I have identified a workaround, which is to replace `&` with `%and%`, which renders correctly as long as one side contains `==`:

```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%
  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) == 29 %and% month(TransactionDate) %in% c(2), 'Y', 'N'))
```
But even this fails if both terms contain `%in%`
```
my_tbl <- con %>% tbl(ident_q("MyDB.dbo.MyTable")) %>%

  mutate(LeapDay = ifelse(day(TransactionDate) %in% c(29) %and% month(TransactionDate) %in% c(2), 'Y', 'N'))
```

The reason this doesn't work is because it renders an `&` in R as an `&` in SQL, which works in a lot of circumstances, but doesn't appear to work in this particular circumstance. Rendering `&` in R as `AND` in SQL would likely solve the problem.

title: MS SQL mutate(ifelse()) translation not working
description:
I'm running into an issue when using mutate and ifelse (or if) on a SQL Server backend. The following sample query:

```
df <- tbl(con, in_schema("schema", "table_name")) %>%
   mutate(field = ifelse(field %in% c('test1', 'test2', 'test3'), 'string1', 'string2') %>%
   collect()
```

... will give the following translation:
```
SELECT CASE WHEN (("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) = 'TRUE') THEN ('string1') 
            WHEN (("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) =  'FALSE') THEN ('string2') 
            END AS "field"
```

Which will return an error. The correct translation should be:
```
SELECT CASE WHEN ("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) THEN 'string1' 
            WHEN ("field" NOT IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) THEN 'string2' 
            END AS "field"
```

Will correcting this in the mssql_if function create any issues in other queries, or is there a better way to do mutate(ifelse()) in mssql?

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/477480e3c488fe6338ce5f142142d280dd61487b/R/db-odbc-mssql.R#L225

description:
With

title: Casting integer -> numeric is not currently possible with SQLlite
description:
I'm not exactly sure why this is happening, but using the sql translation of `CAST(x as NUMERIC)` does not actually cast an integer to a double value in SQLlite.

I would've thought that it would work, because the documentation seems to suggest this would be the expected behavior, but maybe I am reading it wrong.
https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html#affname

At the very least, I think an "easy" solution would just be providing a translation for `as.double` and `as.numeric` that casts to `REAL` or `DOUBLE` rather than the base scalar default of `NUMERIC`


``` r
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
ex <- data.frame(x = 1L)
copy_to(con, ex)
ex_tbl <- tbl(con, "ex")

# it is an integer, as expected
ex_tbl
#> # Source:   table<ex> [?? x 1]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.22.0 [:memory:]
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1

# no conversion done
mutate(ex_tbl, xx = as.double(x))
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.22.0 [:memory:]
#>       x    xx
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1

# sql maybe incorrect?
mutate(ex_tbl, xx = as.double(x)) %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, CAST(`x` AS NUMERIC) AS `xx`
#> FROM `ex`

# confirming that it does not work manually
res_int <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT CAST(x as NUMERIC) as xx FROM ex")

class(res_int$xx)
#> [1] "integer"

# casting to REAL or DOUBLE works
res_dbl <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT CAST(x as REAL) as xx FROM ex")
class(res_dbl$xx)
#> [1] "numeric"

res_dbl2 <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT CAST(x as DOUBLE) as xx FROM ex")
class(res_dbl2$xx)
#> [1] "numeric"
```

title: Case_when translation for ORACLE does not work
description:
*@cderv commented on Apr 18, 2018, 5:20 PM UTC:*

I work with an oracle connection so difficult to make a reprex sorry. I just will use the code as-is as I think it is enough to see the issue in SQL translation.

When using dplyr on an oracle connection, I had this error

```r
tu_cc_pt %>% 
mutate(niv_u = case_when(
  	PT_NIVEAU_TENSION == "90 KV" ~ "HT",
  	PT_NIVEAU_TENSION == "63 KV" ~ "HT",
  	TRUE ~ PT_NIVEAU_TENSION)) %>%
collect()
```

The error message is

```r
Error in new_result(connection@ptr, statement) : nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1344: HY000: ORA-00920: invalid relational operator 
```

A call to `show_query` instead of `collect` gives the following SQL

```sql
SELECT "ID_POSTE_TECHNIQUE", "PT_IDR", "PT_CUR", "PT_TYPE", "PT_STATUT_SEQ", "PT_STATUT_NON_SEQ", "PT_NIVEAU_TENSION", "PT_FILERIE_LIBELLE", "PT_TECHNOLOGIE", "PT_PLAN_PROTECTION", "PT_DT_PREM_MISE_SS_TENSION", "PT_CM", "PT_GMR", CASE
WHEN ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION" = '90 KV') THEN ('HT')
WHEN ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION" = '63 KV') THEN ('HT')
WHEN (TRUE) THEN ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION")
END AS "niv_u"
FROM (DMS_SIDONI_DL_RO.DMBC_CC_PT)
```

This as been mentionned in [#2928](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2928) but not fixed it seems.

I think the problem is with `WHEN (TRUE)` that is not valid with ORACLE. It should be a `ELSE`

```sql
SELECT "ID_POSTE_TECHNIQUE", "PT_IDR", "PT_CUR", "PT_TYPE", "PT_STATUT_SEQ", "PT_STATUT_NON_SEQ", "PT_NIVEAU_TENSION", "PT_FILERIE_LIBELLE", "PT_TECHNOLOGIE", "PT_PLAN_PROTECTION", "PT_DT_PREM_MISE_SS_TENSION", "PT_CM", "PT_GMR", CASE
WHEN ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION" = '90 KV') THEN ('HT')
WHEN ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION" = '63 KV') THEN ('HT')
ELSE ("PT_NIVEAU_TENSION")
END AS "niv_u"
FROM (DMS_SIDONI_DL_RO.DMBC_CC_PT)
```

title: Minimise peak memory usage when doing copy_to from one database to another
description:
*@mungojam commented on Oct 24, 2017, 7:28 PM UTC:*

The copy_to now supports a src_sql source as well as destination, but currently does this via a tibble. This makes it performant only for datasets that fit into available RAM.

It would be good if some sort of streaming or batching were implemented so that the peak RAM usage is much smaller. This is so that we can use dplyr to do an initial large extract from a large remote table into a local SQLite database (for example).

Perhaps this fits better as a DBI feature but it's nice to be able to do a custom select on the source table using dplyr.

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

src1 <- src_sqlite("fileDb1.db", create = TRUE)
src2 <- src_sqlite("fileDb2.db", create = TRUE)

# Create from dataframe
iris_1 <- copy_to(src1, iris, "iris1")

# Create from tbl in another data, currently goes via in-memory tibble containing full dataset
db2 <- copy_to(src2, iris, 'data2', temporary = FALSE)
```

title: Documentation clarification
description:
In the "Introduction to dbplyr" the author recommends the following when deciding to use a database: 

> As well as working with local in-memory data stored in data frames, dplyr also works with remote on-disk data stored in databases. This is particularly useful in two scenarios:
> 
> Your data is already in a database.
> 
> You have so much data that it does not all fit into memory simultaneously and you need to use some external storage engine.
> 
> (If your data fits in memory there is no advantage to putting it in a database: it will only be slower and more frustrating).

This is actually not completely accurate as it's literally written.

I suggest this should be qualified to give the following reasons as well:
1) Dataset is relatively small (up to a million rows or less)
2) It's only a "one-off" project where the overhead of creating the database takes longer than wait times
3) It's a single user project, so data consistency and multi-user concurrency aren't issues 

Or alternatively, make no mention of when a database should be used or not as this is a large subject that depends on too many variables to mention in an introduction

title: Oracle `IN` clause limits
description:
Oracle DBs have a limit on the length of lists (such as those used with `IN` clauses) of 1000 items. See  the discussion [here](http://dbaparadise.com/2016/07/limitations-of-the-in-clause-in-oracle-ora-01795/).

Is this something that `dbplyr` would be open to addressing? If so, would one of the two methods suggested in the article above be preferable?

For example this throws an error:
```
lkp <- as.character(1:1001)
oracle_tbl %>% 
  filter(ID %in% lkp)
```

```
Error in new_result(connection@ptr, statement) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1344: HY000: ORA-01795: maximum number of expressions in a list is 1000
```

title: Ignoring case with remote database table filter operations
description:
*@geotheory commented on Aug 28, 2018, 12:02 PM UTC:*

I've detailed this question on this [SO page](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52047603/case-sensitivity-with-dplyr-rpostgresql-string-matching).

I can't figure out how to apply a non-case-sensitive filter query to a remote PostgreSQL table using `dplyr`. To demonstrate:

```
require(dplyr)
require(stringr)
require(RPostgreSQL)

drv <- dbDriver("PostgreSQL")
con <- dbConnect(drv, dbname="mydb", host="localhost", port=5432, user="username")

# create db table
copy_to(con, iris, "iris", temporary = FALSE)

# dplyr remote database table
iris_pg <- tbl(con, "iris")

iris_pg %>% filter(str_detect(Species, 'setosa')) %>% head(3) %>% collect()
# A tibble: 3 x 5
  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
*        <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
2          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 setosa 
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa

iris_pg %>% filter(str_detect(Species, 'Setosa')) %>% head(3) %>% collect()
# A tibble: 0 x 0

```

To ignore case `stringr::fixed('Setosa', ignore_case=TRUE)` works with tibble filtering. But with the postgres table it has no effect:

```
iris_pg %>% filter(str_detect(Species, stringr::fixed('SETOSA', ignore_case=TRUE))) %>% head(3) %>% collect()
# A tibble: 0 x 0

```

Is there any way around this, or possibly dev plans to accommodate the `ignore_case` arguments or `fixed()` or `regex()` for database table filtering?

*This issue was moved by [romainfrancois](https://github.com/romainfrancois) from [tidyverse/dplyr#3783](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3783).*

title: SQL translation turns aggregation into window function
description:
`dbplyr` is adding an unnecessary `OVER ()` hint with a repro similar to:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
sdf_len(sc, 10) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(average = mean(id)) %>%
    dplyr::show_query()
```
```sql
<SQL>
SELECT `id`, avg(`id`) OVER () AS `average`
FROM `sparklyr_tmp_afe063482375`
```

Which causes performance degradation in Spark cluster, see: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1738

However, this behavior has been around since 2017, probably even earlier, so not a regression at all.

Apparently Oracle has an identifier length limit of 30 characters, which causes problems for generated SQL names that are inherently long (i.e. those generated from a `summarize` statement).

Should we take this into account and truncate names / have an option for doing so? Or is this something that documentation / a better error message would help with?

``` r
library(odbc)

cfg <- config::get(file = "/wrk/db-test-config.yml")
con <- do.call(dbConnect, cfg$oracle)
mytbl <- copy_to(con, iris, "somename")

mytbl %>% summarize(test=sum(Petal.Length + Petal.Width, na.rm=TRUE))
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 1]

title: SQL database specification
description:
In SQL, you can specify both a database and a table at the same time with syntax like `database`.`table`. 

With RMariaDB, if not others, you can create connections that will access any database on the server you're connected to by not including a dbname parameter or using dbname = "".

But I can't find any examples of using dbplyr that specify both the database and the table. All the examples set the database when creating the connection rather than in the `tbl()` call. I've played around with some guesses at what the syntax would be but without any luck.

Please tell me there's a way to do this with an example of how to specify both the database and table to dbplyr. If there's no syntax for this, then this would be a feature request.

Thanks.

Tom

title: calculate median in bigrquery + dplyr
description:

Hello!

I have a large data stored in google cloud platform. I use bigrquery to make the queries in R. I notice some dplyr functions still work but median() doesn't.

```r
library(bigrquery)
library(dplyr)

tbl(con, "episodes") %>%
  filter(Admit_year>=2009) %>%
  mutate(ratio=Total_charges/total_cost) %>%
  group_by(Admit_year)%>%
  summarise_(~median(ratio, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(Admit_year)
```

I tried summarise(median=median(ratio,na.rm=TRUE)) but also failed. The only way it works is if I added "as_tibble()) under the mutate line, then R will "download" the data from the cloud. Then the median function works. My guess is, the median function works "locally", but not as part of a query? The tibble solution works, but it's very time consuming as R needs to download everything before computing. Is there any way to resolve this?

title: Strange printing for postgres integer64
description:
I noticed that I get weird results when I `count` a column with very different value counts. This is a *super* minor issue. Please don't feel compelled to address it!

The issue doesn't seem to happen with SQLite. I'm assuming it's something about printing the `S3: Integer64` column. 

Basic setup of a table to count:
```r

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(),
  user = "my_user", dbname = "my_db")
df <- data.frame(x = c(rep(1, 1000), rep(2, 10)))
dplyr::copy_to(con, df, temporary = TRUE)
remote_df <- dplyr::tbl(con, "df")
dplyr::count(remote_df, x)
```
Result:
```
# Source:   lazy query [?? x 2]
# Database: postgres [my_user@127.0.0.1:5432/my_db]
      x n              
  <dbl> <S3: integer64>
1     2 "  10"         <- What's up with the extra spaces?
2     1 1000     
```
Expected result:
```
# Source:   lazy query [?? x 2]
# Database: postgres [my_user@127.0.0.1:5432/my_db]
      x n              
  <dbl> <S3: integer64>
1     2   10 
2     1 1000     
```
